title: Iowa Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Iowa caps any late fee a lease provides by the size of the monthly rent. If rent is $700 a month or less, the fee may not exceed $12 per day or $60 in total for a month; if rent is more than $700, it may not exceed $20 per day or $100 in total for a month. Iowa requires no grace period. Accepting a late payment can cost you the right to end the lease for that late payment, so if you want to rely on strict deadlines later, say so in writing before the tenant relies on your leniency.

title: Fees Count as Rent in Iowa
bodyText: In Iowa, 'rent' means any payment the tenant must make to you under the rental agreement, so on the statute's plain reading pet rent, utility charges, late fees and other required fees are rent for the three-day nonpayment notice; no reported Iowa case read for this library decides that, and the library's default clause does not end a lease for unpaid late fees alone. Demand only amounts the lease and the law actually allow: an Iowa court threw out an eviction because the nonpayment notice demanded charges the landlord could not lawfully collect, and you must prove any amount you claim.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: You must tell each tenant in writing about a rent increase at least 30 days before it takes effect, and the increase cannot take effect before the original lease, or a renewal or extension of it, expires. So you cannot raise rent in the middle of a fixed term. Whether a rent step written into the original lease counts as an 'increase' under this rule has not been decided in any case read for this library; if a court treats such a step as an increase, it could not take effect before the term ends even with notice, so a step that takes effect at a renewal is the safer course, with the 30 days' written notice. In a month-to-month tenancy each month is a new period, so give the written notice at least 30 days before the rental date on which the increase starts. An increase made because the tenant complained about conditions, or because the tenant became eligible for Iowa's rent reimbursement credit, can be challenged.

title: No Local Rent Control in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no statewide rent control, and cities and counties may not adopt or enforce any limit on the amount of rent charged for private residential property. A city or county may still manage residential property in which it has its own property interest.

title: Returned Check Charge
bodyText: Iowa lets you charge up to $30 for a dishonored check, draft or order, but only if you clearly and conspicuously post a notice of the charge and its amount where rent is usually paid or put it in the tenant's billing statement. You may not charge it when the check bounced because the tenant stopped payment. The statute does not cover failed electronic payments.

title: No Iowa Rule on Application Fees
bodyText: Iowa has no statute limiting or regulating rental application or screening fees. Charge only a fee that reflects real screening costs, describe it before you take it, and apply it the same way to every applicant.

title: No Iowa Fee Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring an all-in rent figure or a list of mandatory fees in advertising or in the lease. The one disclosure close to it: if the tenant will pay you for utilities rather than paying the utility directly, you must fully explain the rates, charges and services before the lease is signed.

title: No Iowa Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a landlord to give a receipt for rent, even for cash. Keep a written record of every payment anyway: in a dispute over a deposit you carry the burden of proof, and an accurate ledger supports any nonpayment notice.

title: No Iowa Rule on Algorithmic Rent Setting
bodyText: Iowa has no statute addressing rent-setting software or algorithmic pricing. Federal antitrust law is not covered by this library.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Iowa's legal rate of interest on money due under a contract, or after it becomes due, is 5 percent a year unless the parties agree in writing to another rate, which may not exceed the maximum lawful rate Iowa's superintendent of banking publishes each month. A written interest term in a lease is lawful within that limit, but the library does not offer one: interest on small rent balances rarely justifies the risk of an error in a fluctuating maximum. A landlord who wants one can add a clause (take advice first).

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: You may not demand or receive more than two months' rent as a security deposit. Every deposit that secures the tenant's performance counts toward that limit, including a pet deposit. Rent paid in advance only as rent, such as last month's rent, is not a deposit and does not count. Iowa has no rule for nonrefundable fees; money taken to secure the tenant's performance is a deposit whatever it is called, and must be held and returned under the deposit rules.

title: Where Deposits Must Be Held
bodyText: Hold every rental deposit for the tenant in a bank, savings and loan association or credit union insured by a federal agency, and never mix it with your personal funds. Deposits may be pooled in a trust account, including an interest-bearing one.

title: Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Iowa does not require you to pay interest on a deposit. Any interest earned during the first five years of a tenancy belongs to you. The statute does not say who owns interest earned after the fifth year; the cautious course is to credit it to the tenant.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText: If you do not return the deposit or send a written statement of specific reasons within 30 days after the tenancy ends and you receive the tenant's mailing address, you lose the right to keep any part of it. Keeping a deposit in bad faith can cost up to twice the monthly rent in punitive damages plus actual damages. In a deposit dispute the court may award attorney fees to the winner, and you carry the burden of proving each deduction.

title: Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: If the tenant gives you no mailing address or delivery instructions within one year after the tenancy ends, the Iowa landlord-tenant statute says the deposit reverts to you and the tenant forfeits it. Iowa's general unclaimed property law also lists security deposits among property that can be presumed abandoned, but the landlord-tenant statute is the specific rule for rental deposits; keep records showing the year passed without an address.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When your interest in the property ends, within a reasonable time either return the deposits (less lawful deductions) to the tenants, or transfer them to your successor and tell each tenant about the transfer and the successor's name and address; doing so ends your liability for them. The successor takes over your deposit obligations, but if a tenant does not object within 20 days after written notice to the tenant of the amount transferred or assumed, which must include a stamped envelope addressed to the successor, the successor owes only that amount.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent
bodyText: A pet deposit is a rental deposit: it counts toward the two-month limit on security deposits and must be held, applied and returned under the deposit rules. Monthly pet rent is rent. You may not charge a pet deposit or pet rent for a service or assistance animal.

title: No Iowa Rule on Holding Deposits
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on deposits taken to hold a unit before a lease is signed. Put the terms in writing: how much, how long the unit is held, and when the money is refunded or credited. Once a lease is signed, money that secures the tenant's performance is a rental deposit under the deposit rules.

title: Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: If rent is unpaid, serve a written notice of nonpayment stating that the lease will terminate if the rent is not paid within three days. Serve it by delivery with a signed and dated acknowledgment from a resident at least 18, by personal service, or by posting it on the main entrance door and mailing it by both regular and certified mail; mailed notice is complete four days after mailing. If the rent is not paid, you may file for eviction without a separate notice to quit. The Iowa Supreme Court has held that the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice applies only to rent defaults that arose during the 2020 moratorium. Courts elsewhere read the federal notice more broadly; see `edu-cares-act-notice`.

title: Notice for Other Lease Violations
bodyText: For a material lease violation, or a failure of the tenant's statutory upkeep duties that materially affects health and safety, serve a written notice that specifies the breach and says the lease will end on a stated date at least seven days after the tenant receives it unless the breach is remedied in seven days. If the breach can be fixed by repairs, paying damages or otherwise, and the tenant fixes it in time, the lease does not end. If substantially the same breach recurs within six months, you may end the lease on at least seven days' written notice without another chance to cure. You may also recover damages, and attorney fees only if the tenant's noncompliance was willful.

title: Clear and Present Danger: Three-Day Termination
bodyText: If a tenant, or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, creates a clear and present danger to the health or safety of other tenants, you, your staff, or others on or within 1,000 feet of the property (for example, assault or threats, illegal use or threatened use of a weapon, or illegal possession of a controlled substance; drug possession by someone other than the tenant counts only if the tenant knew of it), you may serve a single three days' notice of termination and notice to quit and then file for eviction. The notice must state the specific activity and set out the statute's exemption language word for word. A tenant is exempt where someone else did it and the tenant sought a protective order, reported it to police or the county attorney, or sent the statutory trespass letter, and gave you written proof before you sued. Simply keeping a firearm in the unit is never a clear and present danger.

title: Right to Call for Emergency Help
bodyText: You may not limit a tenant's or household member's right to call police or other emergency help for a victim of abuse or crime or anyone in an emergency, and you may not fine, charge or threaten to evict anyone for doing so. Any lease waiver of this right is void. A violation costs a civil penalty of one month's rent plus actual damages, attorney fees and costs. You may still recover the cost of repairing damage caused by the responders, and you may act on other grounds.

title: How Eviction Works in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa evictions are 'forcible entry and detainer' actions, usually filed in small claims court in the county where the property is. Give a three days' written notice to quit before filing, except after a three-day nonpayment notice has already ended the tenancy or where the occupant entered by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth. The court sets a hearing within 8 days of filing (up to 15 if you ask or agree), and the tenant must be served at least three days before the hearing. If you win, the order directs removal within three days, carried out in the daytime by the sheriff. Only a claim for rent, or for other recovery the statute lists (such as your damages after the lease is terminated), may be joined with the case. An employee of an individual owner, or an officer or employee of the property manager, may bring the small claims case without a lawyer. Waiting 30 days of peaceable possession after the cause arises, with your knowledge, bars the action.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: You may recover possession only through the courts, or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit. Removing or excluding a tenant, or willfully cutting off electricity, gas, water or another essential service, lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, and attorney fees. Iowa also abolished distraint: you cannot seize the tenant's belongings for unpaid rent.

title: No General Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no general just-cause or good-cause eviction law for private rentals: when a fixed term ends, or a periodic tenancy is ended by proper notice, you may recover possession without giving a reason. Limits still apply: you may not act in retaliation for code complaints, repair complaints or tenant organizing; you may not evict for calling emergency help; and federally subsidized housing has its own federal rules.

title: Ending a Fixed-Term Lease
bodyText: Two Iowa statutes touch the end of a fixed term. A general statute says a written agreement fixing the date a tenancy ends terminates it on that date without notice. The landlord-tenant act also lets either party end a tenancy longer than month-to-month by written notice at least 30 days before the end of the term. Because no Iowa decision reconciling the two was found, serve a written notice at least 30 days before the last day of the term whenever you want the unit back, using a method the termination-notice statute allows. If the tenant stays after the term without your consent, give a three days' notice to quit before filing for eviction. If you accept rent and let the tenant stay, the tenancy becomes month-to-month.

title: Tenants Who Stay After the Lease Ends
bodyText: If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease ends, you may sue for possession. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may also recover your actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. A separate Iowa statute makes a tenant who holds over after giving notice of intent to quit at a stated time, or who willfully holds over after the term and after a notice to quit, liable for double the rental value for the holdover period. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy continues month to month.

title: Daily Holdover Charge Not Offered
bodyText: Iowa law does not bar a lease from setting a daily holdover charge, but the library does not offer one. Iowa already gives you actual damages and attorney fees for a willful, bad-faith holdover, and a separate statute gives double the rental value after a notice to quit; a fixed charge above your real loss could be attacked as a penalty. The holdover clause instead sets the daily rental value at the Monthly Rent apportioned daily. A landlord who wants a fixed charge can add a clause (take advice first).

title: Accepting Rent Can Waive a Breach
bodyText: If you accept performance that differs from the lease or your rules, such as a late or partial payment, you waive your right to end the lease for that breach. You can grant a temporary waiver for a set number of days without losing your rights, but only if you give the tenant notice of the breach and of the temporary waiver, by a method the notice statute allows, before the tenant acts in reliance on it.

title: When a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the lease would have ended, the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. If you make no reasonable effort, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended when you learned of the abandonment. Iowa's landlord-tenant act does not define 'abandonment'; during an absence of more than 14 days you may enter at reasonably necessary times.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out immediately and, within 14 days, notify you in writing of the intent to end the lease, which then ends on the move-out date; or, if staying is lawful, the tenant may stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the lease ends, return all prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit, accounting for rent as of the date of the casualty. Iowa's statute has no exception for damage the tenant caused, and it gives you no termination right; an optional clause adds one.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: A tenant may not deliberately or negligently damage the property or knowingly let anyone else do so, and you may recover damages for that breach. Several tenant remedies do not apply to a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused: ending the lease for your noncompliance, and the essential-services remedies. But the fire and casualty rights to end the lease or pay reduced rent have no such exception, so a lease cannot take them away even when the tenant caused the damage. The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause keeps those rights and lets you recover repair costs and lost rent as damages.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease-Termination Right
bodyText: Iowa has no statute letting a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early, change locks or receive special notice protections. Iowa protects victims in three ways: a tenant who did not cause a clear and present danger can avoid a three-day termination by taking listed protective steps, and no tenant may be penalized or evicted for calling for emergency help; and a tenant enrolled in the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program can require you to accept a substitute address and not to disclose or display their address and name (`edu-dv-confidentiality-ia`). Related: `edu-no-dv-lockchange-ia`, `edu-no-dv-deposit-timing-ia`, `edu-dv-qualifying-documents-ia`. Federal protections in covered housing programs are not covered here.

title: Protection for Tenants When Others Cause Danger
bodyText: You may not use the three-day clear-and-present-danger termination against a tenant where the dangerous activity was another person's and the tenant sought a protective or no-contact order, reported the activity to law enforcement or the county attorney, or wrote the statutory trespass letter and sent a copy to police, and gave you written proof before you sued. A tenant who relied on the letter once must take one of the other two steps if the person returns.

title: No Iowa Rule When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Iowa has no landlord-tenant statute on what happens when a tenant dies: the lease does not end automatically, and there is no special procedure for the tenant's belongings or deposit. Deal with the estate's personal representative, return the deposit under the normal rules, and recover possession through the courts or a written surrender.

title: Servicemember Lease Rights
bodyText: A tenant who enters military service during a lease, or who receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of at least 90 days, may end the lease by written notice with a copy of the orders. For a monthly lease the termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date; prepaid rent must be refunded within 30 days. You may not hold a servicemember's belongings or deposit for rent accruing after a lawful termination. You may not end the lease of a servicemember or dependents for nonpayment during military service where the rent is under $1,200 a month, except through a court, which may stay the case for up to three months. If the tenant signed before entering service, a court may also grant relief or a stay; whether a residential lease is an 'installment contract' for those purposes is not settled. Federal law also applies.

title: No Retaliation
bodyText: You may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant complained to a code enforcement agency about a health-and-safety violation, complained to you about your maintenance duties, or joined or organized a tenants' union. A good-faith complaint within the past year creates a presumption of retaliation, unless the complaint came after notice of the rent increase or service cut; proof that your legitimate costs rose supports an increase in line with those costs. You may still evict if the tenant's household caused the code violation, if the tenant is behind on rent, or if compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of use of the unit.

title: No Landlord's Lien on Tenant Belongings
bodyText: Iowa does not enforce a landlord's lien on a tenant's household goods (except one perfected before 1979), and distraint for rent is abolished. Do not hold, sell or keep a tenant's property to collect rent.

title: No Iowa Rule for Property Left After Eviction
bodyText: Iowa has no statute telling a landlord what to do with belongings a residential tenant leaves after an eviction or move-out (the abandoned-property procedures in Iowa law apply only to mobile homes in parks). Use the library's Handling of Property Left Behind clause, give written notice before disposing of anything of value, and never keep property to collect rent.

title: Eviction Records Are Public
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or court rule sealing or restricting public access to eviction (forcible entry and detainer) records. Court filings are public unless restricted by law, and clerks may purge old civil files only under the records-retention rules.

title: Removing People Who Were Never Tenants
bodyText: Iowa has no special squatter-removal statute. A person who entered your property by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth can be removed through a forcible entry and detainer action, which needs no three-day notice to quit for that ground; a person who stays after being told to leave may also be committing criminal trespass, a matter for law enforcement.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or your maintenance duties, the tenant may give a written seven-day notice and end the lease if you do not fix it, and may recover damages. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water or essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, buy them and deduct the cost from rent, or recover reduced rental value. In an eviction for unpaid rent, a tenant who told you at least seven days before rent was due, and then in good faith fixed a condition costing no more than one month's rent before receiving your termination notice, can deduct the cost. In a rent case the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court. A tenant may also repair or replace a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm you did not fix within 30 days of written notice and deduct the cost.

title: Lease Terms Iowa Prohibits
bodyText: An Iowa lease may not make the tenant (or landlord) waive rights under the landlord-tenant act, authorize a confession of judgment, agree to pay the other party's attorney fees, or exculpate, limit the liability of, or indemnify the other party for liability arising under law. Such a term is unenforceable. If you willfully use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees. The waiver ban does not apply to a single family residence on agricultural land in an unincorporated area. In federally assisted housing (USDA rural rental assistance and HUD voucher and listed project programs) a lease may not bar lawful firearms in the tenant's own unit.

title: Attorney Fees
bodyText: An Iowa lease may not require either party to pay the other's attorney fees. Fees come only from statutes, which award them in specific situations: for example, to a landlord for a tenant's willful noncompliance or a willful bad-faith holdover; to a tenant for wrongful lockouts, unlawful entry, retaliation, bad-faith deposit retention or a willfully used prohibited lease term; and to the winner of a deposit dispute. The Iowa Supreme Court has held the deposit-dispute fee provision does not reach other claims, such as trespass.

title: Unconscionable Terms
bodyText: An Iowa court may refuse to enforce a lease, or any part of it, that was unconscionable when made, or limit its effect, and it may do the same with a settlement in which a party gave up rights under the landlord-tenant act. Either party gets a chance to present evidence about the setting, purpose and effect of the term.

title: What Iowa's Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Iowa's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act covers residential rental agreements made, extended or renewed after January 1, 1979. Unless an arrangement was created to avoid the Act, it does not cover, among others: residence in an institution incidental to medical, educational or similar services; occupancy under a contract of sale; fraternity and similar housing; hotels and motels; an employee whose occupancy depends on employment at the premises; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; agricultural occupancies; and certain nonprofit transitional and homeless housing. Mobile home parks have their own chapter.

title: Consumer Fraud Law and Leases
bodyText: Iowa's consumer fraud statute defines 'merchandise' to include real estate, and the private-action consumer fraud act covers merchandise 'offered for sale or lease'. Deceptive or unfair practices in advertising or leasing a rental can therefore expose a landlord to claims by the Attorney General and possibly by the tenant. Whether a residential lease is 'consumer merchandise' under the private-action act has not been settled in any case read for this library.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be Signed
bodyText: A lease for a term longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party you will need to enforce it against. If a written lease is not signed by one side but that side accepts rent (landlord) or possession (tenant) without reservation, it takes effect as if signed, but a lease given effect that way that runs longer than one year is effective only for one year.

title: No Iowa Rule on Delivering a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Iowa's residential landlord-tenant act does not require you to give the tenant a signed copy of the lease, although the mobile home park act does. Give one anyway: the required disclosures must be in writing, and a lease neither side has signed can still bind both once rent or possession is accepted without reservation.

title: No Iowa Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Iowa has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the lease to be complete at signing. Fill in every blank before anyone signs: a blank filled later invites a dispute over what was agreed.

title: How to Serve Notices in Iowa
bodyText: Most landlord notices may be served by hand delivery, delivery with a signed and dated acknowledgment from a resident at least 18, personal service, regular plus certified mail, posting on the main entrance door (dated, within the notice period), or any method that results in the tenant actually receiving it. Termination notices and notices to quit are stricter: only signed acknowledgment of delivery, personal service, or posting on the main entrance door plus regular and certified mail. Mailed notice is complete four days after mailing. E-mail is never enough for a termination notice or notice to quit, and works for other notices only if the tenant agreed to e-mail and actually receives it.

title: Landlord's Duty to Keep the Unit Fit
bodyText:
You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; keep supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, in good and safe working order; provide and arrange removal from garbage receptacles; and supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat (unless the tenant controls a unit-only system on a direct utility connection).

A lease cannot waive these duties. In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant handles garbage, water and heat supply and specified repairs or tasks; for any other unit only by a separate signed writing with adequate consideration that does not affect other tenants. You are not liable for injuries caused by things a tenant put in the common areas.

title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText:
The tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, prospective tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least 24 hours' notice and enter only at reasonable times.

You may enter without consent in an emergency, to fix a health-and-safety condition the tenant failed to remedy, during an absence of more than 14 days, or after abandonment or surrender; otherwise only with a court order.

Abusing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages of at least one month's rent plus attorney fees; a tenant's refusal of lawful entry lets you get an injunction or end the lease and recover your actual damages and attorney fees. An entry without consent can also be a trespass: the Iowa Supreme Court upheld per-entry damages, judging consent by what the tenant's conduct led the landlord to believe.

title: When the Property Is Sold or the Manager Changes
bodyText: If you sell in good faith to a bona fide buyer, you are released from liability under the lease for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless you agreed otherwise. A manager is released for events after written notice that the management ended. The disclosure of the manager and owner's agent must be kept current and binds the new owner or manager. Transfer or return the deposits as the deposit statute requires.

title: City Rental Inspection Programs
bodyText: Every Iowa city of 15,000 or more must have a housing code and enforce it with regular rental inspections, inspections on complaint and certification of inspected rental housing. Such a city's program may include a rent escrow to pay for repairs and an ordinance barring recovery of rent for a dwelling that does not comply with the housing code, and cities may charge inspection fees with late penalties. Check your city's ordinance; the library covers state law only.

title: City Utility Bills and Liens
bodyText: Unpaid city utility charges (water, sewer, storm water, solid waste and some others) can become a lien on the rental property. You can protect the property from a lien for charges a tenant pays directly (for water, only if the unit's water is separately metered) by giving the city utility written notice that the property is a rental and the tenant is liable, with the tenant's name, the address and the date occupancy begins; the utility may require a deposit of up to 90 days of usual charges (60 days for gas and electric). Give a new notice within 30 business days after each change of tenant or owner. Repair charges are not covered. If you ask in writing, the utility must also send you its disconnection and lien notices for your tenant's account.

title: Smoke Detectors and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText:
Iowa requires smoke detectors in single-family rental units and multiple-unit residential buildings, and carbon monoxide alarms where there is a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, installed under the rules the director adopts under the statute. Smoke alarms go outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms, in each bedroom, and on every story including the basement. A battery-only smoke alarm installed or replaced since mid-2021 must have a sealed ten-year battery, and hard-wired alarms installed since mid-2016 must be interconnected where more than one is required. Carbon monoxide alarms go near every bedroom (and in a bedroom that has its own fuel-burning appliance or fireplace), unless a listed exception applies.

When a tenant moves in, the carbon monoxide alarms must be installed with working batteries, and you must give one tenant in each unit written information on testing and maintaining them. On request, supply light-emitting devices for a tenant who is deaf or hard of hearing.

Fix an inoperable detector or alarm within 30 days after written notice, or the tenant may repair or install one and deduct the cost from rent. You may require a tenant who has lived there longer than 30 days to provide batteries. Tampering with a required device is a misdemeanor.

title: No Iowa Lock or Rekey Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a landlord to install deadbolts or other security devices or to rekey locks between tenants. Rekeying between tenants is still good practice, and local codes may set requirements.

title: No Iowa Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose mold or setting mold standards for rentals. Mold that makes the unit unfit is still covered by your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable.

title: No Iowa Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment in rentals. An infestation that makes the unit unfit falls under your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable.

title: Radon
bodyText: Iowa does not require a landlord to disclose radon test results to tenants. Results need not be disclosed if they do not exceed the EPA action guideline or if you tested your own building yourself, except in a real estate sale. Certified radon testers report results to the state and may not disclose them to others without the owner's written waiver.

title: No Iowa Methamphetamine Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs. Iowa's clandestine laboratory law makes persons with control over a lab site liable to the state for cleanup costs; an owner is not such a person unless the owner knew the lab existed.

title: No Iowa Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose flood history or flood-zone status to tenants.

title: No Iowa Stigmatized Property Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute saying whether a landlord must disclose that a death, crime or other stigmatizing event occurred at a rental, and none protecting a landlord who stays silent. Answer direct questions truthfully.

title: Superfund (CERCLIS) Listing Disclosure
bodyText: If the property is listed in the federal Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Information System (CERCLIS), you must tell each tenant in writing before the tenancy begins. Check the federal listing before you lease; the optional disclosure clause provides the wording.

title: No Iowa Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Iowa has no statute giving tenants a right to install electric vehicle charging equipment, or requiring landlords to allow it.

title: Towing Vehicles From a Rental Property
bodyText: A vehicle unlawfully parked on private property, or placed there without the owner's consent, for more than 24 hours is an 'abandoned vehicle'. Police may take it into custody, or you may hire a garagekeeper to take custody and dispose of it after the certified-mail notice to the owner and lienholders. Since July 1, 2026, that notice must go out within 10 days of custody, the owner has 20 days to reclaim the vehicle (and may retrieve listed personal items once during that time), the tower must post its storage and impound fees, and the statute preempts county and city ordinances on towing abandoned vehicles. Iowa gives no separate authority to tow a tenant's authorized vehicle for expired registration or because it does not run; handle that through your parking rules and the lease.

title: Iowa Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Iowa Civil Rights Act bars housing discrimination because of race, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability or familial status, including in advertising and in the terms of a rental, and bars discrimination against a tenant because of the race, color, creed, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, age or national origin of the tenant's guests. Gender identity was removed from the Act effective July 1, 2025. Exemptions include an owner-occupied building with two units, rental of fewer than four rooms in an owner-occupied dwelling, an owner-occupied building of up to four units where the owner qualifies for the homestead credit or exemption, housing for older persons, and shared living areas by sex; the small-building exemptions never cover advertising. Federal fair housing law applies separately.

title: Assistance and Service Animals in Iowa
bodyText:
A tenant with a disability and a disability-related need may ask to keep an assistance or service animal; evaluate and respond within a reasonable time, and give a written determination. If the disability or need is not readily apparent, you may ask for information that reasonably supports the need for that particular animal.

Iowa sets out a written finding a listed licensed professional can provide, which must state, among other things, whether the provider has known the person for at least 30 days, and is valid for 12 months or the lease term, whichever is longer; other reliable proof is still allowed. An online registration or certificate is not enough. Do not ask for a diagnosis, severity or medical records.

You may require proof of licensing and vaccination, and you may deny the request for undue financial and administrative hardship, a fundamental alteration of your operations, a direct threat or substantial damage that cannot be reduced by a reasonable accommodation, or because the accommodation is not otherwise reasonable. The tenant is liable for damage the animal causes.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: Iowa law does not bar refusing to rent to a tenant because the tenant uses a federal housing choice voucher or because of the tenant's source of income. Since January 1, 2023, any city or county ordinance requiring landlords to accept vouchers is void, since March 10, 2026 a city or local government may not enact an ordinance that is broader than, or has different categories from, the Iowa Civil Rights Act, and since July 1, 2026 it may not enforce one either. Refusing vouchers as a cover for discrimination on a protected trait is still unlawful.

title: Firearms
bodyText: In most Iowa rentals the lease may restrict firearms, but not in federally assisted housing: if you receive USDA rural rental assistance or HUD voucher or listed project-based payments, the lease may not prohibit or restrict lawful firearms, components or ammunition in the tenant's own unit, though you may reasonably restrict them in common areas and the tenant must store them with reasonable care. Where the law requires you to allow firearms, you are not liable for resulting harm except for willful, reckless or grossly negligent conduct. Merely keeping a firearm in the unit is never a clear and present danger. Iowa's constitutional right to keep and bear arms binds the government; whether it limits a private landlord was not decided in any case read for this library.

title: Marijuana and Medical Cannabidiol
bodyText: Iowa has no recreational marijuana law. Its medical cannabidiol program forbids smoking cannabidiol and expressly does not require anyone who owns, occupies or controls a property to allow marijuana use, possession or growing there, so a lease may ban it. A no-smoking or no-drugs clause is lawful.

title: No Iowa Rule on Tenant Immigration Status
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. Iowa's Constitution gives resident foreigners the same property rights as native-born citizens. Asking only some applicants can be national origin discrimination.

title: Foreign Ownership Limits
bodyText: Iowa bars nonresident aliens, foreign businesses and foreign governments from purchasing or otherwise acquiring agricultural land, with limited exceptions. The restriction is about farmland, not ordinary residential rentals.

title: Sex Offender Residency Restrictions
bodyText: A registered sex offender convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor may not reside within 2,000 feet of a school or child care facility, with exceptions. The restriction is on the offender; Iowa imposes no duty on landlords to screen for it or to disclose registry information.

title: No Iowa Tenant Screening Statute
bodyText: Iowa has no statute regulating tenant screening, criminal-history inquiries or screening reports for rentals. Apply your criteria the same way to everyone; screening that falls harder on a protected group can still raise fair housing problems. Federal consumer reporting law is not covered here.

title: No Iowa Rule on Tenant Cameras
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on tenants installing doorbell or security cameras, or on landlord cameras in rental property.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: Iowa gives tenants no special notice, purchase right or relocation protection when a rental building is converted to condominiums. The conversion itself must meet the local (or state) building code, and the declaration must be filed with the city or county at least 60 days before it is recorded.

title: No Iowa Foreclosure Protection for Tenants
bodyText: Iowa has no state statute giving residential tenants notice or the right to stay after the landlord's property is foreclosed; a person who stays after a foreclosure sale can be removed by a forcible entry and detainer action. Federal law, not covered here, may give tenants of foreclosed property notice rights.

title: Jury Waivers Not Offered
bodyText: An Iowa eviction is tried in equity, without a jury, so a lease jury waiver adds nothing for possession. No Iowa statute addresses a jury waiver for money claims in a residential lease, and the library does not offer one; a waiver of rights under the landlord-tenant act itself is prohibited.

title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal Is a Crime
bodyText: In Iowa, intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or service animal in training, to obtain any right or privilege under state or federal law, is a simple misdemeanor. Because the offense turns on obtaining any legal right, it can reach a request for housing. An online registration, ID card, patch or certificate does not by itself establish a disability or a need for the animal; report suspected misrepresentation rather than deciding a request on suspicion alone.

title: Guide and Hearing Dogs: Lease Restrictions Must Be Waived
bodyText: Iowa requires a landlord to waive lease restrictions on dogs for a blind or partially blind person with a guide dog and for a deaf or hard-of-hearing person with a hearing dog; the tenant is liable for damage the dog does. Denying or interfering with these rights is a simple misdemeanor. Separately, an owner or lessor of property that law requires to be accessible to a person using a service animal is not liable for injury or damage the animal causes if the owner believed in good faith it was a service animal and was not negligent, reckless or willful; whether a private dwelling unit is such property is not settled.

title: No Iowa Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a move-in or move-out inspection, a condition checklist or a damage list. Do one anyway, with dated photos signed by both sides: you must prove every deposit deduction, measured against the unit's condition at the start of the tenancy.

title: Statutory Forms and Prescribed Wording
bodyText: Iowa prescribes no form of residential lease and no form for the ordinary notices to tenants; the 3-day nonpayment notice and the 7-day notice to remedy a breach must say what the statute requires, in your own words. One notice must quote the statute: a 3-day notice of termination and notice to quit for conduct creating a clear and present danger must state the specific activity and set out, in full, the subsection that exempts a tenant who acts against the person causing the danger. Small claims court forms exist for filing an eviction, but they are court forms, not lease or notice forms.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant, but it protects the tenant's possession directly. You may not take possession except after abandonment, surrender or as the act permits, and cutting off electric, gas, water or another essential service counts as taking possession. If you remove or exclude the tenant unlawfully or willfully cut a service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent and attorney fees, and on termination you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit. An unlawful entry, a lawful entry made unreasonably, or repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover at least one month's rent and attorney fees.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: An Iowa lease cannot remove your duty to keep the unit fit. A rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and your maintenance duties under Iowa Code § 562A.15 (code compliance, all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, clean and safe common areas, working facilities and appliances, garbage receptacles, running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat) are the tenant's rights under that chapter. An "as is" clause, a release of your repair duty, or a waiver of the tenant's repair remedies is unenforceable, and if you willfully use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). What Iowa allows is moving who does some of the work, never removing the standard. For a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant handles garbage removal and the water, hot water and heat supply, plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)). For any other unit, the agreement may cover only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by adequate consideration, made in good faith, and not reducing what you owe other tenants (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3)); you may not make it a condition of the lease (Iowa Code § 562A.15(4)). Use `maintenance-allocation-ia` for that agreement. Iowa has no rule letting a tenant accept a defect in exchange for lower rent, and no separate-document rule for a heat agreement beyond these. One exception: the waiver bar does not apply to a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area. Even there, the bar on exculpating you from liability arising under law still applies (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)) and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (Iowa Code § 562A.7); do not rely on a habitability waiver in a farm-home lease without advice. See `edu-habitability-ia` and `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`.

title: Habitability Duties Change Only by Statute
bodyText: Your Iowa maintenance duties do not bend to the lease. Iowa Code § 562A.15 has no "unless otherwise agreed" wording (the act uses that phrase for other subjects, such as where rent is paid and how the tenant uses the unit), and a lease term waiving the duties is barred (`edu-habitability-waiver-ia`). The duty to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat has two built-in exceptions that turn on facts, not on agreement: it does not apply 'where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6)), or where heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Whether a building must be equipped is a question for the building and housing codes that apply to it, including your city's. Iowa's landlord-tenant act (Iowa Code ch. 562A) has no rule letting a lease waive the water duty for a home without a well or utility water. For a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs the garbage duty and the water, hot water and heat supply duty (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)); that moves who does the work, it does not remove the standard. For any other unit, a separate signed agreement may move only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3)). Code compliance and keeping the unit fit and habitable stay yours in every case. See `maintenance-allocation-ia` and `edu-habitability-ia`.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be
bodyText: Iowa sets different thresholds for different tenant remedies. To end the lease over your breach, the tenant needs either a material noncompliance with the lease or a noncompliance with your maintenance duties 'materially affecting health and safety' (Iowa Code § 562A.21(1)); the tenant then gives a written notice naming the breach and a termination date at least seven days after you receive it, and the lease does not end if you adequately remedy the breach before that date. Your code-compliance duty itself reaches the code requirements 'materially affecting health and safety' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)). Damages and a court order need no materiality: the tenant may recover for 'any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or section 562A.15' (Iowa Code § 562A.21(2)), unless you show you used due diligence and the failure was due to circumstances reasonably beyond your control. The essential-services remedies turn instead on a deliberate or negligent failure to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)). In a nonpayment eviction, the tenant's repair-cost defense needs only a failure to comply with the lease or your maintenance duties, seven days' advance notice, a repair costing no more than one month's rent, and the repair actually made in good faith before the tenant receives your written notice to terminate for nonpayment (Iowa Code § 562A.27(4)). Iowa's statutes do not define "material"; that is left to the courts. The same health-and-safety gate applies to the tenant's own maintenance duties (Iowa Code § 562A.17, Iowa Code § 562A.27(1)). Treat every repair request as one you must handle; do not hold back while you decide whether it is material. See `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia` and `edu-habitability-ia`.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: No Iowa statute presumes that a rental is habitable or uninhabitable, whether from a code inspection, a code violation, a rental permit or anything else, and none presumes how long a repair should take. Whether your unit meets your maintenance duties is proved like any other fact. Two nearby rules are not habitability presumptions but matter. First, retaliation: if a tenant made a good-faith complaint to a code agency or to you about your maintenance duties within one year before you raise the rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction, the court presumes your action was retaliation (Iowa Code § 562A.36(2)); the presumption does not arise if the complaint came after notice of a proposed rent increase or cut in services, and evidence that your legitimate costs of owning, maintaining or operating the unit have increased is a defense against the presumption when the rent increase is in step with those costs. Under the act a presumption means the court must find the presumed fact 'unless and until evidence is introduced which would support a finding of its nonexistence' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(8)). Second, in a dispute over a withheld deposit, you carry the burden of proving the reason for withholding, including damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)); move-in and move-out records are your evidence. See `edu-retaliation-ia` and `edu-habitability-ia`.

title: No Habitability Statement Required
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. You do not need such a sentence, because the duty applies by statute whatever the lease says: at the start of the term you must deliver possession 'in compliance with the rental agreement and section 562A.15' (Iowa Code § 562A.14), and throughout the tenancy you must keep the premises fit and habitable (Iowa Code § 562A.15). The library's maintenance and repairs clause (`landlord-maintenance`) covers repairs in the lease, and the statute fills in the rest. Do not write your own shorter version that leaves duties out or makes them depend on the tenant's conduct: a term that cuts down the statutory duties is an unenforceable waiver (`edu-habitability-waiver-ia`). The written disclosures Iowa does require are separate; see `landlord-disclosure-ia` and `edu-habitability-ia`.

title: Rights an Iowa Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Several Iowa statutes keep a lease from taking away a tenant's rights, and they work differently. (1) The act-wide bar: a lease may not have the tenant (or you) waive or give up rights or remedies under Iowa's landlord-tenant act, confess judgment, agree to pay the other side's attorney fees, or exculpate, limit or indemnify the other side's liability arising under law (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)). Such a term is unenforceable, and willfully using a lease with a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Only the waiver bar has an exception: a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area. (2) Calling for help: you may not limit a tenant's or household member's right to summon police or emergency assistance, or penalize them for doing it, and 'Any waiver of the provisions of this subsection is contrary to public policy and is void, unenforceable, and of no force or effect' (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(1)(d)); a violation costs a civil penalty of one month's rent plus actual damages, attorney fees, court costs and an injunction (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(3)). (3) Firearms in USDA- and HUD-assisted housing: the lease may not bar lawful firearms in the tenant's own unit (Iowa Code § 562A.11(2); `edu-firearms-ia`). (4) Late fees above the statutory caps may not be written in (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4); `edu-late-fee-cap-ia`). (5) A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term, or an unconscionable settlement in which a party gave up a claim or right (Iowa Code § 562A.7). Buying a home from an owner in foreclosure and leasing it back: Iowa has no new sale-leaseback rule, but its foreclosure reconveyance law (Iowa Code ch. 714F) has covered these deals since 2008, and a waiver of that chapter is void, apart from a narrow handwritten waiver of the three-day cancellation right (Iowa Code § 714F.6). Get advice before any such deal. Manufactured home community lots follow Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia` and `edu-unconscionability-ia`.

title: Showing Notice Cannot Be Waived in the Lease
bodyText: Iowa sets an entry-notice rule, and it covers showings. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to 'exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors' (Iowa Code § 562A.19(1)), and, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times (Iowa Code § 562A.19(3)). That notice is a right under Iowa's landlord-tenant act, so a lease term waiving it or shortening it for showings is unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using such a term exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). For that reason the library offers no shorter-notice showing clause in Iowa. Iowa's landlord-tenant act has no rule allowing the waiver in a separate signed document instead, and no rule that a tenant's request for service counts as permission to enter. "Impracticable" is not a scheduling tool: ordinary showings can be booked 24 hours ahead. If a tenant agrees at the time to one particular showing on shorter notice, get that agreement in writing for that showing only; consent to entry is judged by what the tenant's conduct led you to believe, and an entry without notice or consent can be a trespass (`edu-landlord-entry-ia`). You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant (Iowa Code § 562A.19(3)). The waiver bar does not apply to a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area; even there, get advice before shortening notice. The lease's entry clause is `landlords-access-mi`.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: The tenant's deposit rights cannot be waived in an Iowa lease. They are rights under Iowa's landlord-tenant act: the two-months'-rent cap, holding the deposit in a federally insured account apart from your own money, return or a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding within 30 days after the tenancy ends and you receive the tenant's mailing address, withholding only for unpaid rent or other funds due under the lease, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, or the cost of recovering possession from a tenant who did not leave in good faith, your burden of proof, and punitive damages of up to twice the monthly rent for bad-faith retention (Iowa Code § 562A.12). A lease term giving any of them up, such as a "deposit is nonrefundable" term, a term letting you keep the deposit as a flat charge, or a term excusing the written statement, is unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). The deposit section has no waiver rule of its own; what it has are forfeitures written by statute, not by the lease: you lose the right to withhold anything if you miss the 30-day statement, and the tenant forfeits the deposit if no mailing address or delivery instructions reach you within one year after the tenancy ends (Iowa Code § 562A.12(4)). After an actual dispute arises, the two of you may settle it, but a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable settlement (Iowa Code § 562A.7(1)(b)). The waiver bar does not apply to a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area; do not rely on that without advice. See `security-deposit-return-ia`, `edu-deposit-cap-ia` and `edu-deposit-return-penalty-ia`.

title: No Exculpatory or Indemnity Clauses
bodyText: An Iowa lease may not excuse or limit your liability, or make the tenant indemnify you. A rental agreement shall not provide that a party 'Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the other party arising under law or to indemnify the other party for that liability or the associated costs' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)). The bar runs both ways and, unlike the general waiver bar, it has no farm-home exception. So leave out "Landlord is not liable for any loss, injury or damage", "Tenant releases Landlord from all claims" and "Tenant will indemnify and hold Landlord harmless" clauses: they are unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). A clause making the tenant pay for damage the tenant, household or guests cause is different: that is the tenant's own liability for breach (Iowa Code § 562A.17(6), Iowa Code § 562A.27(3)), not an indemnity for yours (`tenant-caused-damage-ia`). Some protections come from statute, with no lease term needed: you are not liable for injury caused by objects or materials a tenant puts in the common areas (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(3)); after a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, you are relieved of liability for events after written notice to the tenant of the sale unless otherwise agreed (Iowa Code § 562A.16(1)), as a manager is after notice that management ended (Iowa Code § 562A.16(2)); where Iowa Code § 562A.11(2) makes you allow firearms because you receive the listed USDA or HUD assistance, you are not liable for occurrences involving them except for willful, reckless or grossly negligent conduct (Iowa Code § 562A.16(3)); and a property owner or lessor who believes in good faith that an animal is a service animal is not liable for injury or damage it causes unless the owner was negligent, reckless or willful (Iowa Code § 216C.12(2)). Iowa gives no immunity for removing a residential tenant's belongings after abandonment or at an eviction, or for acting on a police notice (`edu-no-post-eviction-property-rule-ia`). See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`.

title: No Specific Ban on Eviction Charges
bodyText: No Iowa statute specifically bans a lease clause that charges the tenant a fee or penalty for being evicted. Other rules leave little room for one. A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(c)), so an "eviction fee" that covers your lawyer is unenforceable, and knowingly using it exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)); fees come only from statutes, such as for a tenant's willful noncompliance or willful, bad-faith holdover (Iowa Code § 562A.27(3), Iowa Code § 562A.34(4); `edu-attorney-fees-ia`). You may not charge or threaten a tenant for calling police or emergency help (Iowa Code § 562A.27B). What the law does let you recover is actual: rent and damages for the breach, and, from the deposit, the expenses of acquiring possession from a tenant who did not act in good faith in failing to leave after your noncompliance notice (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(3)). Iowa has no general statute deciding when a fixed charge set in advance is an unenforceable penalty rather than valid liquidated damages; the sales-of-goods rule (Iowa Code § 554.2718) does not govern leases of homes, so that question is left to the courts, and you must also mitigate your damages (Iowa Code § 562A.4(1)). The library's Iowa lease therefore carries no fixed eviction charge; document your actual costs instead. See `edu-no-liquidated-damages-rule-ia` and `default-by-tenant-ia`.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: A lease term Iowa Code § 562A.11 prohibits is unenforceable, and using one on purpose costs you money: 'If a landlord willfully uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by the landlord to be prohibited, a tenant may recover actual damages sustained by the tenant and not more than three months' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)) periodic rent and reasonable attorney fees. The penalty covers the terms that section prohibits: a waiver of rights or remedies under Iowa's landlord-tenant act (except in a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area), a confession of judgment, an agreement to pay the other side's attorney fees, an exculpation, limitation or indemnity for liability arising under law, and, in USDA- and HUD-assisted housing, a ban on lawful firearms in the tenant's unit. Two other rules sit outside that section. The right to call police or emergency help (Iowa Code § 562A.27B) has its own voidness clause and its own remedies, including a civil penalty of one month's rent, actual damages, attorney fees, court costs and an injunction. The late fee caps (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4)) say a lease shall not provide for a larger fee but set no penalty of their own. Whether the three-months penalty also reaches those terms, as waivers of rights under the act, has not been settled in anything this library has read, so assume it can. Iowa's consumer fraud statutes list no specific practice of using a void lease term; whether they reach residential leases at all is unsettled (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). A sentence saying "nothing in this lease limits your rights" does not make a prohibited term safe. Use the library's Iowa clauses as written and do not add terms of your own on these subjects. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`.

title: Eviction Notices Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: An Iowa lease cannot shorten or waive the notices that must come before you end a tenancy or file an eviction. The notices in Iowa's landlord-tenant act are rights under that act: the three-day notice to pay rent (Iowa Code § 562A.27(2)), the seven-day notice to remedy a breach (Iowa Code § 562A.27(1)), the three-day notice for a clear and present danger (Iowa Code § 562A.27A), and the ten- and thirty-day notices ending a periodic or fixed-term tenancy (Iowa Code § 562A.34). A lease term waiving or shortening any of them is unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). The three-day notice to quit 'must be given to the defendant in writing' (Iowa Code § 648.3(1)) before most eviction actions. It sits in the eviction chapter, but Iowa's landlord-tenant act governs how it is served on a tenant (Iowa Code § 562A.29A(1)), and no Iowa statute lets a lease dispense with it, so treat it as a notice the lease cannot waive either. The statute supplies the only shortcuts: once a three-day notice to pay rent has ended the tenancy, you may file without a separate notice to quit (Iowa Code § 648.3(1)), and for a tenancy at will ended for nonpayment the three-day notice is the only notice needed (Iowa Code § 648.4). For that reason the library offers no notice-waiver clause. The waiver bar does not apply to a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area; do not rely on a notice waiver there without advice. Farm tenancies are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562, not covered here. See `edu-nonpayment-notice-ia`, `edu-eviction-process-ia` and `edu-notice-service-ia`.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers
bodyText: The library's Iowa lease does not ask the tenant to waive the homestead exemption or the exemptions that protect personal property from creditors. Iowa's homestead 'must embrace the house used as a home by the owner' (Iowa Code § 561.1(1)), so a tenant renting your unit has no homestead in it; no Iowa statute makes a tenant's leasehold a homestead, and a waiver in your lease would at most reach a home the tenant owns elsewhere. Iowa does let a homestead be sold for debts 'created by written contract by persons having the power to convey, expressly stipulating that it shall be liable' (Iowa Code § 561.21(2)), and then only for a deficiency after the other property pledged by the same contract is exhausted; a contract affecting agricultural land of forty acres or more, or dwellings on it, must also carry a signed, boldface waiver statement (Iowa Code § 561.22). Personal property is different: no Iowa statute lets a lease waive the execution exemptions in Iowa Code ch. 627, a debtor does not lose them by failing to designate exempt property unless the levying officer demands it in writing (Iowa Code § 627.3), and household goods are beyond your reach anyway because a landlord's lien on them is unenforceable and distraint for rent is abolished (Iowa Code § 562A.31). Up to five hundred dollars in total of the tenant's rental deposit, utility deposits and prepaid rent is exempt from other creditors, but not from your own claims under the lease (Iowa Code § 627.6(15)). Because the waiver would usually reach nothing and invites a dispute, the library does not offer it. If you lease to a tenant who owns a home and want that home to stand behind the lease, get advice and add your own clause that meets Iowa Code § 561.21(2). A lease still may not let you confess judgment (`edu-confession-of-judgment-ia`). See `edu-landlord-lien-ia`.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your lease cannot take away the tenant's casualty rights or your duty to mitigate. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within fourteen days, or, if staying is lawful, give up the unusable part and pay reduced rent (Iowa Code § 562A.25). If the tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to rent the unit at a fair rental (Iowa Code § 562A.29(3)), and under Iowa's landlord-tenant act 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages' (Iowa Code § 562A.4(1)). These are rights under that act, so a lease term waiving them, such as "Tenant's rent continues even if the unit is destroyed" or "Landlord has no duty to re-rent", is unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Iowa has no separate general casualty statute that an express agreement could override; the only other casualty-termination rule is for self-service storage units. What the lease may do is add rights for you that leave the tenant's untouched: the library's optional `casualty-termination-ia` clause gives you a termination right after a serious casualty, and `tenant-caused-damage-ia` keeps the tenant liable for damage the tenant causes. The waiver bar does not apply to a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area; do not rely on that without advice. See `edu-casualty-ia` and `edu-abandonment-mitigation-ia`.

title: No Statute on Liquidated Damages in Leases
bodyText:
No Iowa statute permits, caps or voids a lease term fixing in advance the damages a tenant pays for breaking the lease.

Iowa's only general liquidated-damages rule is for sales of goods (Iowa Code § 554.2718), and the landlord-tenant act says nothing on the subject, so whether an agreed sum is a valid estimate or an unenforceable penalty is left to the courts under the general law of contracts that supplements the act (Iowa Code § 562A.3).

The act itself points to actual loss: its remedies are administered so the aggrieved party recovers appropriate damages, and the aggrieved party must mitigate (Iowa Code § 562A.4(1)); if a tenant abandons, you must try to re-rent at a fair rental (Iowa Code § 562A.29(3)); you may keep from the deposit only the amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent or other funds due under the lease, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and certain possession costs (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (Iowa Code § 562A.7).

The statute does fix some charges itself: late fees are capped (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4); `edu-late-fee-cap-ia`) and a willful, bad-faith holdover costs actual damages and attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.34(4)).

The library's Iowa lease therefore carries no liquidated-damages clause for a breach. Its early-termination option (`early-termination-ks`) is a fee the tenant chooses to pay to end a fixed term early, not damages for a breach; whether a court would treat it as a penalty has not been researched. Keep records of your actual losses and re-letting efforts. See `edu-abandonment-mitigation-ia` and `edu-no-eviction-penalty-ban-ia`.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: When you break the lease or your maintenance duties, Iowa gives the tenant a set of statutory remedies, summarized in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`: a seven-day notice to remedy or the lease ends, plus damages and an injunction (Iowa Code § 562A.21); buying heat, water, hot water or essential services you deliberately or negligently fail to supply and deducting the cost, or recovering reduced rental value (Iowa Code § 562A.23); a repair-cost defense in a nonpayment eviction (Iowa Code § 562A.27(4)); a counterclaim in a rent or possession case, where the court may order rent paid into court (Iowa Code § 562A.24); rent abatement and termination if you fail to deliver possession (Iowa Code § 562A.22); and possession or termination with actual damages, punitive damages of up to twice the monthly rent and attorney fees for a lockout or utility shutoff (Iowa Code § 562A.26). No Iowa lead or health statute tells tenants to withhold rent until you comply, or bars an eviction while a lead hazard is uncorrected. But a city with a housing code may include in its enforcement procedures 'An escrow system for the deposit of rent which will be applied to the costs of correcting violations' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(5)), and may provide by ordinance that no rent is recoverable for a dwelling that does not comply with the city's housing code until it does (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(8)). Check your city's rental code (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids or Ames); see `edu-rental-inspection-ia`. The remedies cannot be waived in the lease (`edu-habitability-waiver-ia`).

title: Repair Promises: No Form Rule, but They Bind You
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires a promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. A promise still binds you. Iowa's rental agreement can be written or oral (Iowa Code § 562A.6(11)), you must deliver possession in compliance with it (Iowa Code § 562A.14), the tenant must let you in to make 'necessary or agreed repairs' (Iowa Code § 562A.19(1)), and a material failure to do what you agreed lets the tenant give a seven-day notice to end the lease and recover damages (Iowa Code § 562A.21). An unkept promise can also be a consumer-fraud problem: Iowa's consumer fraud act makes a 'false promise' in connection with the lease of merchandise, which includes real estate, an unlawful practice the Attorney General can pursue (Iowa Code § 714.16(2)(a)); whether tenants can sue under the private consumer fraud act is unsettled (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`), and a real estate licensee can be disciplined for a false promise (Iowa Code § 543B.34). Put every promised repair in a written addendum with a completion date, and keep it. See `existing-condition` and `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In an eviction for unpaid rent, or a suit for rent while the tenant still lives in the unit, the tenant may counterclaim for anything the tenant can recover under the lease or Iowa's landlord-tenant act, such as damages for your repair failures. The court then 'from time to time may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing' (Iowa Code § 562A.24(1)), works out what each side owes, and pays the party owed a net amount first from the money paid in. If no rent remains due after that, the tenant wins the possession case. If the counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney fees. When the tenant has moved out, the tenant may still counterclaim but need not pay rent into court (Iowa Code § 562A.24(2)). Ordering rent into court is up to the judge: ask for it when a tenant counterclaims and stays. Nothing in Iowa's landlord-tenant, eviction or small claims chapters (Iowa Code ch. 562, ch. 562A, ch. 631 and ch. 648) makes the tenant pay rent into court before raising other defenses, makes the counterclaim mandatory, or requires rent to be paid because a hearing is continued. An eviction case is tried as an equitable action, set for hearing no later than eight days after filing (fifteen if you ask or agree), and a tenant who appears on short notice may get a continuance (Iowa Code § 648.5); the eviction may be filed together only with a claim for rent or recovery under the listed sections, and cannot itself be the subject of a counterclaim (Iowa Code § 648.19). Iowa's general court rules on counterclaims are not covered here. See `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia` and `edu-eviction-process-ia`.

title: Shifting Maintenance Work to the Tenant
bodyText:
Iowa lets you move some maintenance work to the tenant, on terms that depend on the kind of home. For a single family residence (a unit with direct street access that shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility with another unit), you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant takes over garbage removal and the water, hot water and heat supply, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)). The writing can be in the lease, and the statute names no separate consideration.

For any other unit, the tenant may take on only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only if the agreement is made in good faith, 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3)(a)), and does not reduce what you owe other tenants; you may not make the tenant's performance a condition of the lease (Iowa Code § 562A.15(4)). In either case the work must be specified, and code compliance and keeping the unit fit and habitable stay yours (`edu-habitability-waiver-ia`).

How the library does it: the Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal lease sections bind only in a single family residence; for any other unit, use the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement (`maintenance-allocation-ia`), which states the consideration and the specified tasks.

title: Smoke-Free Common Areas and Smoke Drift
bodyText:
Iowa's Smokefree Air Act bans smoking in your building's enclosed common areas. It bans smoking in public places, which include common areas, and defines a common area to include 'the common use area of a multiunit residential property' (Iowa Code § 142D.2(3)). If you have employees or volunteers (a manager, maintenance or cleaning staff), the enclosed areas they frequent at work, such as hallways, stairways and elevators, are also a place of employment where smoking is banned (Iowa Code § 142D.2(14), Iowa Code § 142D.3(1)(b)). Tenants' own units are private residences and are exempt unless used for child care or as a health care provider location (Iowa Code § 142D.4(1)).

As the owner or manager you must post "no smoking" signs or the international no-smoking symbol in and at every entrance to those areas, remove ashtrays, and tell people who smoke there about the law (Iowa Code § 142D.6(3)-(4), Iowa Code § 142D.8(3)); a failure costs a civil penalty of up to $100 for a first violation, $200 for a second within a year and $500 for each later one, each day counting separately (Iowa Code § 142D.9(2), (6)).

You may declare your whole property nonsmoking, which then binds once the signs are posted (Iowa Code § 142D.5); the library's `smoking-policy` clause bans smoking everywhere on the property.
