No Iowa statute addresses smoke drifting from one unit into another or lets a lease make the tenant give up a claim about it; a lease term excusing your liability arising under law is unenforceable (`edu-exculpatory-clauses-ia`), so do not add a smoke-drift waiver.

title: Notice Before Pest Treatment
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute that makes you tell tenants before pest control or pesticide treatment, and no lease notice on pesticides is required.

Two rules still matter. First, a treatment inside the unit is an entry: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times (Iowa Code § 562A.19(3)); see `landlords-access-mi` and `edu-landlord-entry-ia`.

Second, Iowa's pesticide law makes the Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship set 'the proper notice to be given by a commercial or public applicator to occupants of adjoining properties in urban areas prior to or after the exterior application of pesticides' (Iowa Code § 206.19(3)). That duty is on the applicator, covers outdoor applications only, and arises only 'if an occupant requests that the commercial or public applicator provide the occupant notice in a timely manner prior to the application' (Iowa Code § 206.19(3)); a request expires each December 31 or when the occupant moves. The notice is for occupants of adjoining properties, so a tenant's request covers treatments on neighboring properties, not a treatment at the rental itself. The department's rules give the details; ask your pest control company what notice it gives.

Anyone you hire to apply restricted use pesticides for structural pest control in human dwellings must be certified (Iowa Code § 206.31).

A good practice: tell the tenant in writing which pest is being treated, when, what product the operator will use and how to prepare, and give that notice at least 24 hours ahead. For bed bugs and other pests, see `pest-cooperation-pr` and `edu-no-bed-bug-rule-ia`. City housing codes (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may add rules.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: Iowa has no rule that presumes appliances left in a unit are yours to maintain, and no rule on how a lease excludes them. Your duty turns on what you supply: you must 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)). Two consequences follow. First, equipment a code or statute requires you to supply, such as heat, hot water and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, cannot be excluded at all; see `edu-habitability-ia` and `edu-alarm-duties-ia`. Second, Iowa does not say when an item you leave in the unit for the tenant to use counts as supplied. A lease that leaves an item in place but says you will not repair it could be read as waiving your repair duty or limiting your liability, which an Iowa lease may not do (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a), Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d); `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`). The cautious course: remove any appliance you do not want to maintain before the tenant moves in; list the ones you do supply in the lease (`appliances-included`) and keep them working; and if the tenant brings an appliance, such as a washer, dryer or window air conditioner, say in writing that it is the tenant's own property and the tenant's to maintain. Iowa does not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator at all (`edu-no-stove-refrigerator-duty-ia`). If you want the tenant to take over repairs of something you supply, Iowa allows it only by a good-faith written agreement in a single family residence, or by a separate signed writing with adequate consideration for other units (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2), Iowa Code § 562A.15(3); `maintenance-allocation-ia`). City housing codes (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may require equipment and so make it required to be supplied. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area; the bar on limiting your liability (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)) has no such exception, so the cautious course above applies there too.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no law that makes you provide recycling at a rental or tell tenants where and how to recycle. Your state duty covers trash: you must 'Provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences, accessible to all tenants, for the central collection and removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste incidental to the occupancy of the dwelling unit and arrange for their removal' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(5)). In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant handles this (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2); `maintenance-allocation-ia`). The tenant must 'Dispose from the tenant's dwelling unit all ashes, rubbish, garbage, and other waste in a clean and safe manner' (Iowa Code § 562A.17(3)). Recycling is mostly local. A city or county that collects solid waste 'shall consider as a proposed ordinance, the mandatory curbside collection of recyclable materials which have been separated from other solid waste' (Iowa Code § 455D.21), so your city or hauler may require sorting or set container rules; Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and other cities run their own programs. If you offer recycling, put the sorting and container rules in writing: a lease term or a written rule is enforceable only if it meets Iowa's rules test, and a rule adopted after move-in needs reasonable notice and may not substantially change the lease (Iowa Code § 562A.18; `rules-ia`). Telling tenants where the bins are and what the city accepts is good practice, not a state requirement. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Smart Locks and Keyless Entry
bodyText: Iowa has no law on smart locks, keypads, key cards, app-based entry or other connected devices in rentals. No Iowa statute requires a physical key as a backup, limits what an entry system may record, or lets a domestic violence survivor make you cut off another person's app access. The general rules still apply to a smart lock. Opening the door with a code or an app is an entry, so you still need the tenant's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, and except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, at least 24 hours' notice and a reasonable time (Iowa Code § 562A.19(1), Iowa Code § 562A.19(3); `landlords-access-mi`, `edu-landlord-entry-ia`). You 'shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant' (Iowa Code § 562A.19(3)), and you have no other right of access (Iowa Code § 562A.19(4)). Disabling a tenant's code or app to keep the tenant out is an unlawful exclusion: the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, 'punitive damages not to exceed twice the monthly rental payment, and reasonable attorney fees' (Iowa Code § 562A.26); see `edu-self-help-eviction-ia` and `edu-no-lockout-for-rent-ia`. Data: if your system stores fingerprints or other biometric data with tenants' names, that is personal information under Iowa's breach law (Iowa Code § 715C.1(11)(a)(5)), and if it is breached you must notify the affected tenants (Iowa Code § 715C.2(1)). Iowa's consumer data protection chapter applies only to businesses that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers a year, or 25,000 with more than half their revenue from selling data (Iowa Code § 715D.2(1)), which leaves out most landlords. Good practice: give every tenant a way in that does not depend on a phone or an app working, change or delete codes between tenants (`keys`; `edu-no-security-device-rule-ia`), do not use entry logs to track the tenant, and if a tenant reports domestic abuse, see `edu-no-dv-lockchange-ia`. Federal law may add duties in covered housing; not covered here.

title: No Key Control Law in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no key-control law for rentals. No Iowa statute or held rule makes you adopt a written key-control policy, keep a key log, limit who holds master keys, or run background checks on employees, maintenance workers or managers who can enter units, whatever the size of the building. What Iowa does regulate is entry itself, and it applies to everyone who enters for you: the tenant's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, entry only at reasonable times, and no abuse of the right of access (Iowa Code § 562A.19; `landlords-access-mi`, `edu-landlord-entry-ia`). If an employee enters unlawfully or uses entry to harass, the tenant may get an injunction or end the lease and recover 'actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney fees' (Iowa Code § 562A.35(2)) against you. Good practice for any building: keep keys and codes locked and logged, give staff only the keys a job needs, rekey or change codes between tenants (`edu-no-security-device-rule-ia`, `keys`), and screen anyone who will hold master keys. Screening employees is lawful; employment and consumer-report laws govern how you do it and are not covered here. For keypads and app-based locks, see `edu-no-smart-access-rule-ia`. Code ch. 481-2015).

title: No Alternate Housing Duty in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa does not make you provide or pay for a hotel or other alternate housing while a unit is unfit or being repaired, and, unlike the uniform act it is based on, Iowa's essential-services section does not let the tenant rent substitute housing and stop paying rent. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services, the tenant, after written notice, may buy those services and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from the rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or recover rent already paid for the period of your noncompliance (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)); a tenant who does so may not also end the lease under Iowa Code § 562A.21 for that breach (Iowa Code § 562A.23(2)). For other defects materially affecting health and safety the tenant may give a seven-day notice and end the lease unless you remedy the breach within that time, and may recover damages (Iowa Code § 562A.21); damages could include the reasonable cost of staying elsewhere, a question for the court. See `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`. After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease, or stay in the usable part and pay reduced rent (Iowa Code § 562A.25(1); `edu-casualty-ia`, `casualty-termination-ia`). Two special cases: in a city or county urban revitalization area, a qualified tenant displaced by an owner's work to get the tax exemption must be paid 'compensation of at least one month's rent' (Iowa Code § 404.6), and the city or county may make the owner pay it; and a tenant displaced by a government project gets replacement-housing payments from the displacing agency, not from you (Iowa Code § 316.6). City housing code enforcement must be 'designed to improve housing conditions rather than to displace persons from their homes' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(b)), and city codes (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may require relocation help; this library does not describe them. If you choose to put a tenant up during repairs, agree in writing on who pays, for how long, and what happens to rent; that is lawful but not required.

title: Tenants Sheltering Disaster Evacuees
bodyText: Iowa has no law on tenants who take in friends or family displaced by a fire, flood, tornado or other disaster. No Iowa statute lets a tenant house disaster evacuees despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, bars you from acting on those terms, or limits rent increases for added occupants. Your lease terms apply as written: the guest and occupancy clauses (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`, `permitted-occupants`) and any written rules that meet Iowa's rules test (Iowa Code § 562A.18; `rules-ia`). A new rule adopted after the tenant signs binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.18(2)), so do not tighten guest limits mid-lease in response to a disaster. When the President has declared a major disaster in Iowa, the governor may 'temporarily suspend or modify, for not to exceed sixty days, any public health, safety, zoning, transportation, or other requirement of law or regulation within this state' (Iowa Code § 29C.6(2)) by proclamation, where that is essential to provide temporary housing for disaster victims. Read any proclamation that covers your county; a proclamation may relax a zoning or occupancy rule, but this library has found nothing that rewrites a private lease. Good practice: if a tenant asks to shelter displaced people, agree in writing on who will stay, for how long, and whether rent or utilities change, and apply the same answer to every tenant; guest rules may not treat people differently for protected traits (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). City housing codes set occupancy limits (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`). For your own duties after a disaster, see `edu-disaster-duties-ia`.

title: Your Duties After a Disaster
bodyText: Iowa has no special landlord-tenant rules for declared disasters. A governor's disaster proclamation does not by itself end a tenancy, stop rent, pause evictions or limit rent increases, and Iowa's landlord-tenant act does not mention disasters. The ordinary rules do the work. Fire or casualty: if the unit or premises are damaged 'by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired' (Iowa Code § 562A.25(1)), the tenant may move out at once and give written notice within fourteen days to end the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value (Iowa Code § 562A.25(1)). If the lease ends, you must return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit, accounting as of the date of the casualty (Iowa Code § 562A.25(2)). A storm, flood or tornado is a casualty for this purpose in ordinary usage; there is no special rule for a unit that is undamaged but cannot be reached, a question for case law. See `edu-casualty-ia` and `casualty-termination-ia`. Repairs and services: your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable continues (Iowa Code § 562A.15; `edu-habitability-ia`), and if you deliberately or negligently fail to restore heat, water, hot water or essential services, the tenant has the remedies in Iowa Code § 562A.23 (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`). You need not provide alternate housing (`edu-no-alt-housing-duty-ia`). Entry: in an emergency you may enter without consent (Iowa Code § 562A.19(2)), and during an absence of more than fourteen days you may enter at times reasonably necessary (Iowa Code § 562A.29(2)). Help for tenants: when a proclamation authorizes it, the Iowa Finance Authority may give eligible renters short-term rent help to prevent eviction, paid to the renter or to a local partner (Iowa Code § 16.57C), and rent help for replacement housing if the home is unfit or beyond repair (Iowa Code § 16.57B(6)). Accept such payments for a tenant who qualifies. Under a presidential major-disaster declaration, the governor may by proclamation temporarily suspend or modify some legal requirements to provide temporary housing (Iowa Code § 29C.6(2)). Prices: Iowa's statutes have no disaster price-gouging law; whether the Attorney General's consumer fraud rules reach rent increases during a disaster is in rules this library does not hold, so be cautious about raising rent sharply during a declared disaster (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Who Does a Tenant's Self-Help Repairs
bodyText: Iowa has no rule that lets a lease name the repairer a tenant must use, and no rule that tenant self-help work be done by a licensed or approved contractor. Iowa gives tenants two self-help routes, and neither lets you choose who does the work. First, if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services, the tenant, after written notice, may 'Procure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent' (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)(a)). Second, in a nonpayment case the tenant has a defense if the tenant told you at least seven days before rent was due that the tenant would correct your breach at your expense, the reasonable cost was no more than one month's rent, and the tenant had it corrected in good faith before your termination notice (Iowa Code § 562A.27(4)); see `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`. A lease term requiring the tenant to use your contractor, or to get your consent first, before using either route would take away a right under Iowa's landlord-tenant act, which a lease may not do except for a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using such a term carries a penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3); `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`). What you can do: give the tenant a repair contact in writing (`landlord-disclosure-ia`, Iowa Code § 562A.13) and act fast, since both routes start only after notice to you and your failure to act; you can dispute a cost that was not reasonable. You choose who does your own repairs and who enters for you (Iowa Code § 562A.19(1); `landlords-access-mi`), and when a tenant's breach of the tenant's duties materially affects health and safety and the tenant fails to fix it within seven days after your written notice, you may have the work done and bill it as rent (Iowa Code § 562A.28). For work the tenant chooses to do, such as alterations, you may require your written consent and name the contractor (`no-alterations`). In a written repair agreement under Iowa Code § 562A.15(2) or Iowa Code § 562A.15(3) you may agree who does the work (`maintenance-allocation-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Repair Requests and Notice of Defects
bodyText: Iowa sets the notice for a tenant's repair remedies; it has no rule on how routine repair requests must be made. Remedies that need written notice: to end the lease over your failure to repair, the tenant must 'deliver a written notice to the landlord specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach' (Iowa Code § 562A.21(1)) and give you seven days to fix it; the essential-services remedies start only after the tenant 'may give written notice to the landlord specifying the breach' (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)) and 'do not arise until the tenant has given notice to the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.23(3)). Rights that do not depend on a writing: the notice condition of the repair-and-deduct defense (which has other conditions too, `edu-rent-demand-bar-ia`) is only that the tenant 'notified the landlord at least seven days prior to the due date of the tenant's rent payment' (Iowa Code § 562A.27(4)(b)); the tenant may recover damages for your noncompliance (Iowa Code § 562A.21(2)); and you may not retaliate after the tenant 'has complained to the landlord of a violation under section 562A.15' (Iowa Code § 562A.36(1)(b)), in any form, with a good-faith complaint within a year creating a presumption of retaliation (Iowa Code § 562A.36(2); `edu-retaliation-ia`). How notice may be served: a tenant may hand it to you or your designated agent, mail it by both regular and certified mail, or use 'A method of providing notice that results in the notice actually being received by the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(b)(6)); see `edu-actual-notice-method-ia` and `edu-written-notices-ia`. Your lease may ask the tenant to report repairs promptly and in writing (`landlord-maintenance` does), which gives you a record. Except in a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area, it cannot take away a right Iowa does not tie to a writing (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), so an oral or text complaint still counts for retaliation, and a court may treat it as notice for the repair-and-deduct defense. No Iowa statute says whether inviting phone or app requests in the lease waives the writing that Iowa Code § 562A.21 and Iowa Code § 562A.23 require. The safe course: act on every repair request however it reaches you, log the date, and confirm in writing what you will do and when. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Iowa has no special entry rule for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes, pest treatments, smoke alarm checks or meter readings. Those visits fall under the ordinary entry rule. The tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services' (Iowa Code § 562A.19(1)), and except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give 'at least twenty-four hours' (Iowa Code § 562A.19(3)) notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. That notice is a right under Iowa's landlord-tenant act, so a lease term allowing no-notice or shorter-notice entry for scheduled services is unenforceable, except in a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using one carries a penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)); see `edu-showing-notice-waiver-ia` for the same rule on showings. A regular schedule does not make notice impracticable. Listing the services and their usual schedule in the lease is lawful and helps the tenant plan, but Iowa has not said whether a schedule printed in the lease counts as the 24-hour notice for each visit, so the cautious course is to send a reminder at least 24 hours before each visit, at a reasonable time, and to ask the tenant's permission as `landlords-access-mi` provides. An entry without notice and consent can be a trespass (`edu-landlord-entry-ia`), and abuse of access lets the tenant recover at least one month's rent and attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.35(2)). The library does not offer an Iowa scheduled-services entry clause, because `landlords-access-mi` already covers maintenance and service visits on 24 hours' notice; a landlord who wants a schedule in the lease may add one after taking advice, keeping per-visit notice of at least 24 hours. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Tenant Guest-Rights Law in Iowa
bodyText:
Iowa has no guest-rights law for tenants. No Iowa statute guarantees a tenant's right to have guests, visitors, caregivers or delivery people, bars a lease from limiting guests in buildings of any size, or bars guest fees; Iowa's landlord-tenant act does not use the words guest or visitor.

So guest terms are a matter for your lease: Iowa lets the lease include 'terms and conditions not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)), and the library's guest clauses are `guest-policy` and `guest-policy-day-limit`, with occupants named in `permitted-occupants`. Written building rules about guests must meet Iowa's rules test, including fair application to all tenants (Iowa Code § 562A.18; `rules-ia`).

One firm limit: you may not discriminate against a tenant 'because of the race, color, creed, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, age, or national origin of persons who may from time to time be present in or on the lessee's or owner's premises for lawful purposes at the invitation of the lessee or owner as friends, guests, visitors, relatives, or in any similar capacity' (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(d)); see `edu-fair-housing-ia`. A disabled tenant's need for a live-in or visiting aide is a reasonable-accommodation question (`edu-fair-housing-ia`).

Tenants answer for their guests in several ways: the tenant must not 'knowingly permit a person' (Iowa Code § 562A.17(6)) to damage the premises, must act so as not to disturb neighbors (Iowa Code § 562A.17(7)), and loses some remedies for conditions caused by a person on the premises with the tenant's consent (Iowa Code § 562A.21(1)(c)); see `tenant-caused-damage-ia`.

To keep a particular non-tenant off the property, see `edu-trespass-notice-ia`. A guest fee is not barred by statute, but a charge is collectible only if the lease provides for it, and a fee that is really a penalty may not be enforced (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`, `edu-no-liquidated-damages-rule-ia`).

title: Home Businesses in Iowa Rentals
bodyText:
Iowa's zoning law makes a home-based business a permitted use of residential property, but it leaves your lease in charge. A "home-based business" is one for the manufacture, provision or sale of goods or services 'that is owned and operated by the owner or tenant of the residential property on which the business operates' (Iowa Code § 414.33(1)(b)), and 'The use of a residential property for a home-based business is a permitted use' (Iowa Code § 414.33(2)).

A city may not ban or require a permit for a no-impact home business (one with on-site employees and clients within the occupancy limit, no on-street parking or substantial traffic, activity inside the home or yard, and nothing visible from a neighbor or the street) (Iowa Code § 414.33(1)(c), Iowa Code § 414.33(3)), though it may adopt narrowly tailored health, safety and compatibility rules (Iowa Code § 414.33(4)). Counties have the same rules for unincorporated areas (Iowa Code § 335.35).

That permission 'does not supersede' (Iowa Code § 414.33(2)) 'A deed restriction, covenant, or agreement restricting the use of land' (Iowa Code § 414.33(2)), and a lease is an agreement about the use of the property. Iowa's landlord-tenant act also sets the default: 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit and uses incidental thereto' (Iowa Code § 562A.20).

So you may forbid business use in the lease, as `residential-use-only` does, or allow it on your own conditions.

Whether a quiet home office is a use incidental to a dwelling that a general ban does not reach is a question for case law; if you mean to bar it, say so, and if you will allow remote work or a small home business, say that in writing too, with any conditions on clients, signs, deliveries, storage, insurance and parking. A home-based business also cannot get around your building's HOA or condominium documents (Iowa Code § 414.33(2); `hoa-compliance`). For child care in the home, see `edu-family-child-care-ia`.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Child Care Homes in Iowa Rentals
bodyText:
Iowa does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home, and sets no conditions, such as insurance or a liability waiver, for allowing one. Iowa's child care law expects some home providers to be tenants: a "Child care home" is an unregistered provider caring for five or fewer children at one time, or six or fewer if at least one is school-aged (Iowa Code § 237A.1(5)), and the care must be given in 'a single-family residence that is owned, rented, or leased by the person or program providing the child care' (Iowa Code § 237A.3(3)), which 'includes an apartment, condominium, townhouse, or other individual unit within a multiple unit residential dwelling' (Iowa Code § 237A.3(3)). Larger providers register as child development homes (Iowa Code § 237A.1(6)).

Paid child care in the home is also a home-based business, which Iowa zoning law treats as a permitted use but which does not override 'A deed restriction, covenant, or agreement restricting the use of land' (Iowa Code § 414.33(2)); see `edu-home-business-ia`.

Your lease decides: unless otherwise agreed, the tenant must occupy the unit 'only as a dwelling unit and uses incidental thereto' (Iowa Code § 562A.20), and `residential-use-only` bars commercial use.

If you allow child care, put it in writing: the type of care and the number of children, compliance with state child care rules, renter's liability insurance naming the business use (`edu-no-renters-insurance-rules-ia`), use of yards and common areas, and parking for drop-off. A lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for your own legal liability or limit that liability (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)).

A home used as a child care home is a public place under Iowa's smokefree air law, so no one may smoke there (Iowa Code § 142D.2, Iowa Code § 142D.3; `smoking-policy`). Do not refuse or restrict tenants because they have children; that is a separate question of familial status (`edu-fair-housing-ia`).

title: Hunting Rights on Rented Farmland
bodyText: Iowa has no statute that decides whether hunting and fishing rights on rented farmland go with the farm lease or stay with the owner. The farm lease decides, so say it in writing. Two Iowa rules treat a tenant like an owner. First, trespass to hunt is 'Entering upon or in property without the express permission of the owner, lessee, or person in lawful possession with the intent to' (Iowa Code § 716.7(2)(a)(1)) hunt, fish or trap there, so a farm tenant in possession can lawfully give someone permission to hunt unless the lease says otherwise. Second, 'Owners or tenants of land, and their minor children, may hunt, fish or trap upon such lands' (Iowa Code § 483A.24(1)) without a license, except for the special deer and wild turkey licenses; owners and tenants of farm units also have their own special landowner-tenant deer and turkey licenses (Iowa Code § 483A.24(2)). No one may shoot at game within two hundred yards of an inhabited building or a feedlot 'unless the owner or tenant has given consent' (Iowa Code § 481A.123(1)). Iowa's recreational use law limits the duty of care a "holder" of land, which includes a tenant or lessee, owes to people hunting there for free (Iowa Code § 461C.2, Iowa Code § 461C.3). If you want to keep the hunting rights, or lease them separately to a hunter, reserve them expressly in the farm lease and say whether the tenant and the tenant's family may hunt. Farm leases are not governed by Iowa's residential landlord-tenant act, which does not apply to 'Occupancy under a rental agreement covering premises used by the occupant primarily for agricultural purposes' (Iowa Code § 562A.5(7)); see `edu-scope-ia`. A farmhouse let to a tenant who does not farm the land is a residential tenancy, and hunting on the surrounding land is then a separate question for the owner and the farm operator.

title: Elevators, Pools and Other Facilities
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty, two Iowa safety laws reach facilities common in rental buildings: elevators and pools. The general duty: you must maintain 'all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)) and keep common areas clean and safe (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(3)). "Premises" includes 'grounds, areas and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(7)), so a laundry room, fitness room, garage, storage area or playground you offer is part of what you must keep safe; see `edu-habitability-ia`. Elevators: Iowa's conveyance safety law covers elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, lifts and wheelchair lifts (Iowa Code § 89A.1(2)), except a conveyance 'installed in any single private dwelling residence' (Iowa Code § 89A.2(1)(a)). Each conveyance must be inspected at least annually unless the safety board's rules set another interval (Iowa Code § 89A.6(3)); the owner must get an operating permit and may not run the conveyance without one after the time allowed (Iowa Code § 89A.9(1)); the permit 'shall be posted conspicuously in the car of an elevator' (Iowa Code § 89A.9(2)) or near other equipment; and 'Every conveyance shall be maintained by the owner in a safe operating condition and in conformity with the rules adopted by the safety board' (Iowa Code § 89A.14). Pools and spas: Iowa's pool law 'applies to all spray pads, swimming pools, and spas owned or operated by local or state government, or commercial interests or private entities including but not limited to facilities operated by' (Iowa Code § 135I.2) apartments and condominiums, among others, but not to facilities intended for single-family use, with a narrow exemption for some homeowners' associations and housing cooperatives of seventy-two or fewer units. The state registers and regulates those pools; ask the state or your local board of health what registration and inspection apply. No Iowa statute or held rule regulates automatic garage door openers in rentals or puts a product-safety duty on you for them; if you supply one, it is a facility you must keep in safe working order under Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4). Fair rules for shared facilities may be adopted under Iowa Code § 562A.18 (`rules-ia`, `common-area-use`); for boilers, see `edu-no-radiator-cover-rule-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Parking Rules in Iowa Leases
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on parking rules in residential leases. Nothing requires you to deliver parking rules before signing, use a set heading, state in the lease whether parking is included or what it costs, limit the vehicle information you ask for, or make a parking permit run with the lease; and no Iowa statute gives residents of an apartment lot a waiting period or posted notice before a tow for expired registration. Iowa's general rules test fills the gap. A written rule about use of the premises, including parking, binds the tenant only if its purpose is convenience, safety or welfare, protecting your property, or fair distribution of facilities; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it 'applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner' (Iowa Code § 562A.18(1)(c)); it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; it is not meant to evade your obligations; and the tenant had notice of it at signing (Iowa Code § 562A.18(1)). A rule adopted later binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and if 'it does not work a substantial modification of the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.18(2)), so do not add a parking fee or take away a promised space mid-lease by a new rule. Parking you promise or hold out for tenants is part of the "Premises" (Iowa Code § 562A.6(7)) you must keep clean and safe. See `rules-ia`. Put the parking terms in the lease: `parking-ks-oh-ca`, `assigned-parking-space` and `parking-vehicle-rules-id`; any parking charge must be stated in the lease (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1); `edu-fees-as-rent-ia`, `edu-no-unbundled-parking-rule-ia`). Towing: a vehicle unlawfully parked on private property for more than 24 hours can be handled as an abandoned vehicle; see `edu-towing-ia` for the notice and reclaim rules. For an authorized tenant's car with expired registration, follow your lease and rules and give written notice before any tow. Iowa's disabled-parking quotas apply to public and nonresidential parking (Iowa Code § 321L.5(3)), not apartment lots; accessible spaces for residents are a fair housing and building code question (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). Cities (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others) regulate on-street parking and may regulate towing. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText:
No Iowa statute requires your lease to say anything about children, and Iowa's landlord-tenant law has no separate rule about a child joining the household during a tenancy. What applies is the Iowa Civil Rights Act's ban on familial-status discrimination. Familial status means a household where anyone under 18 lives with a parent, a legal custodian or the custodian's written designee, and it also covers a person who is pregnant or is getting legal custody of a child (Iowa Code § 216.2(11)).

You, and anyone acting for you, may not refuse to rent, set different terms, rules or services, or otherwise make housing unavailable because of familial status, and may not advertise that families with children are unwelcome (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(a)-(c)). Iowa sets no grace period or notice rule for a child born, adopted or taken into custody during the tenancy. Treat ending, or refusing to renew, a tenancy because a child has joined the household as barred by the same ban.

Exemptions: an owner-occupied building with two units; fewer than four rooms rented in a home the owner or occupant lives in; an owner-occupied building of up to four units where the owner qualifies for Iowa's homestead credit or exemption; and qualifying housing for older persons (55 and over, or 62 and over) (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(b)-(e)). The small-building exemptions never cover advertising (Iowa Code § 216.12(2)). Federal fair housing law (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604) applies separately and has different exemptions; see `edu-portfolio-thresholds-ia`.

Occupancy limits: the Act does not affect a reasonable local or state limit on how many people may occupy a dwelling (Iowa Code § 216.20(1)(a)), so you may apply your city's housing code limit (see `edu-rental-inspection-ia`). Count children and adults alike, apply one limit to everyone, and do not set a limit tighter than the code unless you have a sound reason that has nothing to do with children.

Practical steps: list every occupant, children included, in the occupants clause (`permitted-occupants`); never use wording such as "adults only" or "no kids"; don't steer families to particular units or floors; and apply pool, yard and noise rules to everyone.

In a civil rights agency hearing, a violation can bring actual damages, attorney fees and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for a first violation (Iowa Code § 216.15A(11)). For the other protected classes see `edu-fair-housing-ia`.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here, though the Civil Rights Act applies there too.

title: No Separate Ban on Protected-Class Questions
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or held rule that separately bars you from asking an applicant or tenant about a protected characteristic, or from keeping a record of one. What Iowa bars is the discrimination itself: refusing to rent, setting different terms or services, and advertising or 'in any other manner' indicating that people of a protected class are unwelcome (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(c); see also Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(a)-(b), Iowa Code § 216.8A(1)-(3)). The one express inquiry limit is for assistance and service animals: you may not ask for information that discloses a diagnosis, the severity of a disability or medical records, and where the disability or need is not obvious you may ask only for information that reasonably supports the need for that particular animal (Iowa Code § 216.8B(3), Iowa Code § 216.8B(6)(a); `edu-assistance-animals-ia`). No separate ban is not permission to ask. A question about race, color, creed, religion, sex, sexual orientation, national origin, disability or familial status that serves no lawful purpose, or a written answer kept in your file, is evidence a complainant can use to show discrimination, and a question that tells a class of applicants they are not wanted can itself be a statement the advertising ban reaches. Practical steps: ask every applicant the same questions; ask only what your written screening criteria use (income, rental history, references, the number of people who will live there); don't ask about pregnancy, plans for children, marriage or family relationships, religion, birthplace, accent or health; and if a government program makes you collect demographic data, keep it apart from the screening file and out of the decision. Age is protected in Iowa housing only as to a tenant's guests (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(d)), so confirming that an applicant is an adult who can sign a lease is ordinary. Federal fair housing law (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604) and its rules apply separately and were not read for this row. For screening generally see `edu-tenant-screening-ia`; for immigration status see `edu-no-immigration-rule-ia`; for the protected classes and exemptions see `edu-fair-housing-ia`. Code ch. 161-9).

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Iowa's Civil Rights Act gives applicants and tenants with a disability two rights you must honor. Accommodations: you must make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they are needed to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling (Iowa Code § 216.8A(3)(c)(2)). Examples: a reserved parking space near the door, a rent due date that matches when disability benefits arrive, or allowing a live-in aide. Modifications: you must allow reasonable modifications of the premises, at the tenant's expense, when they are needed for full enjoyment of the premises (Iowa Code § 216.8A(3)(c)(1)), such as grab bars, a ramp or lever handles. Where reasonable, you may condition permission for a modification on the tenant's agreement to restore the interior to its condition before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Iowa law does not require that restoration condition to appear in the lease, and it sets no special restoration deposit or escrow account. Money you take to secure restoration is a rental deposit under Iowa law, so the two-months'-rent cap and the holding and return rules apply to it (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12), Iowa Code § 562A.12; `edu-deposit-cap-ia`, `edu-deposit-holding-ia`). Federal rules may add conditions on restoration deposits and were not read for this row. The rights cover the applicant or tenant, anyone who will live in the unit, and anyone associated with them (Iowa Code § 216.8A(3)(a)-(b)). You need not rent to a person whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property (Iowa Code § 216.8A(3)(e), Iowa Code § 216.20(1)(b)). Buildings of four or more units first occupied after January 1, 1992, must also meet accessible design and construction standards: all units where there is an elevator, otherwise the ground-floor units (Iowa Code § 216.2(5), Iowa Code § 216.8A(3)(c)(3)). The owner-occupied small-building exemptions (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(b), (c) and (e)) reach these rules too, but federal law may still apply; see `edu-portfolio-thresholds-ia`. Assistance and service animals follow their own Iowa procedure: `edu-assistance-animals-ia` and the `assistance-animal-accommodation` clause. Your lease's alterations clause (`no-alterations`) already preserves modifications the law allows. Good practice: treat any request, spoken or written, as a request; answer promptly; ask for disability-related information only when the disability or the need is not obvious, and never for a diagnosis or medical records; if a request is unreasonable, discuss an alternative instead of a flat refusal; and put each modification agreement (scope of work, contractor standards, insurance, restoration) in writing for that request. A refusal can lead to a civil rights complaint with actual damages, attorney fees and civil penalties (Iowa Code § 216.15A(11)). Code ch. 161-9).

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant law applies the same way whether you rent one unit or a thousand. No Iowa statute or held rule exempts small landlords from it, or adds duties once you own more than a set number of units. The only size tests that matter for most Iowa landlords are the fair housing exemptions, and Iowa's are tied to the building you live in, not to how many properties you own. Under the Iowa Civil Rights Act the housing rules do not apply to: renting a unit in a building with no more than two units if you live in the other one; renting fewer than four rooms in a home you live in; and renting a unit in a building with no more than four units if you live in one of them and it qualifies for Iowa's homestead credit or exemption (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(b), (c), (e)). Every part of an exemption must be met: a three-unit building does not qualify under the two-unit test even if you live there, and living in a four-unit building does not qualify unless your unit also qualifies for the homestead credit or exemption. None of these exemptions covers advertising (Iowa Code § 216.12(2)). Federal fair housing law has different exemptions (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)). One is portfolio-based: a private individual who owns no more than three single-family houses and rents one without a broker or rental agent and without a discriminatory advertisement. Another covers an owner who lives in a building of up to four units. Federal advertising rules apply even then. The gap matters: Iowa has no single-family-house exemption, so an individual renting one, two or three houses without a broker may be outside federal law but is fully covered by Iowa's Act. And an owner living in a three- or four-unit building whose unit does not qualify for the Iowa homestead credit or exemption may be exempt federally but not in Iowa. Plan as if the fair housing rules apply to every rental you own. Other Iowa size tests count buildings or cities, not your portfolio: accessible design rules for newer buildings of four or more units (`edu-disability-accommodation-ia`), alarm rules for multiple-unit buildings (`edu-alarm-duties-ia`), and city housing codes and inspections (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). See also `edu-fair-housing-ia` and `edu-children-occupancy-ia`.

title: Out-of-State Owners and Iowa Agents
bodyText: Iowa does not make a nonresident owner of an ordinary house or apartment appoint an agent who lives in Iowa, and it does not stop a nonresident individual owner from suing until one is named. What Iowa requires of every landlord, resident or not: before the tenancy starts, give the tenant in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices (Iowa Code § 562A.13(1); `landlord-disclosure-ia`), and keep that information current (Iowa Code § 562A.13(2)). The address need not be in Iowa. If you skip the disclosure, whoever signed the lease for you or manages for you becomes your agent for service and for performing your duties as landlord (Iowa Code § 562A.13(3)). Being sued: a nonresident who makes a contract with an Iowa resident to be performed in Iowa, such as a lease of an Iowa home to an Iowa tenant, is treated as appointing the Iowa secretary of state to accept service in suits arising from it, with notice mailed to the nonresident (Iowa Code § 617.3(2)-(3)). Other ways to serve someone outside Iowa are in the Iowa Rules of Civil Procedure, which were not read for this row. Manufactured home communities are different: a community landlord who is not an Iowa resident, or is a corporation not authorized to do business in Iowa, must file a written designation of an Iowa agent for service with the secretary of state (Iowa Code § 562B.6(2)). Communities are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B and not covered further here. Owning through a company: an out-of-state LLC or corporation doing business in Iowa must register with the secretary of state and name a registered agent in Iowa (owning and maintaining property alone is not doing business, Iowa Code § 489.905(1)(j), Iowa Code § 490.1505(1)(j); whether renting it out is, the statutes don't say, so register to be safe), and it cannot maintain a suit in an Iowa court, an eviction included, until it registers; its leases stay valid and it can still defend a suit (Iowa Code § 489.902, Iowa Code § 489.903(1), Iowa Code § 490.1502, Iowa Code § 490.1503(1)). See `edu-entity-landlord-representation-ia`. Trade names: an individual who rents under a business name other than the owners' own surnames must first record a verified statement with the county recorder (Iowa Code § 547.1). Breaking that rule is a misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 547.4), but Iowa's trade-name chapter does not bar a suit. Taxes and reporting: Iowa's withholding law treats anyone who pays, or controls payment of, taxable Iowa income to a nonresident as a withholding agent, and requires withholding from a nonresident's Iowa-taxable income that is not otherwise subject to withholding (Iowa Code § 422.16(1), Iowa Code § 422.16(2)(b)), unless the nonresident has a Department of Revenue certificate after paying estimated tax (Iowa Code § 422.17). How the department applies this to rent that a tenant or property manager pays to a nonresident owner is set by department rules not read for this row, so get tax advice. A person or agent in Iowa who pays rent to an individual may also have to file an Iowa information return (Iowa Code § 422.15(1)). Foreign persons who hold agricultural land have their own reporting duties (`edu-foreign-ownership-ia`). Cities: some cities with rental registration or inspection programs (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames) may ask for a local contact; check the city's rules (`edu-landlord-registration-ia`). Practical steps for an out-of-state owner: hire or name an Iowa manager or agent, put that person's name and address in the lease disclosure, make sure mail sent there reaches you, and get tax advice on Iowa withholding and filing.

title: Police Requests and Reporting Duties
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or held rule that makes you join a crime-free housing program, sign a police cooperation agreement, report a tenant's suspected crimes to the police, or hand over tenant records just because an officer asks. Any local crime-free or nuisance-property program (for example in Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids or Ames) is a matter of local ordinance, not covered here. What Iowa law does say: Court-ordered surveillance help. When a court order for a wiretap, pen register or trap-and-trace device directs it, a landlord must give law enforcement the information, facilities and technical help needed, with as little disruption to the tenant as possible. You are paid reasonable expenses, and good-faith reliance on the order is a complete defense (Iowa Code § 808B.5(5), Iowa Code § 808B.13). Deaths and human remains. Any person present at a death that affects the public interest, which includes violent, unexpected or unexplained deaths, must report it to the county or state medical examiner (Iowa Code § 331.802(1), (3)). Anyone who discovers human remains must notify the medical examiner or a law enforcement agency as soon as reasonably possible, and failing to do so is a serious misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 523I.316(6)). If you or your staff find a tenant dead in a unit, call 911 and leave the scene alone. Police entry. Your own right to enter is limited to the tenant's consent, emergencies, court orders, the entries Iowa Code § 562A.28 and Iowa Code § 562A.29 allow, and abandonment or surrender (Iowa Code § 562A.19). Whether your consent lets police search a tenant's home is a question of constitutional search law (Iowa Const. art. I, § 8) and case law not searched here. The safe course: don't admit police to an occupied unit without the tenant's consent, a warrant or a genuine emergency unless your lawyer agrees. Calls for help. You may not limit or penalize a tenant's calls for police or emergency help (`edu-emergency-assistance-ia`). Crime at the property. Iowa's three-day termination for a clear and present danger, and the tenant's exemption where the tenant reported the activity to law enforcement or the county attorney, are covered in `edu-clear-present-danger-ia` and the `criminal-activity-ia` clause; crime-free addenda in `edu-no-drug-free-addendum-ia`; nuisance exposure in `edu-nuisance-ia`. A tenant in Iowa's address confidentiality program may ask you to protect the address (`edu-dv-confidentiality-ia`). Abuse reporting duties under Iowa law bind listed professionals, not landlords as such. Good practice for police requests: ask to see the warrant, subpoena or court order; give only what it covers; keep a record of what you gave and when; and call a lawyer before answering a broad request for tenant files.

title: Habitability Rules Iowa Does Not Have
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Iowa counterpart. (1) No cooling duty. Iowa does not require you to supply air conditioning or keep a unit below a maximum temperature. If you do supply air conditioning, you must keep it in good and safe working order (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)), and the tenant must use it reasonably (Iowa Code § 562A.17(5)). Heat and hot water are required (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6); `edu-heating-ia`). For a tenant's own window or portable unit see `edu-no-portable-cooling-rule-ia`. (2) No duty to provide other housing while repairs are made (`edu-no-alt-housing-duty-ia`). (3) No right for either side to end the lease because a repair costs too much (`edu-no-repair-cost-termination-ia`). (4) No statutory presumption of uninhabitability and no habitability statement to give tenants (`edu-no-habitability-presumption-ia`, `edu-no-habitability-statement-ia`). (5) No water heater temperature rule (`edu-no-water-heater-temperature-rule-ia`), no window guard, radiator cover or balcony inspection rule (`edu-no-window-guard-rule-ia`, `edu-no-radiator-cover-rule-ia`, `edu-no-balcony-inspection-rule-ia`), and no duty to supply a stove or refrigerator (`edu-no-stove-refrigerator-duty-ia`). (6) No mold or bed bug disclosure rule (`edu-no-mold-disclosure-ia`, `edu-no-bed-bug-rule-ia`) and no lock or security device standard (`edu-no-security-device-rule-ia`). What Iowa does require: comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, and keep the premises fit and habitable (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a); `edu-habitability-ia`). These duties cannot be waived (except in a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area, Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and only limited repair and maintenance work can be shifted to a tenant, in good faith and in writing (`edu-habitability-waiver-ia`, `edu-maintenance-duty-shift-ia`). The tenant's remedies are in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia` and `edu-landlord-breach-remedy-ia`. City housing codes often add duties, and larger cities inspect rentals (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`), so check the city's code.

title: Other Rules Iowa Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states do not exist in Iowa. (1) No ban on a payment-method fee. No Iowa statute bars or caps a convenience or card fee for paying rent a particular way. Any fee must be in the lease, and it cannot be a disguised penalty or unconscionable (`acceptable-payment-methods`, `edu-no-fee-transparency-rule-ia`, `edu-unconscionability-ia`). (2) No special right to end a tenancy because the rental application was false. Make the application part of the lease (`rental-application-accuracy`), so a material falsehood is a material noncompliance handled through the usual notice steps (Iowa Code § 562A.27(1); `edu-noncompliance-cure-ia`). (3) No statute bars renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period (`edu-no-double-letting-rule-ia`). (4) No smoke or carbon monoxide alarm shield: Iowa's alarm statute does not make a missing or broken alarm inadmissible as evidence of negligence, and does not limit what an insurer may do (Iowa Code § 10A.518; `edu-alarm-duties-ia`). (5) No Iowa rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs (`edu-tenant-bankruptcy-ia`). (6) No lease type-size, initialing or plain-language rule, and no general translation duty (`edu-no-lease-type-size-ia`, `edu-no-lease-initials-requirement-ia`, `edu-no-plain-language-rule-ia`, `edu-translation-duty-ia`). (7) No tenant guest-rights statute, key-control law or recycling notice rule (`edu-no-guest-rights-statute-ia`, `edu-no-key-control-policy-ia`, `edu-no-recycling-notice-ia`). For out-of-state owners, entity landlords, trade names, service of court papers and reporting duties that bind everyone, see `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ia`.

title: Checked Across the Whole Iowa Code
bodyText: Iowa's whole statute book was searched, not only the landlord-tenant chapters, for things landlords ask about. (1) No special squatter-removal procedure. Remove an unauthorized occupant through a forcible entry and detainer action, and use the criminal trespass law (`edu-no-squatter-statute-ia`). (2) No duty to give a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash, and no general statute requiring a receipt for cash. Give one anyway and keep a ledger; in a deposit dispute you carry the burden of proof (`edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-ia`). (3) No state rule makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of getting a possession judgment. Rental certification is local (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), and whether a city's rules affect an eviction there is not covered here (`edu-landlord-registration-ia`). State law does stop a city or county from revoking or refusing to renew a rental certificate because someone was a victim of abuse or crime, or called for police or emergency help for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency where the caller reasonably believed help was necessary or it was actually needed (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(2)(a)-(c)). General business and other laws that reach landlords: (4) An out-of-state LLC or corporation cannot maintain a suit in an Iowa court, an eviction included, until it registers with the secretary of state; its leases stay valid and it can still defend (Iowa Code § 489.902(2)-(3), Iowa Code § 490.1502(2)-(3)). Whether renting homes counts as doing business in Iowa is a case-law question, so register before you file (`edu-entity-landlord-representation-ia`). (5) An individual renting under a business name other than the owners' surnames must record a verified statement with the county recorder (Iowa Code § 547.1). Each day of violation is a separate misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 547.4, Iowa Code § 547.5), but the trade-name chapter does not bar a suit. (6) Service on an owner who lives out of state: the lease disclosure of an owner or agent for service (Iowa Code § 562A.13(1)(b)), and service through the Iowa secretary of state on a nonresident who contracts with an Iowa resident (Iowa Code § 617.3(2)). See `edu-nonresident-owner-agent-ia`. (7) Reporting duties that bind everyone, landlords included: report a death that affects the public interest if you are present (Iowa Code § 331.802(1)) and human remains you discover (Iowa Code § 523I.316(6)); see `edu-law-enforcement-cooperation-ia`. A person or agent in Iowa who pays rent to an individual may owe an Iowa information return (Iowa Code § 422.15(1)), and Iowa's withholding law reaches taxable Iowa income paid to nonresidents (Iowa Code § 422.16(2)(b)); see `edu-nonresident-owner-agent-ia`.

title: No Iowa Tenant Solar Right
bodyText:
Iowa gives tenants no right to install solar panels or plug-in (balcony) solar devices, and no Iowa statute limits what your lease may say about them. Iowa's solar access chapter lets owners obtain solar access easements, and lets a city or county bar unreasonable restrictions on solar collectors in deeds for new subdivisions (Iowa Code § 564A.8); it does not reach leases.

Utility safety rules matter more. A solar device that feeds power into the building's wiring is likely to count as a distributed generation facility under Iowa utility law. The Iowa Utilities Commission must have safety rules for those connections, including a disconnection device next to the meter and notice to the local fire department, and a utility may deny or disconnect service to a person who does not comply (Iowa Code § 476.58(1)-(2)). If the electric account is in your name, an unapproved tenant device could put your service at risk.

You may require your written consent and any utility approval before a tenant installs or connects a solar, battery or other generating device, and require removal and repair at move-out; the optional `portable-solar-mo` clause does this. A tenant with a disability may still ask for a reasonable modification (`edu-disability-accommodation-ia`). Cities may have their own building or electrical permit rules (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), not covered here.

title: No Iowa Rule on Portable Cooling Devices
bodyText:
Iowa gives tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no Iowa statute limits what your lease may say about cooling devices. Iowa also has no statute voiding restrictions on cooling equipment in leases, deeds or community rules.

Iowa does not make you supply air conditioning. If you do supply it, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and that duty cannot be waived in the lease except for a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4); Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a); `edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-ia`).

So list in the lease exactly what cooling equipment you supply. You may let tenants use plug-in portable units and fans, and require your consent before a window or through-the-wall unit is installed. Window units can fall, block an escape window or overload a circuit, so set installation conditions and require removal and repair at move-out; the optional `portable-cooling-device-ia` clause does this.

A tenant with a disability may ask for a cooling device as a reasonable accommodation or modification (`edu-disability-accommodation-ia`).

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. City housing codes may add rules (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), not covered here.

title: EV Charging: Iowa Tax, License and Utility Rules
bodyText:
Iowa gives tenants no right to install an electric vehicle charger (`edu-no-ev-charging-rule-ia`). If you allow one, the optional `ev-charger-installation-ia` clause sets consent, licensed installation, insurance, electricity reimbursement and what happens at move-out.

Rules that apply when charging is provided:

Tax and license. Iowa taxes electric fuel at 2.6 cents per kilowatt hour when it is delivered into a vehicle at a location other than a residence, and no one may sell or dispense electric fuel at a location other than a residence without a Department of Revenue license for that location; licensed charging stations are inspected for accuracy every two years (Iowa Code § 452A.41(1), (4), Iowa Code § 452A.42(1), (3); 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1139, § 26). A residence is the place where a person lives, permanently or temporarily (Iowa Code § 452A.40(6); subsection 7 in the 2027 Code after 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1139, § 30 added a definition). A charger at a single-family rental's own garage or driveway serves the tenant's residence. Whether a charger in a shared apartment lot is at a residence is not settled by any statute or held rule read here, so ask the Department of Revenue before you sell charging to tenants or the public.

Utility status. A commercial or public charging station that takes all its power from the local electric utility is not a public utility (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.20(1)), but it must follow the tax and other laws that apply (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.20(4)).

Billing a tenant for charging electricity. In a master-metered building, what you collect for electricity cannot exceed the utility's bill for the same period (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(c); `edu-electric-submetering-ia`), and if a tenant pays you for utilities you must explain the rates and charges before the lease is signed (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`).

Money you hold to secure the tenant's charger obligations counts toward the two months' rent deposit limit (Iowa Code § 562A.12(1)). Condominium or association rules may also apply (`edu-hoa-ia`). Cities set electrical permit rules (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), not covered here.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking Areas
bodyText: Iowa has no rule on electric vehicle chargers in shared parking areas. No Iowa statute gives a tenant a right to put a charger in a lot or garage other tenants use, sets a fee for reserving the space, or says who pays for damage to a shared-area charger. Your lease decides. If you allow a charger in a shared area, use the optional `ev-charger-installation-ia` clause and name the specific space there; assign that space to the tenant in the lease (`assigned-parking-space`), set any parking charge as part of the rent or a stated fee, and say who is responsible for damage to the charger and the surrounding property, including after the tenant moves out. If you sell charging from a shared charger, Iowa's electric fuel tax and license rules may apply, and whether a shared apartment lot counts as a residence is unsettled (`edu-ev-charging-requirements-ia`). In a condominium or other association, the association's rules on common areas control (`edu-hoa-ia`, `hoa-compliance`).

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends. No Iowa law says the charger stays the tenant's property, gives the tenant a right to remove or sell it, or makes you buy it. Decide it in the lease. The optional `ev-charger-installation-ia` clause makes you choose: the tenant removes the charger and repairs any damage, or leaves it and it becomes yours. If the lease is silent, whether a hard-wired charger has become part of the building is a question of fixture law, which comes from case law not searched here, so don't leave it silent. You may use the deposit for the cost of restoring the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted, with a written statement of the reasons within 30 days after the tenancy ends and you receive the tenant's mailing address (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(2); `security-deposit-use-ia`, `security-deposit-return-ia`). If the tenant leaves a removable charger behind, follow the lease's abandoned-property procedure (`abandoned-property-ia`).

title: No Iowa Rule on Screening Apartment Staff
bodyText: Iowa has no rule on screening apartment employees. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you, or a property manager, to run criminal background checks on leasing staff, maintenance workers or anyone who holds master keys, whatever the size of the building, and none bars you from doing so. Screening is still wise. You answer for how your staff use entry: entry needs the tenant's consent (which may not be unreasonably withheld), at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency or where impracticable, and reasonable times, and abuse of access can cost you an injunction or the tenant's damages and attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.19, Iowa Code § 562A.35(2); `edu-landlord-entry-ia`, `edu-no-key-control-policy-ia`). How you screen is governed by employment and consumer-report law, which this library does not cover. Federal law sets rules for background reports from a screening company, and cities may have their own rules (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), not covered here. If someone other than your own regular employee manages or rents your units for pay, that person generally needs an Iowa real estate license (`edu-landlord-registration-ia`).

title: Campaign Signs and Political Activity at Rentals
bodyText: Iowa has no statute giving candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators a right to enter apartment buildings or other rental property, and none requiring you to let tenants use common areas for political meetings. Two Iowa laws do touch political activity at rentals. Campaign signs. Iowa's campaign law allows campaign signs, with the permission of the property owner or the lessee, on property leased for residential purposes, including apartments, condominiums, college housing and houses, but only on leased space the tenant actually occupies (Iowa Code § 68A.406(1)(c)). No one may place a campaign sign on property without the owner's or the lessee's permission (Iowa Code § 68A.406(2)(a)(3)). The statute does not say whether a lease may forbid a tenant's signs, and no case law was searched. The cautious course: don't ban campaign signs in the tenant's own leased space (a window, or the yard of a rented house); neutral limits on size, number, attachment and removal at move-out, applied to every sign whatever its message, carry less risk; signs on common areas and building exteriors are yours to allow or refuse. Large signs and signs fixed to buildings need a paid-for-by statement, which is the campaign's duty (Iowa Code § 68A.406(3)). Cities also regulate signs (for example Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames), not covered here. Tenant organizing. You may not retaliate by raising rent, cutting services or bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization (Iowa Code § 562A.36(1)(c); `edu-retaliation-ia`). Political views are not a protected class under Iowa's fair housing law, but creed and religion are (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(a); `edu-fair-housing-ia`, `edu-no-religious-display-rule-ia`). Put any sign or common-area rule in your written rules and apply it evenly (`rules-ia`).

title: Unlawful Use Does Not Void an Iowa Lease
bodyText: No Iowa statute makes a lease void, or lets you treat it as annulled, just because the tenant uses the home for an unlawful purpose. You still have to end the tenancy through Iowa's notice and court process. But Iowa law does push you to act: Prostitution. If you know, or have reason to know, that a tenant is using the property for prostitution and you do not immediately end the tenancy or effectively stop the practice, you commit a serious misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 725.4). Nuisance. Anyone who owns or leases a building used for prostitution or unlawful gambling is guilty of a nuisance; the court can order the building's contents sold and the building closed against any use for a year (Iowa Code § 99.1A(1), Iowa Code § 99.21; `edu-nuisance-ia`). How to end it. For a clear and present danger, such as threatened violence, illegal weapons or illegal drugs, you may use a single three-day notice (Iowa Code § 562A.27A; `edu-clear-present-danger-ia`). Other unlawful use is a material noncompliance handled with the seven-day notice (Iowa Code § 562A.27(1); `edu-noncompliance-cure-ia`). Never lock the tenant out (`edu-self-help-eviction-ia`). Your lease should limit use to a private residence and bar criminal activity (`residential-use-only`, `criminal-activity-ia`); crime-free addenda are covered in `edu-no-drug-free-addendum-ia`.

title: No Iowa Religious Display Right
bodyText: Iowa has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on the door frame, a wreath, a cross or a prayer flag, or to fly a flag, and none limiting what a lease may say about displays. What does apply is the Iowa Civil Rights Act. You may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or in services or facilities, because of a tenant's creed, religion, race, color or national origin (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(b)), and the religion or national origin of a tenant's guests is protected too (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(d)). So a rule that singles out religious or cultural items, or that you enforce against one faith or culture but not others, invites a civil rights complaint. A neutral rule, for example on what may be attached to doors, hallways or building exteriors, or a fire-safety rule on hallway decorations, applied the same way to everyone, carries much less risk. Small door-frame items such as a mezuzah cause little damage; allowing them avoids disputes. Put any display rule in your written rules and apply it evenly (`rules-ia`). Campaign signs are covered in `edu-political-access-ia`; association rules in a condominium or planned community also bind tenants (`edu-hoa-ia`). Religious institutions may set religious qualifications in limited cases (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(a)). Federal fair housing law applies separately, not covered here.

title: No Work Card for Staff in 55-Plus Housing
bodyText: Iowa has no work card, permit, registration or required background check for maintenance, housekeeping or management staff in housing for people 55 or older, or in any other rental housing. Screening your staff is your own policy. What Iowa does have on senior housing is a fair housing exemption. The Iowa Civil Rights Act's housing sections do not apply to 'Discrimination on the basis of familial status involving dwellings provided under any state or federal program specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons ... and housing for older persons' (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(d)). Housing for older persons means housing intended 'For eighty percent occupancy by at least one person fifty-five years of age or older per unit' (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(d)(1)), with significant facilities and services designed for older residents and published policies showing that intent, or housing 'For and occupied solely by persons sixty-two years of age or older' (Iowa Code § 216.12(1)(d)(2)). The Iowa Civil Rights Commission's rule reads the exemption as reaching familial status only (Iowa Admin. Code r. 161-9.3): a 55-plus building may turn away households with children, but every other protected class still applies. See `edu-fair-housing-ia` and `edu-children-occupancy-ia`. Federal fair housing law has its own older-persons exemption with its own tests; not covered here. If your building also delivers care, it may stop being plain rental housing. Assisted living means 'provision of housing with services which may include but are not limited to health-related care, personal care, and assistance with instrumental activities of daily living to three or more tenants' (Iowa Code § 231C.2(2)), and a certified assisted living program or elder group home must run abuse registry and criminal record checks on an employee who 'provides direct services to consumers' (Iowa Code § 135C.33(5)(a)(5)); see also Iowa Code § 135C.33(5)(a)(4). A business that provides care may also ask the state for a national fingerprint check of staff who have access to the elderly (Iowa Code § 692C.1(2)); that check is optional. Ordinary 55-plus apartments without care services are not covered by either. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Renting to Students in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no student-housing licence, registration or special lease regime. If you rent an apartment or house to students, Iowa's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to you exactly as it does to any other tenant: the same deposit, notice, repair and eviction rules. Iowa's only student-housing rule is a scope line. The Act does not govern 'Residence at an institution, public or private, if incidental to detention or the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar service' (Iowa Code § 562A.5(1)), or 'Occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the portion of a structure operated for the benefit of the organization' (Iowa Code § 562A.5(3)). Both exclusions fail if the arrangement was 'created to avoid the application of this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.5). So a college residence hall, where living there goes with being enrolled, sits outside the Act, and fraternity and sorority houses do too. A privately owned building that rents to students on ordinary leases is not housing incidental to an educational service, and the Act applies in full, even if it markets itself as student housing or is near campus. Whether a private building master-leased to or run for a college crosses the line turns on the facts and on case law; if you are in that position, take advice and assume the Act applies. The Board of Regents runs the state university dormitories and sets their rents (Iowa Code § 262.35). See `edu-scope-ia`. Student status is not a protected class under Iowa's fair housing law (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(a)), so you may choose whether to rent to students, but you must not use student status as a stand-in for familial status, disability or any other protected class (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). Roommate groups: a city may not, after January 1, 2018, 'adopt or enforce any regulation or restriction related to the occupancy of residential rental property that is based upon the existence of familial or nonfamilial relationships between the occupants of such rental property' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(b)), so a city cannot cap the number of unrelated students sharing a rental; it may still set space-based occupancy limits in its housing code (`edu-no-single-family-zone-lease-limit-ia`, `edu-rental-inspection-ia`). Iowa City, Ames, Cedar Falls and other college towns run their own rental codes and inspection programs; check yours. Lease practice for student renters: list every occupant (`permitted-occupants`), decide whether roommates are jointly liable (`joint-liability`), and use a guarantor if you want one (`edu-guarantor-renewal-ia`). Iowa sets no academic-year term limit (`edu-lease-term-limitation-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Sharing Tenant Information in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no statute that bars a landlord from sharing what it knows about a tenant, former tenant or applicant, and none sets a consent rule for doing so. No Iowa law lists tenant information as confidential in your hands. Three narrower rules can still apply. First, address confidentiality. If a tenant tells you in writing that they are in the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program for victims, you must accept their designated address (Iowa Code § 9E.5(1)), must not knowingly disclose their real address once notified on the Secretary of State's form, except to someone who lives, works or goes to school there or with the tenant's written consent (Iowa Code § 9E.5(5)), and 'shall not allow the display of the program participant's name at an address otherwise protected under this chapter' (Iowa Code § 9E.7(4)). See `edu-dv-confidentiality-ia`. Second, Iowa's consumer data protection law.
