It reaches only a business that in a calendar year 'Controls or processes personal data of at least one hundred thousand consumers' (Iowa Code § 715D.2(1)(a)), or at least twenty-five thousand consumers while earning over half its revenue from selling personal data (Iowa Code § 715D.2(1)(b)). A very large management company could cross that line; most landlords will not. A covered business must protect the data, give a privacy notice listing the categories of data it shares and with whom, and honor consumers' rights, including the right to opt out of the sale of personal data (Iowa Code § 715D.3, Iowa Code § 715D.4). A lease clause cannot trade those rights away: 'Any provision of a contract or agreement that purports to waive or limit in any way consumer rights pursuant to section 715D.3 shall be deemed contrary to public policy and shall be void and unenforceable' (Iowa Code § 715D.4(4)). Only the attorney general enforces the chapter (Iowa Code § 715D.8(1)). Third, data breaches. If you keep a tenant's name with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or bank or card numbers with their access codes in computer form and someone gets them without authorization, Iowa's breach law makes you notify the tenant (Iowa Code § 715C.2(1)); see `edu-tenant-records-ia`. Practical course: share tenant information only for a business reason the tenant would expect (screening, collections, utilities, repairs, a lawful court or police request, a reference the tenant asked for), don't sell it, and get the tenant's written consent for anything else. Fair credit reporting rules for screening reports are federal; see `edu-tenant-screening-ia` and `edu-fcra-adverse-action-notice`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays at Iowa Rentals
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute that gives tenants a right to display a flag, sign or religious item, and none that bars a landlord or an association from limiting displays.

One election-law rule matters. Iowa's campaign law says 'Campaign signs may be placed with the permission of the property owner or lessee' (Iowa Code § 68A.406(1)) on, among other places, 'Property leased for residential purposes including but not limited to apartments, condominiums, college housing facilities, and houses if placed only on leased property space that is actually occupied' (Iowa Code § 68A.406(1)(c)). A campaign sign must not go up 'On any property without the permission of the property owner or lessee' (Iowa Code § 68A.406(2)(a)(3)).

Read together, your tenant may lawfully put a campaign sign on the part of the property the tenant actually occupies, such as the unit's window or a house's yard, without asking you, and may not put one on common areas or other parts of the building. Whether a lease clause or rule can take away the tenant's permission for the occupied space is not settled by statute. The cautious course is to allow campaign signs in the tenant's own occupied space and regulate only size, safety and placement there, and to keep common areas sign-free for everyone.

Flags and other signs: no Iowa statute protects a tenant's display of the United States flag or any other flag at a rental. Iowa's flag statutes cover public buildings, schools, state proclamations and flag desecration, not private rentals. Federal law protects flag display by condominium and association members; not covered here.

Religious items: Iowa's fair housing law bars different terms, conditions or privileges because of religion (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(b)), so a rule that removes one faith's door decoration but leaves another's is unlawful; a neutral rule applied to every display is not. See `edu-fair-housing-ia`, `edu-political-access-ia` and `edu-no-religious-display-rule-ia`.

Your own display rules: you may put limits on signs, flags and exterior decorations in the lease or in written rules, as long as each rule is reasonable, applies to all tenants fairly and, if adopted after move-in, does not work a substantial change in the bargain (Iowa Code § 562A.18; `rules-ia`). Make the rule content-neutral: limit size, number, location, attachment method and damage, not message. Association rules also bind your tenant where your lease or the declaration makes them; see `hoa-compliance` and `edu-hoa-ia`.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Housing Your Employees in Iowa
bodyText: If you rent a unit to someone who also works for you, under an ordinary lease that does not depend on the job, Iowa's landlord-tenant act applies to that tenancy in full. The act does not govern 'Occupancy by an employee of a landlord whose right to occupancy is conditional upon employment in and about the premises' (Iowa Code § 562A.5(5)), such as a resident manager, caretaker or maintenance worker housed on site as part of the job, unless the arrangement was 'created to avoid the application of this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.5). See `edu-scope-ia`. Iowa has no statute that requires a signed disclosure of the occupancy and vacating terms for employee housing, sets a move-out period when the job ends, or makes you offer a lease to a former employee. Iowa's eviction statute does not name employees or caretakers: it reaches a person who entered by force or stealth, a lessee holding over or holding contrary to the lease, nonpayment of rent and a few other cases (Iowa Code § 648.1). Whether a former employee whose housing was tied to the job is a lessee, a tenant at will entitled to thirty days' written notice (Iowa Code § 562.4; `edu-tenancy-at-will-ia`), or something else is a case-law question. The cautious course: put the housing terms in a separate signed written agreement that says the occupancy ends with the job and how much time the employee then has to move out; give at least thirty days' written notice when the job ends; and if the person does not leave, go to court rather than changing locks or removing belongings (`edu-self-help-eviction-ia`, `edu-eviction-process-ia`). Rent taken out of pay: an employer may not withhold wages unless required or permitted by law or 'The employer has written authorization from the employee to so deduct for any lawful purpose accruing to the benefit of the employee' (Iowa Code § 91A.5(1)(b)), so get that written authorization before deducting rent. Licensing: a resident manager who lives in the building and leases units as part of the job does not need a real estate license (Iowa Code § 543B.7(8)). Farm and seasonal workers: housing for seven or more migrant agricultural workers is a migrant labor camp, which needs a state permit (Iowa Code § 138.1(8), Iowa Code § 138.2) and must meet the chapter's sanitation and repair standards. A rental charge or wage deduction for camp housing is barred 'unless such migrant is fully informed of all such rental charges or deductions to be made prior to the time the migrant contracts for employment as an agricultural or migrant worker' (Iowa Code § 138.17). Iowa has no filing rule for guest-worker rent agreements. Federal law may add duties for agricultural and guest-worker housing; not covered here. A farm home rented with farmland is also outside the act where the premises are used primarily for agricultural purposes (Iowa Code § 562A.5(7)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: Rent ledgers: Iowa has no statute that makes you keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a statement of account or payment history on request, or attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice, and none sets how long to keep tenant records. Keep a ledger anyway. In a deposit dispute 'the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, the reason for withholding all or any portion of the rental deposit shall be on the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)), and a clear payment record supports any rent notice or eviction (`edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-ia`, `security-deposit-return-ia`, `edu-nonpayment-notice-ia`). A licensed broker who manages property owes trust-account records and accountings to the owner under the real estate commission's rules (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-2013.1, Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-2015.1), not a ledger to the tenant. Keep records once a complaint arrives: when a civil rights complaint has been served on you, you 'shall preserve all records relevant to the investigation until the complaint is finally adjudicated' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 161-3.6(1)), including applications and records about other applicants, and a judge may infer that destroyed evidence was adverse to you (Iowa Admin. Code r. 161-3.6(2)). Applicant and tenant data: Iowa's data-breach law reaches landlords. 'Personal information' means a person's name with a Social Security number, a driver's license or other government ID number, a financial account or card number together with the code that gives access to the account, or biometric data (Iowa Code § 715C.1(11)(a)), and the law covers paper copies printed from computer files (Iowa Code § 715C.1(1)). If that data, held in your business, is acquired without authorization, you must notify each affected Iowan 'in the most expeditious manner possible and without unreasonable delay' (Iowa Code § 715C.2(1)), say what happened and what was taken (Iowa Code § 715C.2(5)), and, if more than five hundred Iowans must be told, notify the attorney general's consumer protection division in writing within five business days after notifying them (Iowa Code § 715C.2(8)). You may skip notice only after an investigation or consultation with law enforcement shows no reasonable likelihood of financial harm, documented in writing and kept for five years (Iowa Code § 715C.2(6)). A violation is an unlawful practice the attorney general enforces (Iowa Code § 715C.2(9)). Iowa does not require an ordinary landlord to have a written information security program. Two exceptions: a business large enough to fall under Iowa's consumer data protection law must 'adopt and implement reasonable administrative, technical, and physical data security practices' (Iowa Code § 715D.4(1)); see `edu-no-tenant-information-statute-ia` for its thresholds. And any business may choose to keep a written cybersecurity program conforming to a recognized framework, which gives it an affirmative defense if sued in tort after a breach (Iowa Code § 554G.2(1), Iowa Code § 554G.2(4)). Good practice: collect Social Security and bank numbers only when you need them for screening, keep them encrypted or locked away, limit who can see them, and shred paper copies before disposal. Federal rules on screening reports and their disposal may also apply; not covered here. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Tenant Organizing in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa protects tenant organizing through its anti-retaliation rule. You may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction after the tenant 'has organized or become a member of a' (Iowa Code § 562A.36(1)(c)) tenants' union or similar organization. If you do, the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees and has a defense to your possession action (Iowa Code § 562A.36(2)). The one-year presumption of retaliation in the same subsection is triggered by a good-faith complaint, not by organizing, so a tenant claiming retaliation for organizing must prove the link without that presumption. You may still bring a possession action if the tenant is behind on rent or in the other cases listed in Iowa Code § 562A.36(3). See `edu-retaliation-ia`. Iowa law gives apartment and house tenants no further organizing rights: no statute lets them meet in your common rooms, distribute literature door to door, or bring in organizers, and none bars you from applying neutral rules on common-area use, solicitation and guests (`common-area-use`, `rules-ia`). Apply those rules the same way to organizing as to any other activity, and never enforce them more strictly against tenants who organize, since selective enforcement can itself be retaliation. Manufactured home community lots are different: there a landlord may not 'Prohibit meetings between tenants in the manufactured home community or mobile home park relating to mobile home living and affairs in the manufactured home community or park community or recreational hall if such meetings are held at reasonable hours and when the facility is not otherwise in use' (Iowa Code § 562B.19(3)(f)); those lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered further here. Federal rules for subsidized housing may give tenant organizations more rights; not covered here.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant in Iowa
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Iowa property law does not use; the word appears nowhere in Iowa's statutes, Constitution or the held rules. Iowa's counterpart is the life estate, for example a surviving spouse who elects a life estate in the homestead (Iowa Code § 633.240) while the children hold the remainder. Iowa has a statute on exactly what happens to a lease you sign as a life tenant when your life estate ends. For a home that is not a farm: 'Upon the termination of a life estate, a tenancy granted by the life tenant which is not a farm tenancy shall continue until one of the following first occurs' (Iowa Code § 562.9): the end date already agreed for the tenancy; for a tenant at will, the thirty-day notice period (Iowa Code § 562.4); for a tenancy of less than one year, 'sixty days after the end of the month in which the life estate terminated' (Iowa Code § 562.9(3)); and for a tenancy of a year or more, 'one year after the end of the month in which the life estate terminated' (Iowa Code § 562.9(4)). Which item fits a month-to-month tenancy under the landlord-tenant act is not spelled out, so a successor ending one should allow at least sixty days after the end of that month and also give the act's written notice (`periodic-tenancy-notice-ia`, `edu-tenancy-at-will-ia`). While the tenancy continues, the holder of the next interest is entitled to 'a rental amount equal to the prevailing fair market rental amount in the area' (Iowa Code § 562.10), and either side may ask the district court to set it. Farm tenancies have their own rule (Iowa Code § 562.8). Making the lease run its full term: the continuation rules give way 'if the lease is binding upon the holder of the successor interest by the provision of a trust or by specific commitment of the holder of the successor interest' (Iowa Code § 562.9(4)). If you are a life tenant and want your tenant protected for the whole term, get the remainder holders (or the trustee) to sign a written commitment to be bound by the lease. That is their decision, not a term you can put in the lease alone. Rent at death: your executor may recover 'the proportion of rent which had accrued at the time of the death of such life tenant' (Iowa Code § 562.1), and under the landlord-tenant act rent is apportionable day to day unless otherwise agreed (Iowa Code § 562A.9(3)). Practical course: tell the tenant in writing, before signing, that you hold the property for life and what happens when your interest ends; keep the term within what you can deliver or get the remainder holders' commitment; and remember that every duty of the landlord-tenant act still applies to you as landlord. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa gives private landlords no tax credit, fee waiver, guarantee fund or other incentive for renting to veterans, and sets no veteran preference in private rental housing. Veteran or military status is also not a protected class in Iowa housing: the fair housing ban covers race, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability and familial status (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(a)). Many veteran applicants are still protected on another ground, most often disability (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). State money can help a veteran tenant pay you. The state veterans trust fund may pay 'Rental housing assistance for veterans who meet the definition of homeless, as set out in 42 U.S.C. §11302, for payment of rental application fees needed for obtaining rental housing' (Iowa Code § 35A.13(8)(n)), one-time homelessness prevention help of up to one thousand dollars (Iowa Code § 35A.13(8)(o)), and emergency temporary housing assistance (Iowa Code § 35A.13(8)(j)). Each county may also pay for 'shelter, utilities' (Iowa Code § 35B.14(1)) for indigent veterans and their families through its county commission of veteran affairs. These payments go through the veteran's application, not a landlord program; accept them like any other rent payment. Iowa also offers home-purchase help for military members (Iowa Code § 16.54), which does not reach rentals. Active-duty tenants have Iowa lease-termination and nonpayment protections; see `edu-servicemember-ia`. Federal law adds more; not covered here. Voluntary veteran discounts: no Iowa law bars you from offering veterans a rent concession, waived fee or other benefit. If you do, put it in the lease as a credit against full rent (`rent-concession-ia`, `edu-rent-concession-ia`), offer it to every eligible veteran on the same terms, accept a simple proof of service, and don't ask about disability, medical history or the character of discharge.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires a residential lease to be written in plain language, to pass a readability test, or to be divided into captioned sections. The readable-form rules Iowa does have govern other documents: rent-to-own agreements for household goods (Iowa Code § 537.3606), continuing care and senior living contracts, which must be 'written in nontechnical language easily understood by a lay person' (Iowa Code § 523D.6), and some service, funeral, cemetery and loan contracts. Write clearly anyway. A court may refuse to enforce a lease term that was unconscionable when made, or limit it (Iowa Code § 562A.7; see `edu-unconscionability-ia`), and deceptive practices in leasing can draw a consumer fraud claim (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Use headings, define each term once, and keep each subject in its own section.

title: No Front-Page Consumer Statement Rule
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires a residential lease to carry a front-page statement listing the terms that protect you or the rights the tenant gives up, and none sets a readability test, offers Attorney General preapproval of a lease form, or turns on a dollar threshold. Iowa takes a different route: it bars certain terms outright. A lease may not have the tenant 'waive or to forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), confess judgment, pay your attorney fees, or excuse or indemnify you for your own legal liability, and a barred term 'is unenforceable' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Willfully using a lease you know contains one can cost you the tenant's actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`, `edu-nonwaivable-rights-ia` and `edu-knowing-use-penalty-ia`; for clear drafting see `edu-no-plain-language-rule-ia`. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act
bodyText: Iowa has no truth-in-renting act. No state agency publishes a statement of tenant rights that you must hand out with the lease, and no statute makes you warn the tenant that a lease term may be unenforceable. Iowa does the same work another way. Certain lease terms are barred and unenforceable, and if you willfully use a lease 'containing provisions known by the landlord to be prohibited' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)), the tenant may recover actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (`edu-knowing-use-penalty-ia`, `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`). Deceptive practices in leasing can also draw a consumer fraud claim (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Keep barred terms out of your lease and do not add terms copied from other states' forms. If you run a licensed assisted living program or elder group home, its occupancy agreement has its own content rules (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-ia`).

title: Where Iowa Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant act sets several defaults that your lease can change. A lease that says nothing takes the default. (1) Rent: 'Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(3)), periodic rent is due at the start of each month (or of any term of one month or less), and rent is apportioned day to day. With no agreement on rent at all, the tenant owes the fair rental value (Iowa Code § 562A.9(2)). State the amount, due date, place and method (`rent-payment`). (2) Term: unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case (Iowa Code § 562A.9(5)). (3) Late fee: there is none unless the lease provides one, and the statute caps it (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4); `late-fee-ia`). (4) Use: 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit and uses incidental thereto' (Iowa Code § 562A.20; `residential-use-only`). (5) Absence notice: the lease may require the tenant to tell you of an anticipated extended absence; only then can you recover damages when the tenant willfully fails to (Iowa Code § 562A.20, Iowa Code § 562A.29(1); `extended-absence-notice-ks`). (6) Chores and repairs: in a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant handles trash, water, hot water and heat and specified repairs; in other units only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)-(3); `maintenance-allocation-ia`). (7) Sale: unless otherwise agreed, a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser relieves you of liability for later events once the tenant has written notice (Iowa Code § 562A.16(1); `edu-sale-management-change-ia`). (8) Deposit: you may withhold for 'other funds due to the landlord pursuant to the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(1)), so a charge the lease never mentions has nothing to attach to. (9) Rules: a valid rule adopted under the act is part of the rental agreement (Iowa Code § 562A.6(11); `rules-ia`). Anything else you add must be a term 'not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)), and the lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the act (`edu-nonwaivable-rights-ia`). For a lease that includes an option to buy, see `edu-lease-option-ia`.

title: Leases With an Option to Buy
bodyText: A lease that gives the tenant an option to buy is lawful in Iowa, but the library does not offer an option clause: it mixes a sale into the lease and carries sale-law duties. If you want one, have your own clause drafted after taking advice. Three things to know. (1) Seller disclosure. Iowa's real estate disclosure law covers a 'transfer or conveyance by sale, exchange, real estate contract, or any other method by which real estate and improvements are purchased' of a property with one to four dwelling units (Iowa Code § 558A.1(7)), and the disclosure statement must be delivered before the seller makes or accepts a written offer (Iowa Code § 558A.2(1)). The statute does not say whether granting an option counts or only its exercise. The cautious course is to deliver the statement before the lease with the option is signed. (2) Once the tenant exercises the option and occupies as buyer under a contract of sale, the landlord-tenant act no longer governs (Iowa Code § 562A.5(2)). (3) Foreclosure lease-backs. If you buy a home from an owner in foreclosure, forfeiture or tax sale and let the owner stay under a lease, a lease with an option to buy or a contract for deed, Iowa's foreclosure reconveyance law applies (Iowa Code ch. 714F): a written contract in at least 12-point bold type in the language used to negotiate, with set terms and notices (Iowa Code § 714F.2, Iowa Code § 714F.3, Iowa Code § 714F.5), a cancellation right of about three business days (Iowa Code § 714F.4), no waiver and no arbitration clause (Iowa Code § 714F.6, Iowa Code § 714F.7), proof the owner can afford the lease payments and the purchase (Iowa Code § 714F.8(1)(a)), and no lease terms that are 'unfair or commercially unreasonable' (Iowa Code § 714F.8(4)). Violations carry damages, attorney fees and criminal penalties (Iowa Code § 714F.9). Get advice before any such deal. Iowa's rent-to-own act covers household goods only, not homes.

title: Required Iowa Disclosures at a Glance
bodyText: Iowa's list of required disclosures is short. Before or at the start of the tenancy, in writing: (1) the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices, kept current (Iowa Code § 562A.13(1)-(2); `landlord-disclosure-ia`); (2) if the tenant pays you rather than the utility company, a full explanation of utility rates, charges and services before the lease is signed (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`); (3) whether the property is on the federal Superfund (CERCLIS) list (Iowa Code § 562A.13(6); `superfund-disclosure-ia`); (4) your written rules, which bind the tenant only if the tenant 'has notice of it at the time the tenant enters into the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.18(1)(f); `rules-ia`); (5) for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet (`lead-based-paint`). During the tenancy: 30 days' written notice of a rent increase (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ia`), and written notice when you sell or change managers (`edu-sale-management-change-ia`). What Iowa does not require: no state lease form or required first page (`edu-statutory-forms-ia`), no rent-law coverage notice (local rent control is barred, `edu-rent-control-ia`), no radon, mold, flood or bed bug disclosure (`edu-radon-ia`, `edu-no-mold-disclosure-ia`, `edu-no-flood-disclosure-ia`, `edu-no-bed-bug-rule-ia`), and no duty to disclose a wind or solar facility waiver. Three special cases: a lease with an option to buy may bring the seller disclosure statement, and a foreclosure lease-back has its own contract rules (`edu-lease-option-ia`); and if you are a real estate licensee providing brokerage services in a deal where you act for yourself, your family or your firm, you must give all parties written disclosure of that interest (Iowa Code § 543B.56(3)(b)); the real estate commission's rules may say more and were not reviewed here. Mobile home park lots follow Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant act says which notices must be written, and a lease cannot make any of them oral (`edu-nonwaivable-rights-ia`). Your notices that must be in writing: the manager and owner disclosure and the Superfund disclosure (Iowa Code § 562A.13(1), (6)); a rent increase, at least 30 days ahead (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)); your rules, which bind the tenant only if written (Iowa Code § 562A.18(1)); the deposit statement when you keep any of the deposit, and the notice to the tenant when a deposit passes to a new owner (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3), (6)); notice of a sale or a change of manager (Iowa Code § 562A.16); the 7-day notice to remedy a breach, the 3-day notice to pay rent (Iowa Code § 562A.27(1)-(2)) and the 7-day notice before you fix a tenant-caused problem yourself (Iowa Code § 562A.28); the 3-day clear-and-present-danger notice (Iowa Code § 562A.27A); notice ending a periodic tenancy or a term that renews (Iowa Code § 562A.34(1)-(3)); and the 3-day notice to quit (Iowa Code § 648.3). The tenant's notices that must be in writing include the 7-day notice of your breach (Iowa Code § 562A.21), notice ending the lease when you fail to deliver possession (Iowa Code § 562A.22), notice of a failure to supply heat, water or essential services (Iowa Code § 562A.23), notice of termination after a fire or casualty (Iowa Code § 562A.25) and notice ending a periodic tenancy (Iowa Code § 562A.34). The 24-hour notice before you enter need not be written (`landlords-access-mi`), but a written or e-mailed record protects you. How to serve each notice: `edu-notice-service-ia`, `notices` and `electronic-notice-ia`. A lease itself may be written or oral (`edu-statute-of-frauds-ia`).

title: No Initials Requirement for Lease Terms
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease provisions or notices, or to sign any lease term separately. Two separate-signature rules sit next to the lease. In a unit other than a single family residence, an agreement that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling must be 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3)(a); `maintenance-allocation-ia`). And if a real estate licensee represents you or the tenant in the rental, the licensee's written agency disclosure must be acknowledged by the represented party's separate signature before an offer is made or accepted (Iowa Code § 543B.57(2)(b)). You may still ask for initials, for example beside your rules to show the tenant had them at signing (`rules-ia`), but initials do not rescue a term Iowa bars (`edu-prohibited-terms-ia`).

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Iowa has no state-published statement of tenant rights that you must give with the lease, attach as its first page, or have the tenant sign for, and nothing makes delivery of one a condition of an eviction or rent suit. One group of landlords is different: a certified assisted living program or elder group home must sign a written occupancy agreement with each tenant before move-in that 'shall clearly describe the rights and responsibilities of the tenant and the program' (Iowa Code § 231C.5(2)), with a matching rule for elder group homes (Iowa Code § 231B.5(2)), and Iowa's landlord-tenant act also applies to them (Iowa Code § 231C.19, Iowa Code § 231B.18). Those programs are not covered by this library. Federally assisted housing may carry its own notice duties; not covered here. For what Iowa does require you to disclose, see `edu-required-disclosures-ia`; for why Iowa has no truth-in-renting notice, `edu-no-truth-in-renting-ia`.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: Iowa publishes no landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that you must hand the tenant before signing or at renewal, and no statute calls for a signed acknowledgment of one. Some Iowa cities run their own rental programs and may hand out material of their own (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames among them); check your city (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). The one statutory rights-description rule applies to assisted living programs and elder group homes, not ordinary rentals (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-ia`).

title: Lease Language and Translation
bodyText: Iowa law does not require you to translate a residential lease or to sign it in the language you used to negotiate, and it prescribes no lease text in any language. Iowa's English-language law makes English the language of government documents; it does not govern a private lease (Iowa Code § 1.18). One exception: if you buy a home from an owner in foreclosure, forfeiture or tax sale and lease it back to them, the reconveyance contract must be 'in the same language principally used by the foreclosure purchaser and foreclosed homeowner to negotiate the sale of the residence in foreclosure' (Iowa Code § 714F.2), and its cancellation notice in the contract's language (Iowa Code § 714F.5(2)); see `edu-lease-option-ia`. In court, a party with limited English is entitled to an interpreter (Iowa Code § 622A.2). If you negotiate in another language, a translation helps the tenant understand the lease and helps you show the terms were explained; misleading a tenant in any language can still draw a consumer fraud claim (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Federal fair housing rules may bear on language-based practices; not covered here.

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText: Iowa sets no maximum term for a residential lease and no special signing formalities for a long one. What does apply: (1) A lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed by the party it will be enforced against (`edu-statute-of-frauds-ia`); a written lease that one side never signed but that takes effect because rent or possession was accepted 'is effective only for one year' (Iowa Code § 562A.10(3)). (2) No seal is needed: private seals are abolished, and adding one changes nothing (Iowa Code § 537A.1). (3) An agent under a power of attorney with general authority over real property may sign a lease for you (Iowa Code § 633B.204(2)). (4) Spouses: no Iowa statute makes a spouse join in a lease of the owner's property. But if you rent out part of the home you live in as your homestead and you are married, Iowa says a 'conveyance or encumbrance' of the homestead is not valid unless your spouse signs it too (Iowa Code § 561.13(1)), and the statute does not say whether a lease counts. The cautious course is to have your spouse sign that lease as well. Agricultural land has its own term and recording rules, not covered here.

title: No Parity Rule for Lease Types
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires you to offer both month-to-month and fixed-term leases, to give a month-to-month tenant the same terms as a tenant on a lease, or to limit how much more you charge for one than the other. Iowa's landlord-tenant act treats the two kinds alike in what it does say: a lease that fixes no definite term is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly), and either kind ends on written notice (Iowa Code § 562A.9(5), Iowa Code § 562A.34; `periodic-tenancy-notice-ia`). Differences you choose must not track a protected class (`edu-fair-housing-ia`), and a rent increase needs 30 days' written notice and cannot take effect before the current term ends (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ia`). Mobile home park lots follow Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: No Iowa statute sets a minimum type size for a residential lease, and none bars a small-print lease from evidence. Two type-size rules can touch a landlord. If you record a lease or a memorandum of lease with the county recorder, preprinted text must be at least 8 point and other text at least 10 point, or the recorder will refuse it (Iowa Code § 331.606B(1)(b)). And a foreclosure lease-back contract must be in at least 12-point bold type, with its required notices in 14-point bold (Iowa Code § 714F.2, Iowa Code § 714F.3(1)(h), Iowa Code § 714F.5(1); `edu-lease-option-ia`). Use a readable size anyway (`edu-no-plain-language-rule-ia`).

title: Notice by Any Method That Arrives
bodyText: Iowa already lets either side use any delivery method for most notices, as long as the notice actually reaches the other person: you may serve a tenant by 'A method of providing notice that results in the notice actually being received by the tenant' (Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(a)(6)), and the tenant may serve you the same way (Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(b)(6)). No lease term is needed to use a text message, an app message or a hand-delivered note under that rule; the risk is proof. If the tenant later says it never arrived, you must show it did, so keep a reply, a read receipt or the tenant's acknowledgment. If you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically (Iowa Code § 554D.106(2)), an electronic message counts as received under Iowa's electronic transactions law once it reaches a system the tenant uses, even if no one has read it (Iowa Code § 554D.117(2), (5)), but whether that is notice 'actually being received' (Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(a)(6)) is not settled; do not rely on delivery alone. This rule does not reach termination notices or notices to quit, which must be served only by the methods Iowa Code § 562A.29A and Iowa Code § 648.3 list (`edu-notice-service-ia`). The library offers an optional e-mail notice clause (`electronic-notice-ia`) but no separate text-message clause, because the statute already permits any method that actually arrives and a text term adds little beyond it; if you want one, add your own after taking advice, and never for termination notices.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule
bodyText:
No Iowa statute requires you to give tenants an emergency or after-hours phone number, to staff a 24-hour line, or to print a hotline or website notice in the lease, and none regulates a tenant's emergency contact.

What Iowa does require is the written name and address of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices (`landlord-disclosure-ia`). A city may require the owner of a short-term rental to give it an emergency contact (Iowa Code § 414.1), and counties have the same power (Iowa Code § 331.301); short-term rentals are outside this library.

Giving tenants a number to call is still wise: an emergency the tenant cannot report quickly can become a repair you owe under the habitability duty (`edu-habitability-ia`). The library's optional clause collects a tenant's own emergency contact (`emergency-contact-co`); emergency contact data used for that purpose is exempt from Iowa's consumer data protection act (Iowa Code § 715D.2).

title: Tenant Portals and Electronic Records
bodyText: No Iowa statute deals with tenant portals as such. We searched Iowa's statutes (Iowa Code 2026, with the 2025 and 2026 Iowa Acts) and Constitution. Payment: rent is payable 'at the time and place agreed upon by the parties' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(3)), so the lease may name an online portal as a payment method; keep at least one practical alternative (`acceptable-payment-methods`). Signatures and records: Iowa's electronic transactions law applies only where both sides agreed to deal electronically (Iowa Code § 554D.106(2); `electronic-signatures`), and a party who agreed 'may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means' (Iowa Code § 554D.106(3)) and that right 'may not be waived by agreement' (Iowa Code § 554D.106(3)). So a lease term making every future signature or document portal-only cannot stop a tenant from asking for paper later. A portal that keeps the tenant from printing or saving a record cannot hold the tenant to it (Iowa Code § 554D.110(3)). Notices: posting in a portal never serves a termination notice or notice to quit (`edu-notice-service-ia`); for other notices it works only if the tenant actually receives it (`edu-actual-notice-method-ia`, `electronic-notice-ia`).

title: No Preset Deposit Charges in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no statute that lets a lease pre-set what you will deduct from the security deposit, and none that sets a carpet-cleaning or other cleaning charge. What controls instead is the deposit statute's own limit: 'The landlord may withhold from the rental deposit only such amounts as are reasonably necessary for the following reasons' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)). Those reasons are unpaid rent or other money due under the lease, restoring the unit 'to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(2)), and some costs of regaining possession from a tenant who stays on in bad faith. You must prove the reason for any amount you keep (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)). So a price list in the lease does not decide what you may keep. Deduct only what the unit's actual condition reasonably required. A flat charge taken whatever the condition, or one that covers ordinary wear and tear, risks being a waiver of the tenant's deposit rights, and an Iowa lease may not contain one (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)); a prohibited term is unenforceable and knowingly using it carries a penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Bad-faith retention can cost punitive damages of up to twice the monthly rent on top of actual damages (Iowa Code § 562A.12(7)). A schedule you show the tenant at move-in can still work as an honest estimate, but charge only the cost the condition justified and keep the receipts. The library offers no preset-charge clause. See `security-deposit-use-ia`, `security-deposit-return-ia` and `edu-deposit-return-penalty-ia`; for carpet cleaning, `edu-no-carpet-cleaning-rule-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: No Deposit Installment Right in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, and none requires you to offer a payment plan or forbids one. You may agree to installments if you choose. If you do, put the amounts and due dates in a signed addendum, because the library's deposit clause `security-deposit-use-ia` calls for the whole deposit before occupancy. The total of all installments, plus any other deposit such as a pet deposit, must stay within the two-month limit (Iowa Code § 562A.12(1); `edu-deposit-cap-ia`). Each installment you receive is part of the rental deposit and must be held and returned under the deposit rules (`edu-deposit-holding-ia`, `security-deposit-return-ia`). An unpaid installment is money due under the lease, but whether it counts as rent for a three-day nonpayment notice is not settled; treat a missed installment as a lease breach rather than as unpaid rent unless you have taken advice (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`).

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText:
Iowa treats rent paid in advance and a security deposit as different things. A rental deposit is money that secures the tenant's performance, 'other than a deposit which is exclusively in advance payment of rent' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12)). So last month's rent that you collect up front only as rent is not a deposit: it does not count toward the two-month deposit limit and is not subject to the deposit holding and return rules. If your lease lets you keep that money for damages or other unpaid charges, it is no longer exclusively advance rent, and on that reading it becomes a deposit that counts toward the limit (`edu-deposit-cap-ia`). Label it plainly as rent for the last month and apply it only to that month's rent.

Several statutes make you give back all prepaid rent when the lease ends early for your fault or a casualty, for example 'the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 562A.12' (Iowa Code § 562A.25(2)); see also Iowa Code § 562A.21(4), Iowa Code § 562A.22 and Iowa Code § 562A.26.

No Iowa statute lets a tenant use the security deposit as the last month's rent, and none forbids it. The library's deposit clause says the deposit does not relieve the tenant of paying rent and may not be applied to rent without your written consent (`security-deposit-use-ia`). A tenant who holds back the last month's rent owes it, and you may withhold unpaid rent from the deposit (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(1)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Clock
bodyText:
In Iowa the only tenant act that starts your deposit deadline is giving you a mailing address or delivery instructions. You have thirty days 'from the date of termination of the tenancy and receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)) to return the deposit or send the written statement of what you kept. If the tenant gives you no address or instructions within one year after the tenancy ends, the deposit reverts to you (Iowa Code § 562A.12(4); `edu-deposit-reversion-ia`). The statute does not say the address must be in writing or on a form, so count the thirty days from the day you receive it in any form.

No Iowa statute makes the refund depend on the tenant's advance notice of moving out, on returning the keys, or on a move-out inspection. A lease term that forfeits the deposit for a missed move-out notice would take away the tenant's deposit rights, which an Iowa lease may not do (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)).

What you may keep is limited to the statutory grounds: unpaid rent and other money due under the lease (including rent owed because the tenant did not give the required termination notice, `periodic-tenancy-notice-ia`), restoring the unit beyond ordinary wear and tear, and some costs of regaining possession from a tenant who stays on in bad faith (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)). The library's return clause asks the tenant for a written address at move-out (`security-deposit-return-ia`).

The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: No Posted Deposit Standards Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no rule that makes you post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, whatever the size of your property, and no rule that every tenant must pay the same deposit. You may set each deposit by your own criteria, within the two-month limit (Iowa Code § 562A.12(1); `edu-deposit-cap-ia`). The Iowa Civil Rights Act still applies: you may not discriminate because of a protected characteristic 'in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the sale, rental, lease assignment, or sublease' of housing (Iowa Code § 216.8(1)(b)), and a deposit amount is a term of the rental (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). Write your deposit criteria down (for example, by credit result or pet), apply them the same way to every applicant, and keep the record; that is your evidence if a higher deposit is ever challenged. Federal fair housing law may add duties in covered housing; not covered here. Some Iowa cities have their own civil rights ordinances; check yours (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames among them).

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no fast-track or optional procedure for settling a security deposit: no quicker refund in exchange for giving up the written statement, no processing fee, and no separate rule for evictions or abandonment. One rule applies however the tenancy ends. Within thirty days after the later of the end of the tenancy and your receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, return the deposit or send a written statement of the specific reasons for keeping any of it (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a); `security-deposit-return-ia`). You may always return it sooner. After an eviction, the deposit may also cover 'expenses incurred in acquiring possession of the premises from a tenant who does not act in good faith in failing to surrender and vacate' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(3)), but not a fee for handling the deposit itself, which is not one of the statutory grounds. If you and the tenant disagree, either of you may sue; you must prove why you kept any amount (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)), and the court may award reasonable attorney fees to the winner (Iowa Code § 562A.12(8)). A money claim of $6,500 or less is a small claim (Iowa Code § 631.1(1)(b)).

title: Fees in Place of a Deposit
bodyText: No Iowa statute regulates a fee, bond or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit. Iowa neither authorizes nor forbids one, and sets no offer-to-all, switch-to-deposit or credit-reporting rules for it. The risk is how the deposit statute treats the money. A rental deposit is 'a deposit of money to secure performance of a residential rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12)). If you collect and keep money that secures the tenant's performance, it is a deposit whatever you call it: it counts toward the two-month limit and must be held and returned under the deposit rules (`edu-deposit-cap-ia`, `edu-deposit-holding-ia`). A premium the tenant pays to a separate insurer or surety is less likely to be a deposit, but no Iowa authority read for this library decides it. A required monthly charge you collect is also 'rent' under the act's definition (Iowa Code § 562A.6(10); `edu-fees-as-rent-ia`). The library offers no deposit-alternative clause, because whether a given program is a deposit, and how insurance law treats it, depends on the product. If you want to offer one, take advice and add your own clause.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on nonrefundable deposits or fees, and none that requires a notice before you take one. What decides the question is what the money is for. A rental deposit is 'a deposit of money to secure performance of a residential rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12)). Any money you take to cover the tenant's performance (damage, cleaning, pet damage, unpaid rent) is a deposit whatever you call it. It counts toward the two-month limit, must be held for the tenant, and must be returned except for the deductions the statute allows (Iowa Code § 562A.12; `edu-deposit-cap-ia`, `security-deposit-use-ia`, `security-deposit-return-ia`). So a nonrefundable deposit does not work in Iowa: calling it nonrefundable does not let you keep it, and a lease term that takes away the tenant's deposit rights is unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a), (3)). A genuine fee for something else, such as an application or administrative charge, is not a deposit, and Iowa does not regulate it (`edu-no-application-fee-rule-ia`, `edu-no-fee-transparency-rule-ia`). A pet deposit is a deposit (`edu-pet-deposit-ia`). If you charge a fee, state its amount and purpose in the lease and make sure the purpose is not to secure the tenant's performance. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Iowa has no rule requiring a separate written notice, a separate signature or particular wording for a nonrefundable fee or deposit. Because money taken to secure the tenant's performance is a deposit whatever it is called (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12)), a notice cannot make it nonrefundable; see `edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-ia`. For a genuine fee, state its amount and purpose in the lease itself.

title: Charging for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Iowa statute specifically bars you from charging a tenant for a service, amenity or utility you do not provide. Other rules make it a bad idea. If the tenant pays you for utilities rather than paying the utility directly, you must 'fully explain utility rates, charges and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`). If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services contrary to the lease or your maintenance duties, the tenant may, after written notice, buy them and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages for the lower rental value, or recover rent paid for the period (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)); willfully cutting off utilities carries larger remedies (Iowa Code § 562A.26; `edu-self-help-eviction-ia`). Iowa's consumer fraud statute treats deception or misrepresentation 'in connection with the lease, sale, or advertisement of any merchandise' as unlawful (Iowa Code § 714.16(2)(a)), and how far it and the private-action act reach a residential lease is unsettled (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Charge a service fee only for a service the tenant actually receives, describe each one in the lease, and stop or credit the fee when the service stops.

title: Late Fee Limits in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa caps late fees in residential leases by the monthly rent: no more than $12 a day or $60 a month where rent is $700 a month or less, and no more than $20 a day or $100 a month where rent is more (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4)). See `edu-late-fee-cap-ia` for the rule and `late-fee-ia` for the clause. Manufactured home community lots have the same figures in their own chapter (Iowa Code § 562B.10(4)), with no separate penalty. The self-storage statute is different and does not apply to homes: it lets a storage rental agreement provide a reasonable late fee and says a monthly fee of $20 or 20% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater, 'shall be reasonable and is not a penalty' (Iowa Code § 578A.5(4)). Nothing like that applies to a dwelling lease. The cap sits outside the list of prohibited provisions in Iowa Code § 562A.11, but whether the penalty for willfully using a prohibited provision (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)) also reaches an over-cap late fee, as a waiver of the tenant's rights under the act, is not settled (`edu-knowing-use-penalty-ia`), so assume it can; keep your figures within the cap.

title: Iowa Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Iowa sets only a few money limits on a residential lease. (1) Security deposit: no more than two months' rent, counting every deposit including a pet deposit (Iowa Code § 562A.12(1); `edu-deposit-cap-ia`). (2) Late fees: no more than $12 a day or $60 a month where rent is $700 a month or less, and no more than $20 a day or $100 a month where it is more (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4); `edu-late-fee-cap-ia`). (3) Returned checks: a charge of up to $30 for a dishonored check, draft or order, only if you post the required notice, and never where the tenant stopped payment (Iowa Code § 554.3512; `edu-dishonored-check-ia`). (4) Interest: 5% a year unless the tenant agrees in writing to a higher rate within the published maximum (Iowa Code § 535.2; `edu-legal-interest-ia`). (5) Rent: no statewide limit on rent or rent increases, and cities and counties may not cap rent (`edu-rent-control-ia`). No Iowa statute caps application, pet, cleaning, administrative or other fees. The penalties you face are capped too: bad-faith retention of a deposit, up to twice the monthly rent plus actual damages (Iowa Code § 562A.12(7)); knowingly using a prohibited lease term, actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)); unlawful ouster or utility shutoff, up to twice the monthly rent plus actual damages and attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.26). Money claims of $6,500 or less go to small claims (Iowa Code § 631.1(1)(b)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: No Iowa statute lets you pass a city or other government fine on to a tenant by lease, and none makes the tenant liable to you for fines or nuisance-abatement costs unless the lease says otherwise. Housing-code penalties and fines are charged to the owner, and unpaid ones become a lien on the property (Iowa Code § 364.17). Be careful with a lease clause that makes the tenant reimburse you for a fine. An Iowa lease may not have the tenant agree 'to indemnify the other party for that liability or the associated costs' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)), meaning the other party's liability arising under law, and a fine imposed on you is your liability under law. Such a clause risks being unenforceable, and knowingly using a prohibited term carries a penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). The library therefore offers no fine-reimbursement clause. What you can do instead: the tenant must comply with the housing-code obligations that fall primarily on tenants and must not damage the property (Iowa Code § 562A.17(1), (6)), and you may recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance (Iowa Code § 562A.27(3)). If the tenant's own breach caused a fine, claim it as damages for that breach, with the citation as evidence; whether a court will treat the fine as recoverable damages has not been decided in any case read for this library. Never charge a tenant a fine, fee or penalty because the tenant or a household member called the police or other emergency help: 'A landlord shall not impose monetary or other penalties on a resident or tenant who exercises the resident's or tenant's right to summon law enforcement assistance or other emergency assistance' (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(1)(b)), and a violation costs a civil penalty of one month's rent plus damages and fees (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(3); `edu-emergency-assistance-ia`). You may still recover the cost of repairing damage caused by emergency personnel the tenant summoned (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(1)(e)). Your city's housing code may say more (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames among them).

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Iowa has no state rental registration or licence fee. Cities with housing codes run rental inspection and certification programs and 'may establish reasonable fees for inspection and enforcement procedures' (Iowa Code § 364.17(5)), which they charge to the owner (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). No Iowa statute says whether you may have the tenant reimburse such a fee. A lease promise that the tenant will repay whatever the city charges you is risky: an Iowa lease may not have the tenant agree to indemnify you for your liability arising under law 'or the associated costs' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)), and whether a city fee counts has not been decided in any case read for this library. The library therefore offers no reimbursement clause. The safer course is to build the cost into the rent, or to state a fixed fee amount in the lease's list of fees (`fees-and-charges-vi`). Either way it is rent (Iowa Code § 562A.6(10)), so you cannot add or raise it during the lease term, and a later increase needs 30 days' written notice (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5); `edu-rent-increase-notice-ia`). Never pass on a reinspection fee or penalty caused by your own failure to correct a violation. Check your city's ordinance (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames among them).

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute lets a lease charge a set fee for removing or tampering with a smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm. Iowa makes tampering an offense instead: 'No person may render inoperable a smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm which is required to be installed by this section by tampering' (Iowa Code § 10A.518(8)), and a violation is a simple misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 10A.518(9)). The library's alarm clause already forbids tampering (`smoke-alarm-battery-ia`; `edu-alarm-duties-ia`). If a tenant damages, removes or disables an alarm, recover the actual cost of repair or replacement as damages: the tenant may not deliberately or negligently damage or remove a part of the premises (Iowa Code § 562A.17(6)), and you may recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance (Iowa Code § 562A.27(3)), or deduct the cost from the deposit at move-out (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(2)). A fixed charge set in advance could be attacked as a penalty rather than a fair estimate of your loss; that is a question of case law, so the library offers no fixed fee. Keep the receipt for the replacement.

title: Carpet Cleaning and the Deposit
bodyText: No Iowa statute lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and none sets an age or condition test for carpet or paint. The deposit statute decides what you may charge. You may withhold only what is reasonably necessary 'To restore the dwelling unit to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(2)), or to cover unpaid rent and other money due under the lease, and you must prove the reason (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)). So you may charge for cleaning carpets the tenant left stained, soiled or damaged beyond normal use, but not for routine cleaning between tenants or for carpet or paint worn out by ordinary living. A lease term that makes the tenant pay for professional cleaning whatever the carpets' condition would enlarge the statutory grounds, which an Iowa lease may not do (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)). The tenant must keep the unit as clean as its condition permits (Iowa Code § 562A.17(2)). Record the carpets' condition and age at move-in and move-out with dated photos, charge only the actual reasonable cost, and describe the damage in your written deposit statement (`security-deposit-return-ia`). The library offers no carpet-cleaning clause; see `edu-no-deposit-cost-schedule-ia` and `security-deposit-use-ia`. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Two Iowa rules limit what you may add to a tenant's unpaid balance when you collect it. First, an Iowa lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(c); `edu-attorney-fees-ia`). A collection charge that includes or stands in for a lawyer's fee is barred, and knowingly using a prohibited term carries a penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Attorney fees come only from the statutes that award them, for example for a tenant's willful noncompliance (Iowa Code § 562A.27(3)). Second, Iowa's debt collection law covers an obligation from a transaction that would have been a consumer credit transaction 'if a lease was of an interest in land' (Iowa Code § 537.7102(3)), and a debt collector includes a person collecting its own debts (Iowa Code § 537.7102(5)). On those words it can reach you and any agency you hire when you collect unpaid rent. It bars collecting any 'charge, fee or expense incidental to the principal obligation unless the interest or incidental charge, fee, or expense is expressly authorized by the agreement creating the obligation and is legally chargeable to the debtor, or is otherwise legally chargeable' (Iowa Code § 537.7103(5)(d)), and bars saying fees may be added when they may not (Iowa Code § 537.7103(4)(h)). So never add a collection fee the lease does not state. Even a stated fee must be legally chargeable, and whether a flat or percentage collection fee is enforceable against an Iowa tenant has not been decided in any case read for this library. The library offers no collection-fee clause. Collect unpaid amounts by demand, from the deposit where the statute allows (`security-deposit-use-ia`), or in small claims court.

title: No Notice or Eviction Fees in Iowa Leases
bodyText: No Iowa statute lets a lease charge the tenant a fee for serving a notice (a three-day notice to pay, a seven-day notice to cure, a notice to quit) or for filing an eviction, and none sets such a fee. The costs of a court case are handled by the court, not the lease: 'Costs shall be recovered by the successful against the losing party' (Iowa Code § 625.1). In a small claims case the filing and service fees are paid in advance and 'assessed as costs in the action' (Iowa Code § 631.6(1)), and an eviction judgment carries 'a clause commanding the officer to collect the costs as in ordinary cases' (Iowa Code § 648.22). A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(c); `edu-attorney-fees-ia`), so an eviction or notice fee that covers a lawyer's work is barred. A flat notice fee could also be attacked as a penalty, and adding a fee to a tenant's balance that is not legally chargeable can break Iowa's debt collection law (`edu-collection-fee-ia`). Do not add a notice fee to a nonpayment notice: a notice that demands amounts you cannot lawfully collect may fail (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`). The library offers no notice or eviction fee clause. If a tenant who acted in bad faith forces you to go to court for possession, the deposit may cover your 'expenses incurred in acquiring possession' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(3)).

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: Iowa has no rule about late fees when a housing subsidy or voucher pays part of the rent. No Iowa statute bars a late fee on the subsidy-paid share, and none measures the fee on the tenant's own share. The general Iowa cap applies to every tenancy, subsidized or not: where 'the rent does not exceed seven hundred dollars per month, a rental agreement shall not provide for a late fee that exceeds twelve dollars per day or a total amount of sixty dollars per month' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4)), and above $700 a month the limits are $20 a day and $100 a month (Iowa Code § 562A.9(4)). Iowa does not say whether the $700 test uses the full contract rent or the tenant's share. The cautious course is to use the lower limits whenever the tenant's own share is $700 or less. Charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, never because a housing authority's payment arrived late, and say so in the lease. If you have a housing assistance payments contract, that contract, the program's rules and any required lease addendum control what you may charge; federal law may add duties in covered housing, not covered here. Iowa law does not require you to accept vouchers (`edu-source-of-income-ia`). See `late-fee-ia`, `edu-late-fee-cap-ia` and `edu-fees-as-rent-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on passing property tax increases to a residential tenant. Nothing requires a tax clause to state the tenant's share or to refund an abatement, and nothing bans such a clause outright. But a tax pass-through is rent, because Iowa defines rent as 'a payment to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(10)). That brings in the rent increase rule: 'Each tenant shall be notified, in writing, of any rent increase at least thirty days before the effective date' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)), and the 'effective date shall not be sooner than the expiration date of original rental agreement or any renewal or extension thereof' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)). So a clause that makes the tenant pay a tax increase in the middle of a fixed term risks being an increase Iowa does not allow, and no case read for this library says whether an increase scheduled in the lease itself escapes that rule. The cautious course is to build expected tax costs into the rent you set for each term, and to raise the rent at a renewal with at least 30 days' written notice. The library offers no tax pass-through clause for Iowa for that reason; if you want one, take advice and add your own. A higher tax bill also helps if a tenant claims an increase was retaliation: proof that your 'legitimate costs and charges of owning, maintaining or operating a dwelling unit have increased' (Iowa Code § 562A.36(2)) is a defense to the retaliation presumption when the increase matches the cost. Do not raise rent because the tenant gets or qualifies for Iowa's rent reimbursement; that is a defense to a nonpayment action (Iowa Code § 425.35). See `edu-rent-increase-notice-ia`, `edu-retaliation-ia`, `edu-fees-as-rent-ia` and `edu-rent-escalation-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Sales and Lodging Tax on Rent
bodyText: Ordinary residential rent in Iowa carries no state tax. Iowa's sales tax chapter (Iowa Code ch. 423) does not list renting a home among the sales and services it taxes. The tax that can reach rent is the hotel and motel tax: 'A tax of five percent is imposed upon the sales price for the renting of any lodging if the lodging is located in this state' (Iowa Code § 423A.3), and a city or county may add a local hotel and motel tax of up to seven percent (Iowa Code § 423A.4(1)). "Lodging" is broad. It includes rooms and apartments in a rooming house, cabin, apartment or 'residential property' (Iowa Code § 423A.2(1)(e)), so a short-term rental of a house or apartment can be taxed. A rental of more than 31 consecutive days to the same person is exempt (Iowa Code § 423A.5(1)(a)). There is one important exception: for a room or sleeping quarters in a rooming house, a hotel, a motel or similar transient lodging, the exemption starts only 'for the period beginning after ninety consecutive days of rental by such person' (Iowa Code § 423A.5(1)(b)). So if you rent rooms to roomers in a rooming house, the first 90 days of each roomer's stay may be taxable even under a longer agreement. Where the tax applies, you as the lodging provider collect it from the occupant, add it to the price and show it as a separate item (Iowa Code § 423A.5A(3)). A standard lease of an apartment or house to the same person for more than 31 consecutive days owes no hotel and motel tax, and the library's lease has no tax clause. Short stays in a hotel or motel are outside Iowa's landlord-tenant act altogether (Iowa Code § 562A.5(4); `edu-scope-ia`). Iowa has no statute about passing a repealed local tax through to tenants. Ask the Iowa Department of Revenue or a tax adviser before charging any tax. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Rent and the Repair Duty Go Together
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant act states as one of its purposes 'To ensure that the right to the receipt of rent is inseparable from the duty to maintain the premises' (Iowa Code § 562A.2(2)(c)), and the act 'shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying purposes and policies' (Iowa Code § 562A.2(1)). Unlike the uniform act and Iowa's manufactured home chapter (Iowa Code § 562B.12), ch. 562A has no separate section voiding an assignment, deed, trust deed or security instrument that lets someone collect rent free of the repair duty. The purpose clause is what a court would apply. In practice: whoever takes the rent should expect to owe the duty to keep the unit fit and habitable (Iowa Code § 562A.15; `edu-habitability-ia`). Do not rely on a lease term, a management contract or an assignment of rents to a lender to move that duty away from the party collecting rent. A lease may not waive the tenant's rights under the act (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a); `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`). The only lawful shifts are the tenant repair agreements Iowa Code § 562A.15(2) and Iowa Code § 562A.15(3) allow (`maintenance-allocation-ia`). If you do not disclose your manager and owner, the person who signed for you becomes your agent for performing your duties and must spend 'all rent collected from the premises' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(3)(b)) for that purpose (`landlord-disclosure-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: Scheduled Rent Increases in the Lease
bodyText: Iowa has no statute on rent escalation clauses. Every rent increase falls under one rule: 'Each tenant shall be notified, in writing, of any rent increase at least thirty days before the effective date' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)), and the 'effective date shall not be sooner than the expiration date of original rental agreement or any renewal or extension thereof' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)). No case read for this library says whether a step increase written into the original lease is a "rent increase" under that rule. If it is, a step in the middle of a fixed term cannot take effect, even though the tenant signed it. The cautious course: set one rent for each fixed term. Change the rent only when a new term, renewal or extension starts, and give each tenant written notice of the new rent at least 30 days before it takes effect, even if the lease already names the figure. The library offers no mid-term escalation clause for Iowa for this reason. A renewal-rent clause adds little, because the 30-day written notice alone sets the rent for the next term; if you want either kind of clause, take advice and add your own. Iowa's notice period is a fixed 30 days; it is not measured against the notice the lease requires of the tenant. Retaliation: you may not raise rent because the tenant made a good-faith code complaint, complained to you about repairs, or joined a tenants' union (Iowa Code § 562A.36(1)). The retaliation presumption does not arise if the tenant complained after notice of a proposed increase, and proof that your costs rose is a defense when the increase matches them (Iowa Code § 562A.36(2)). Iowa has no extra safe harbor that depends on an escalation clause in the lease. Do not raise rent because the tenant gets or qualifies for Iowa's rent reimbursement: the state may order the rent reduced (Iowa Code § 425.33) and it is a defense to a nonpayment action (Iowa Code § 425.35). Cities may not impose rent control (`edu-rent-control-ia`). See `edu-rent-increase-notice-ia`, `edu-retaliation-ia` and `edu-tax-escalation-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Rent Concessions in Iowa
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute about rent concessions, free months or move-in specials, so you may offer one. Put it in the lease (`rent-concession-ia`). Write it as a credit against the full Monthly Rent for named months, not as a lower rent that later goes up. Iowa does not let a 'rent increase' take effect before the end of the term (Iowa Code § 562A.13(5)), and a discounted rent that rises mid-term could be read as one.

Never tie a concession to the tenant finding you other renters. Iowa's consumer fraud law makes it an unlawful practice to rent 'any merchandise at a price or with a rebate or payment or other consideration to the purchaser which is contingent upon the procurement of prospective customers provided by the purchaser' (Iowa Code § 714.16(2)(b)), and 'merchandise' includes real estate (Iowa Code § 714.16(1)(e)). The penalty is severe: the practice renders 'any obligation incurred by the buyer in connection therewith, completely void and a nullity' (Iowa Code § 714.16(2)(b)), which could cost you the tenant's lease obligations, not just the referral credit. A flat move-in special or loyalty discount that does not depend on referrals is outside that rule.

Advertise concessions accurately. Deceptive advertising in connection with the lease of merchandise is an unlawful practice under Iowa Code § 714.16(2)(a) (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`).

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Iowa has no rent-reporting statute. Nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting, nothing bars a lease from mentioning it, and no Iowa law requires a special notice before you report late or unpaid rent to a credit bureau. Iowa's debt collection law can still apply when you collect unpaid rent, because it covers obligations from a transaction that would have been a consumer credit transaction 'if a lease was of an interest in land' (Iowa Code § 537.7102(3)), and a debt collector includes a person collecting for itself (Iowa Code § 537.7102(5); `edu-collection-fee-ia`). That law lets you tell the tenant you may report the debt to a credit bureau and lets you report it (Iowa Code § 537.7103(3)(a)). It forbids 'False accusations made to a person, including a credit reporting agency, or the threat to falsely accuse, that a debtor is willfully refusing to pay a just debt' (Iowa Code § 537.7103(1)(c)). So report only amounts the tenant truly owes, correct errors promptly, and never threaten a report you do not intend or are not entitled to make. Do not report a disputed amount as a willful refusal unless the tenant has ignored requests for payment or refused to negotiate in good faith (Iowa Code § 537.7103(1)(c)). Anyone who reports to a credit bureau also takes on duties under federal consumer reporting law; federal law may add duties, not covered here. The library offers no rent-reporting clause: you need no lease term to report accurate information, and if you want to offer a reporting program, take advice and add your own clause. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Iowa does not let you lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even with notice and even if the lease says you may. 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.33). Iowa's act permits no lockout for delinquent rent, so changing the locks, removing the tenant, or cutting off utilities to force payment is unlawful. If you do it, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, punitive damages of up to twice the monthly rent, and reasonable attorney fees; if the lease ends you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit (Iowa Code § 562A.26). A lease clause allowing a lockout would have the tenant give up rights under the act, which an Iowa lease may not do, except a lease of a single-family home on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), and knowingly using such a clause carries a further penalty (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Seizing the tenant's belongings for rent is also abolished (Iowa Code § 562A.31(2)). For unpaid rent, serve the three-day notice and, if the tenant does not pay, file an eviction (`edu-nonpayment-notice-ia`, `edu-eviction-process-ia`). See `edu-self-help-eviction-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Rent Reimbursement and Property Tax Statements
bodyText: Iowa has a rent reimbursement program for some elderly and disabled renters with low incomes. It treats part of their rent as property tax: "rent constituting property taxes paid" is 'twenty-three percent of the gross rent actually paid' (Iowa Code § 425.17(9)) for the right to occupy the home. No Iowa statute requires you to give tenants a yearly statement of the property-tax share of their rent, or to certify the rent they paid. The tenant, not you, must prove the claim, including 'the name and address of the owner or manager of the property rented' (Iowa Code § 425.26(2)(b)), and the department of health and human services may require more proof (Iowa Code § 425.26(3)). If a tenant asks for a written statement of the rent you received, giving one is good practice; see `edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-ia`. Three rules protect tenants in this program. The department may order you to reduce rent you raised primarily because the tenant is eligible (Iowa Code § 425.33). Such an increase is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment (Iowa Code § 425.35). And 'Discrimination by a landlord in the rental of or in rent charges for a homestead because the tenant has received or is eligible for reimbursement under this subchapter is a simple misdemeanor' (Iowa Code § 425.36). If you and the tenant are related or did not deal at arm's length, the department may treat excessive rent as a lower amount (Iowa Code § 425.17(3)). See `edu-rent-escalation-ia` and `edu-tax-escalation-ia`.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no statute that requires you to rent or price parking separately from the home, and none that forbids it. You may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately.
