Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Time Limits for Rent and Lease Claims
bodyText: Time limits for suing a tenant. A claim for unpaid rent must be brought within five years: 'Those founded on claims for rent, within five years' (Iowa Code § 614.1(5)(b)), even under a written lease. Other claims on a written lease have ten years (Iowa Code § 614.1(5)(a)), but claims on an unwritten lease and claims 'for injuries to property' have five (Iowa Code § 614.1(4)), and a claim for a statute penalty has two (Iowa Code § 614.1(2)). Because a damage claim may be read as an injury-to-property claim, treat five years as your limit for anything a tenant owes. Since July 1, 2026 the statute adds that these 'time limitations may only be altered by an Act of the general assembly' (Iowa Code § 614.1; 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1150, § 1), so do not put a clause in your lease that shortens or lengthens them; a term limiting the tenant's time to sue under the landlord-tenant act could also be a barred waiver (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)). Reviving an old debt. A contract claim is revived 'by an admission in writing, signed by the party to be charged, that the debt is unpaid, or by a like new promise to pay the same' (Iowa Code § 614.11). The statute does not say that a partial payment alone restarts the clock; that is case law not read here, so when a former tenant agrees to a payment plan, get the agreement in writing and signed. Time does not run while the former tenant lives outside Iowa: the periods are computed 'omitting any time when' (Iowa Code § 614.6(1)) the defendant is a nonresident (Iowa Code § 614.6(1)(a)); how far that reaches a defendant who could have been served out of state is case law not read here, so do not rely on it to sue late. A case that fails for a reason other than negligence can be refiled within six months as a continuation (Iowa Code § 614.10). Evictions. Act promptly once a notice expires or a lease ends: thirty days of 'peaceable possession with the knowledge of the plaintiff after the cause of action accrues is a bar to this proceeding' (Iowa Code § 648.18). Judgments. A judgment for rent becomes void and unenforceable twenty years after entry in a court of record (ten for a court not of record), and only two years after entry if you sell or assign it for value to anyone other than a state or federally chartered bank or credit union (Iowa Code § 615.1A). Related rows: `edu-entity-landlord-representation-ia` (who may sue for an entity, foreign-entity registration, trade names, serving a nonresident), `edu-legal-interest-ia`. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area, but even there a lease may not alter the time limits (Iowa Code § 614.1).

title: Landlord Registration and Rental Permits
bodyText: Iowa has no statewide landlord or rental registry. No state statute makes you register with the state, a county assessor or a water utility before you rent, requires an out-of-state owner to hire an Iowa broker or name an Iowa agent, or puts a general business licence on landlords. Registration and certification are local, and a state statute requires them in larger cities. Every city of 15,000 or more must enforce a housing code with a program for 'regular rental inspections, rental inspections upon receipt of complaints, and certification of inspected rental housing' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)), and smaller cities may do the same (Iowa Code § 364.17(6); `edu-rental-inspection-ia`). Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own rental codes; check the city's ordinance before you rent, because this library does not cover local codes. State law limits what a city may demand. A city 'shall not adopt or enforce any regulation, restriction, or other ordinance related to residential property rental permit caps on single-family homes or duplexes' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(d)). 'A city shall not require a license or permit fee for a short-term rental property in the city' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(e)(4)). A city or county may not register or license rental manufactured or mobile homes 'unless a similar registration or licensing system, or registration or license fees, or safety or sanitary standards are required for other rental properties intended for human habitation' (Iowa Code § 364.3(5); counties, Iowa Code § 331.304(9)). A city may not make you take or show compliance with any action, or pay a fee, before you sell, refinance or transfer the property (Iowa Code § 364.3(3)(d)). And no city or county may punish you or a tenant for calling police or emergency help by 'The actual or threatened revocation, suspension, or nonrenewal of a rental certificate, license, or permit' (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(2)(c)(3); `edu-emergency-assistance-ia`). No Iowa statute separately bars a city from inspecting rentals without probable cause. Courts 'may issue administrative search warrants, in accordance with the statutory and common law requirements for the issuance of such warrants' (Iowa Code § 808.14) for inspections a city is authorized to make; when entry needs consent or a warrant is a constitutional and case-law question not covered here. What state law does require of you directly: give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the manager and of an owner or agent for service of notices (Iowa Code § 562A.13(1); `landlord-disclosure-ia`). If someone else rents, manages or collects rent for you for pay, that person generally needs an Iowa real estate broker licence (Iowa Code § 543B.3); you, as owner or lessor acting for yourself, and your regular full-time employees are excluded (Iowa Code § 543B.7(1)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Recording a Lease in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no lease registry, and no statute requires a residential lease to be recorded or registered. Recording is optional. A lease is an instrument 'in any manner relating to real estate' (Iowa Code § 558.1), and 'An instrument affecting real estate is of no validity against subsequent purchasers for a valuable consideration, without notice, ... unless the instrument is filed and recorded in the county in which the real estate is located' (Iowa Code § 558.41(1)). A document must be acknowledged before a notary to be lawfully recorded (Iowa Code § 558.42). Whether a tenant's possession under an unrecorded lease gives a later buyer or lender notice is a case-law question; Iowa has no statute on it, and none like Nebraska's rule for leases to relatives. Recording changes one statutory right. In a court challenge to an eminent domain taking, 'a tenant occupying the property under a recorded lease shall also have standing to bring such action' (Iowa Code § 6A.24(1)), and the acquiring agency's own petition must be served on that tenant (Iowa Code § 6A.24(2)); see `edu-eminent-domain-ia`. A lease of agricultural land must be recorded within 180 days unless it runs five years or less with renewals (Iowa Code § 558.44(2)); an ordinary home lease is not caught unless it is part of such a farm lease. Separately, a lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed to be proved (Iowa Code § 622.32(3); `edu-statute-of-frauds-ia`). A lease term forbidding the tenant to record the lease is not barred by Iowa's landlord-tenant act, and Iowa's rule voiding no-recording clauses covers residential real estate installment sales contracts, not leases (Iowa Code § 558.41(3)). The library does not offer such a clause: residential leases are rarely recorded, and a lease that is not acknowledged cannot be lawfully recorded anyway. If you want one, add your own clause after taking advice. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Single-Family Zone Rental Limit in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute limits renting a house in a single-family zone, makes renting depend on the owner living on the lot, or sets up a state lot-split or two-unit program with occupancy or rental-term conditions. Iowa law runs the other way: it limits what cities may do to rentals in residential zones. A city 'shall not adopt or enforce any regulation, restriction, or other ordinance related to residential property rental permit caps on single-family homes or duplexes' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(d)). 'A city shall not, after January 1, 2018, adopt or enforce any regulation or restriction related to the occupancy of residential rental property that is based upon the existence of familial or nonfamilial relationships between the occupants of such rental property' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(b)). On a lot with an accessory dwelling unit, neither a city nor a county may restrict occupancy of the house or the unit by 'requiring the property owner to be a resident' (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(b)(4); Iowa Code § 331.301(29)(b)(4); `edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-ia`). A rental of thirty days or less is a short-term rental, and 'A short-term rental property shall be classified as a residential land use for zoning purposes' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(e)(2)); cities and counties may regulate it only for listed purposes such as fire and building safety, sanitation, noise and nuisance, and may not charge a licence or permit fee (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(e)(3)-(4); Iowa Code § 331.301(18)). Ordinary zoning still applies: a city may regulate the 'density of population, and the location and use of buildings' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(a)), and a city's rental housing code and inspection program apply to houses as well as apartments (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`, `edu-landlord-registration-ia`). Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames have their own zoning and rental codes; check them, because this library does not cover local ordinances. Private limits are separate: a deed restriction or a homeowners association rule may limit renting, and it binds you as owner (`hoa-compliance`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa law lets you build and rent an accessory dwelling unit (a second home on a house lot, attached or detached, such as a unit over a garage), and stops cities and counties from blocking it. Since July 1, 2026, 'A city shall allow a minimum of one accessory dwelling unit on the same lot as a single family residence within a zoning district where a single family residence is an allowed principal use' (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(a), 2027 early release; 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1013, § 3); counties must do the same (Iowa Code § 331.301(29)(a); 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1013, § 1). The unit must meet the building code and may not exceed 1,000 square feet or half the size of the house, whichever is larger; 'The size calculation of an accessory dwelling unit shall exclude unfinished basements' (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(a)(2), 2027 early release). What a city may not do: require you to live on the lot ('requiring the property owner to be a resident' (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(b)(4))), require a family, marital or employment tie between the occupants of the house and the unit, or limit the unit's occupants by income or age (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(b)(4)); impose 'Regulations on the use of an accessory dwelling unit as a rental property that are more restrictive than those provided for in subsections 9 and 16 of this section' (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(b)(2)), the short-term rental rules and Iowa's landlord-tenant act; require extra parking; or require separate utility lines unless the unit cannot have full utility access with a separate meter for billing (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(b)(3), (5)). A conforming permit application must be approved without discretionary review, and a denial must be in writing with the remedy (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(c)). The county rules match (Iowa Code § 331.301(29)(b)-(c)). What can still stop you: a deed restriction or a rule of a homeowners association or other common interest community, and historic-area review (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(a)(3), 2027 early release). Iowa sets no minimum rental term for the unit; a rental of thirty days or less is a short-term rental under Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(e) (`edu-no-single-family-zone-lease-limit-ia`). Once rented, the unit is a dwelling unit under Iowa's landlord-tenant act, so every rule in this library applies to it, including the utility disclosure when the unit shares a meter with the house (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`). Check your city's ordinance (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames have their own codes); an ordinance that conflicts with the state rule is void (Iowa Code § 364.3(23)(d)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Local Health Board Rules for Rentals
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires you to give a tenant a copy of local health rules on request, or to refer a tenant to a health board or district. Iowa has no special health-district rental regulations of its own; public health is local. Every city, county or multi-county district board of health has 'jurisdiction over public health matters' in its area (Iowa Code § 137.103), must 'Enforce state health laws and the rules and lawful orders of the state department' (Iowa Code § 137.104(1)(a)), and may make 'reasonable rules and regulations not inconsistent with law and the rules of the department as may be necessary for the protection and improvement of the public health' (Iowa Code § 137.104(1)(b)), which take effect only after a public hearing, approval by the city council, board of supervisors or district board, and newspaper publication (Iowa Code § 137.104(1)(b)(1)-(4)). By agreement with a city, it may enforce the city's public health ordinances (Iowa Code § 137.104(2)(d)). Those rules can reach rental housing, and they bind you: breaking a local board of health rule or lawful order is a simple misdemeanor, each day after notice is a separate offense, and the board may impose a civil penalty of up to $750, or $1,000 for a repeat offense (Iowa Code § 137.117). A health rule may cover rental manufactured or mobile homes only if it also applies to other rental properties or to owner-occupied housing (Iowa Code § 364.3(5); Iowa Code § 331.304(9)). A tenant who has a health or safety complaint can go to the city's housing inspector or the local board of health on their own; you may not retaliate for a good-faith complaint to a government body charged with enforcing a building or housing code (`edu-retaliation-ia`). Check with your local board of health and city (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames have their own housing codes; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`), because this library does not cover local rules. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Lead-Safe Unit Certificate in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate for rental units, and nothing to attach to a lease as an exhibit. The federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978 still applies (`lead-based-paint`). Iowa's lead certification is for people, not units. The state certifies lead inspectors, lead abaters and lead-safe renovators, and 'a person ... shall not perform renovations on target housing or a child-occupied facility, unless the person has completed a training program approved by the department and has obtained certification pursuant to this section' (Iowa Code § 10A.902(3)). Target housing is, in general, 'housing constructed prior to 1978' (Iowa Code § 10A.901(2)), apart from housing for the elderly or for persons with disabilities and housing with no bedroom, unless a child under six lives or is expected to live there. This matters to you as a landlord. An owner who does lead inspection, abatement or renovation on the owner's own home 'is not required to obtain certification to perform these measures, unless the residential dwelling is occupied by a person other than the owner' (Iowa Code § 10A.902(2)) or the owner's immediate family while the work is done. So if you renovate, repaint or remodel an occupied pre-1978 rental yourself, you need the state certification and must follow the state work practice standards; if you hire someone, hire a certified renovator. A violation carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each offense (Iowa Code § 10A.902(4)). Anyone paid to renovate, remodel or repaint target housing must give the owner and the occupant an approved lead hazard pamphlet before starting (Iowa Code § 10A.903(1)(a); `edu-no-lead-state-notices-ia`). The state's detailed rules on certification and work practices are administrative rules this library has not read; follow them, and federal renovation rules may also apply. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Iowa Lead Notices With the Lease
bodyText:
Iowa adds no lead notice, certificate or information packet that you must deliver with a lease. The only lead disclosure for a rental is the federal one for housing built before 1978, with the federal pamphlet (`lead-based-paint`).

Three Iowa lead rules sit nearby and do not attach to the lease. First, anyone paid to renovate, remodel or repaint target housing 'shall provide an approved lead hazard information pamphlet to the owner and occupant of the housing or facility prior to commencing the services' (Iowa Code § 10A.903(1)(a)); a civil penalty of up to $5,000 applies (Iowa Code § 10A.903(2)). If you hire a contractor for work in an occupied pre-1978 unit, expect your tenant to receive that pamphlet; if you do the work yourself, see `edu-lead-safe-certification-ia`.

Second, Iowa's seller disclosure statement must report lead service lines (Iowa Code § 558A.4(1)(a)), but it applies to sales and other transfers of homes with one to four units (Iowa Code § 558A.1), not to leases.

Third, the state childhood lead poisoning program makes rules on 'Maximum blood lead levels in children living in targeted rental dwelling units' (Iowa Code § 135.102(3)) and offers model lead hazard remediation regulations that cities and counties may adopt when a child is found lead poisoned (Iowa Code § 135.102(6); Iowa Code § 135.105B). A local board of health or city that has adopted such rules may order you to fix lead hazards; check with your local board of health (`edu-no-health-district-rental-rules-ia`).

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Repair Orders and Receivership in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no receivership statute aimed at substandard rental buildings as such, and nothing limited to buildings with two or more units. Code enforcement against a rental is mainly local, backed by state statutes in four ways. First, a city's housing code program may include 'Authority for the issuance of orders requiring violations to be corrected within a reasonable time' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(2)), citations, injunctions, and, if other methods fail, authority for an officer to contract to have the work done, with the cost 'assessed to the violator' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(4)) and a lien on the property until paid (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). Second, any city may 'Require the abatement of a nuisance, public or private, in any reasonable manner' (Iowa Code § 364.12(3)(a)) and 'Require the removal, repair, or dismantling of a dangerous building or structure' (Iowa Code § 364.12(3)(c)); if you do not act within the time stated in the notice, the city may do the work and assess the cost against the property like a property tax (Iowa Code § 364.12(3)(h)). Third, in a municipal infraction case the court may order you to abate the violation, authorize the city to correct it, and enter the cost as a judgment against you or assess it against the property (Iowa Code § 364.22(10)(a)). Fourth, Iowa's receivership chapter for abandoned and nuisance buildings, Iowa Code ch. 657A, applies only where the city or county has adopted it by ordinance (Iowa Code § 657A.10A(1)) and does not reach agricultural land (Iowa Code § 657A.10A(2)). After a building official's inspection and written findings, the city, the county, a neighbor within 500 feet or a housing nonprofit may petition the district court; the court may order you to correct the conditions, and if no owner or other interested person undertakes the work, may appoint a receiver (Iowa Code § 657A.1A, Iowa Code § 657A.2, Iowa Code § 657A.3, Iowa Code § 657A.4). A receiver may be empowered to 'Take possession and control of the property, operate and manage the property, establish and collect rents and income, lease and rent the property, and evict tenants' (Iowa Code § 657A.6(1)), and may borrow against the property on a receiver's mortgage with priority (Iowa Code § 657A.6(9), Iowa Code § 657A.7). The chapter targets abandoned buildings: the petition is tied to the official's findings or to six months of abandonment (Iowa Code § 657A.2(1)), and it is unlawful to force, intimidate, harass or coerce a lawful occupant to leave so the property can be called vacant (Iowa Code § 657A.6A). A city or county may instead ask a court to order the owner to correct a public nuisance (Iowa Code § 657A.10C). A city may also condemn a residential building found to be a public nuisance and convey it for rehabilitation or rebuilding (Iowa Code § 364.12A; `edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-ia`). Check your city's ordinances (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own codes). Your tenant's own repair remedies are separate (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant about an outstanding housing inspection order, code violation notice, repair order or condemnation affecting the unit. Iowa's lease-time disclosures are the owner and manager names, utility charges, rent increase notice and a federal Superfund listing (Iowa Code § 562A.13; `edu-required-disclosures-ia`), and none covers code orders. The duty behind the order still binds you: you must 'Comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)), and an unremedied violation gives the tenant the repair remedies in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`. A city's housing code may let the city bar you from recovering rent for a dwelling that does not comply with the code (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(8); `edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-ia`), and a city may condemn a residential building found to be a public nuisance (Iowa Code § 364.12A). Cautious course: before a tenant signs, say in writing whether any inspection, repair or vacate order is open on the unit, and do not rent a unit a city has ordered vacated. Concealing a known order can expose you to claims outside the landlord-tenant act (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`), and a local code may require notice or posting; Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own rental codes, which this library does not cover. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa does not require you to tell a tenant about a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving such a notice out, and no Iowa statute makes you forfeit the deposit or pay double or treble for skipping an inspection (`edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-ia`). The deposit penalties that do exist turn on the written statement and on bad faith. If you do not return the deposit or send the written statement of specific reasons within thirty days after the tenancy ends and you receive the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, you 'shall forfeit all rights to withhold any portion of the rental deposit' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(4)). 'The bad-faith retention of a deposit by a landlord, or any portion of the rental deposit, in violation of this section shall subject the landlord to punitive damages not to exceed twice the monthly rental payment in addition to actual damages' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(7)); see `edu-deposit-return-penalty-ia`. An inspection still protects you: you carry the burden of proving each deduction (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b)), measured against the unit's condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(2)). Do a dated, photographed walk-through with the tenant at move-in and move-out. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Rent on Condemned or Noncompliant Units
bodyText: No Iowa statute itself bars you from collecting rent after a unit is condemned, placarded or ordered vacated. But a state statute lets cities adopt that bar locally. A city with a housing code under Iowa Code § 364.17 (every city of 15,000 or more, and any smaller city that opts in) may include in its enforcement program 'Authority by ordinance to provide that no rent shall be recoverable by the owner or lessee of any dwelling which does not comply with the housing code adopted by the city until such time as the dwelling does comply with the housing code adopted by the city' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(8)), and 'An escrow system for the deposit of rent which will be applied to the costs of correcting violations' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(5)). Where your city has adopted such an ordinance, you may be unable to recover rent for a noncompliant unit until it complies. Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own housing codes; check the ordinance, because this library does not cover local codes. State law also cuts or redirects rent in other ways (`edu-rent-demand-bar-ia`): after fire or casualty the tenant may leave and owe rent only to the date of the casualty, or, 'If continued occupancy is lawful' (Iowa Code § 562A.25(1)(b)), stay in the usable part at reduced rent; a tenant may recover or deduct for essential services you deliberately or negligently fail to supply (Iowa Code § 562A.23); and a court-appointed receiver may collect the rents of an abandoned or nuisance building (Iowa Code § 657A.6(1); `edu-substandard-property-receivership-ia`). Cautious course: do not rent, or collect rent for, a unit a city has ordered vacated or declared unfit, and fix code violations promptly; you must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Code Variance Notice in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no state sanitary or housing code variance that you must give to tenants or attach to a lease, and no statute requiring notice of a code exception or waiver. Housing code variances in Iowa are local. A city with a housing code under Iowa Code § 364.17 'may provide reasonable variances for existing structures which cannot practicably meet the standards in the code but are not unsafe for habitation' (Iowa Code § 364.17(4)); the statute says nothing about telling tenants. If your city grants you a variance, keep the written decision with your records and follow any condition the city attaches, including any notice or posting its ordinance requires. Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own housing codes, which this library does not cover. A variance does not lower your duty under the lease law to keep the unit fit and habitable (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2); `edu-habitability-ia`). Cautious course: if a variance affects something a tenant would notice, such as ceiling height, room size or egress, tell the tenant in writing before signing. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the building has a certificate of occupancy, to give a copy, to post it, or to attach a rental certificate to the lease. Certificates themselves are local. Under the state building code, local building departments 'Issue certificates of occupancy or use, permits, licenses, and other documents in connection with the construction of buildings or structures as may be required by ordinance' (Iowa Code § 103A.19(2)(d)), and a certificate of occupancy or use, until set aside, is binding on state and local agencies as to the matters it states (Iowa Code § 103A.19(2)(d)(2)). Larger cities must also certify inspected rental housing under their housing codes (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a); `edu-rental-inspection-ia`, `edu-landlord-registration-ia`). Whether you need either certificate before renting, and whether you must post it, depends on your city's ordinance; Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own codes, which this library does not cover. A city may not revoke, suspend or refuse to renew 'a rental certificate, license, or permit' (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(2)(c)(3)) because someone called police or emergency help (`edu-emergency-assistance-ia`). Cautious course: before renting a new, converted or altered space (a basement, attic or garage unit, or an accessory dwelling unit, `edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-ia`), confirm it has any certificate or permit the city requires and keep a copy; renting space the code does not allow can breach your duty to comply with building and housing codes (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Tenant Purchase Right in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no tenant opportunity-to-purchase law. When you sell a rental building, no Iowa statute requires you to notify tenants before the sale, offer the building or a unit to them first, give them a right of first refusal, or wait for a tenant association. A condominium conversion gives tenants no purchase right either (`edu-conversion-ia`). Iowa's statutory first-purchase rights in real estate belong to others, not tenants: for example a former farm mortgagor's right to repurchase after a sheriff's deed (Iowa Code § 654.16A), the right of an owner or person in possession of agricultural land to a first refusal when a foreclosure receiver leases it (Iowa Code § 654.14(2)), and a prior owner's right to buy back condemned land before the agency sells it (Iowa Code § 6B.56); none reaches a residential tenant. What a sale does require: within a reasonable time, transfer the deposits to the buyer and notify each tenant of the transfer and the buyer's name and address, or return the deposits (Iowa Code § 562A.12(5)(a); `edu-deposit-on-sale-ia`); keep the owner and manager disclosure current, which binds the new owner (Iowa Code § 562A.13(2)); and give the tenant written notice of the sale to be released from liability for later events (`edu-sale-management-change-ia`). The lease survives the sale. You may give a tenant an option to buy or a right of first refusal by contract, but the library does not offer such a clause (`edu-lease-option-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Purchase-Right Exemption Notice in Iowa
bodyText: Because Iowa has no tenant opportunity-to-purchase law (`edu-no-tpa-notice-ia`), there is no exemption notice, exemption filing or statement of exempt sale to give tenants or file with any agency when you sell a rental property. Nothing to file or send on an ordinary sale beyond the deposit transfer notice and the updated owner disclosure (Iowa Code § 562A.12(5)(a), Iowa Code § 562A.13(2); `edu-deposit-on-sale-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Sunset on Iowa Tenant Laws
bodyText: No Iowa tenant-protection statute is on a dated repeal clock. Iowa's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Iowa Code ch. 562A), the general landlord and tenant chapter (Iowa Code ch. 562), the eviction chapter (Iowa Code ch. 648) and the manufactured home community act (Iowa Code ch. 562B) carry no sunset date, and no 2025 or 2026 act amends or repeals them. Treat these rules as permanent until the legislature changes them. Changes do come by ordinary amendment instead. For example, the 2025 and 2026 sessions narrowed what local governments may do on rentals and civil rights (2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1002 on local civil rights laws; accessory dwelling units, `edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-ia`). Check each year's new laws, which generally take effect on July 1 unless the act says otherwise (Iowa Code § 3.7(1)). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Voucher Inspections and Refusals in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute addresses refusing to rent because a housing assistance program requires an inspection of the unit, and none sets a deadline for a program to inspect or approve a unit. Iowa law does not require you to accept a housing choice voucher at all: a city or county may not adopt or enforce an ordinance that stops an owner from refusing to rent to a person because of the person's 'use of a federal housing choice voucher issued by the United States department of housing and urban development' (Iowa Code § 364.3(16); counties, Iowa Code § 331.304(13)), and Iowa's civil rights act has no source-of-income category (`edu-source-of-income-ia`). If you do rent to a voucher holder, the program inspects the unit under its federal rules, and HUD's tenancy addendum becomes part of your lease (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`); federal program rules are not covered in detail here. Federal housing quality standards are also one of the codes an Iowa city may adopt as its housing code (Iowa Code § 364.17(1)(e)). Two limits remain. Refusing a voucher must not be a cover for refusing someone on a protected trait such as race, disability or familial status (`edu-fair-housing-ia`). And apply the same policy to every applicant (`edu-tenant-screening-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Repair Escrow Exemption in Iowa
bodyText: Some states let a small landlord opt out of a tenant's rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving notice. Iowa has no such exemption and no exemption notice: its tenant repair remedies apply to every landlord covered by the landlord-tenant act, whatever the number of units (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`), and the act's rights cannot be waived in the lease (`edu-nonwaivable-rights-ia`). Iowa has no statewide rent escrow for repairs either. Rent goes into court only inside a case: when you sue for possession for nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant is in possession, and the tenant counterclaims, 'the court from time to time may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing' (Iowa Code § 562A.24(1); `edu-rent-into-court-ia`). Locally, a city housing code program may include 'An escrow system for the deposit of rent which will be applied to the costs of correcting violations' (Iowa Code § 364.17(3)(a)(5)); whether your city has one, and whether it exempts anyone, is a matter of local ordinance (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own codes, which this library does not cover). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Special District Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: No Iowa statute requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, that the property lies in a special taxing, assessment or improvement district. Iowa has such districts, for example self-supported municipal improvement districts taxed under Iowa Code ch. 386 (Iowa Code § 386.1) and real estate improvement districts under Iowa Code ch. 358C, and cities levy special assessments for public improvements, but these are charges on the owner and the property, not on the tenant. Iowa once had a statute on disclosing a real estate improvement district's special assessments; it was repealed in 2008 (Iowa Code § 358C.24, a repeal note only). If you want the tenant to bear a share of property taxes or assessments, the lease must say so; see `edu-tax-escalation-ia`. Otherwise these costs stay with you. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Government Approval Needed for an Iowa Lease
bodyText: Iowa has no communal, clan or native land system, and no Iowa statute requires a government officer to approve a residential lease before it is valid. An ordinary lease between private parties needs no government approval. One special case: the Meskwaki Settlement (the Sac and Fox Indian settlement in Tama County). Iowa civil law applies there and Iowa courts hear civil cases arising there (Iowa Code § 1.12), and tribal ordinances or customs consistent with state civil law are given effect (Iowa Code § 1.14). But nothing in those sections authorizes 'the alienation, encumbrance, or taxation of any real or personal property ... belonging to any Indian or Indian tribe, band, or community that is held in trust by the United States or is subject to a restriction against alienation imposed by the United States' (Iowa Code § 1.13), or regulation of that property inconsistent with federal law. So whether and how land held in trust for the tribe or a tribal member may be leased is a federal and tribal question, not covered here; get advice before leasing such land. Separately, a lease of agricultural land for more than five years must be recorded, and some foreign owners face farmland limits (`edu-lease-registration-ia`, `edu-foreign-ownership-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Submetered Electricity and Gas
bodyText: Iowa has no statute requiring a special lease disclosure for submetered electricity or gas, and no statute saying whether a landlord who resells it to tenants becomes a regulated utility. Iowa's utility law covers anyone owning or operating facilities for 'Furnishing gas by piped distribution system or electricity to the public for compensation' (Iowa Code § 476.1(2)(a)); whether billing your own tenants counts is not settled by any statute or held rule, so don't treat a submeter as a business of its own. The Iowa Utilities Commission's rules for rate-regulated electric and gas utilities allow an owner to pass master-metered energy on to occupants, within a limit: 'If a multitenant building is master-metered, the end-user occupants may be charged for electricity as an unidentified portion of the rent, condominium fee, or similar payment, or, if some other method of allocating the cost of the electric service is used, the total charge for electric service shall not exceed the total electric bill charged by the utility for the same period' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(c)). The gas rule says the same for natural gas (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.3(1)(c), in the version effective December 16, 2026). So if you submeter or otherwise allocate gas or electricity, keep the total you collect from all tenants at or below the utility's bill for the same period, with no markup or added fee. The same rules require the utility to meter each unit of a multitenant building separately unless an exception applies: central heating, cooling, water-heating or ventilation systems; facilities designated for elderly or handicapped persons; buildings where 'submetering or resale of service was permitted prior to 1966' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(b)(3)); buildings where individual meters are impractical; and buildings that qualify for a master meter by projected energy savings (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(b); Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.3(1)(b)). Ask the utility before changing how a building is metered. Municipal utilities and electric cooperatives follow other rules, not covered here. If the tenant pays you rather than the utility, you must fully explain the utility rates, charges and services before the lease is signed (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4)); record that with `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`. See also `edu-utility-apportionment-ia` and `edu-utility-allowance-cap-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Charging for Shared or Unmetered Utilities
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute that bars or limits a lease term making the tenant pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit, such as a share of the building's water, sewer or trash bill or of common-area electricity, and no rule tied to a lease-signing date. You may include such a term (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)) if you follow these rules.

First, if the tenant pays you rather than the utility, you must 'fully explain utility rates, charges and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4)); write the sharing method into `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`.

Second, for gas or electricity from a master meter, the total you charge all tenants may not exceed the utility's bill for the same period (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(c); Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.3(1)(c), version effective December 16, 2026; `edu-electric-submetering-ia`).

Third, for water: the Utilities Commission's rule for the water utilities it regulates says 'Separate premises will be separately metered and billed. Submetering is not permitted' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-21.3(1)(b)). Most Iowa water comes from city utilities, which that rule does not reach (Iowa Code § 476.1(3)), and city rules differ. Whether the rule bars a landlord's own water submeters is not settled; before installing submeters, ask the water utility, and otherwise share the building's water bill by a stated formula.

Amounts the lease requires the tenant to pay you are rent under Iowa's definition (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`), and unpaid city utility charges on an account in your name can become a lien on the property (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`).

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Shutting Off Utilities You Supply
bodyText: Iowa has no special procedure that lets a landlord who submeters, resells or supplies electricity, gas or water disconnect a tenant, for nonpayment or anything else. The utility disconnection rules bind the utility, not you (`edu-utility-shutoff-statute-ia`). What binds you is a flat bar: if you 'willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant' (Iowa Code § 562A.26), the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent and attorney fees; and you may not take possession that way (Iowa Code § 562A.33; `edu-self-help-eviction-ia`). Cutting service can also be unlawful retaliation after a code or repair complaint (Iowa Code § 562A.36). If a tenant does not pay utility charges the lease makes payable to you, treat them as unpaid rent and use the nonpayment notice and the courts (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`, `edu-nonpayment-notice-ia`), never the meter. For repairs, you may enter with at least 24 hours' notice to make necessary repairs or supply services (Iowa Code § 562A.19), but no statute sets rules for planned service outages. Keep them short, give notice beforehand unless there is an emergency, and restore service promptly: an outage you cause deliberately or negligently can trigger the tenant's remedies for failure to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services (Iowa Code § 562A.23; `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`). The library offers no clause letting you interrupt service, because a term limiting those remedies would be unenforceable (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a), (d)); if you want one, take advice and add your own. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area; the bar on limiting your liability (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(d)) has no such exception, so do not add an interruption clause there either without advice.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules
bodyText:
Iowa limits when gas and electric utilities may disconnect a home, mainly for the occupant's protection; the rules bind the utility, and the debt is still owed. Rate-regulated utilities, and city-owned gas and electric utilities, follow Iowa Code § 476.20 and the Iowa Utilities Commission's rules (Iowa Code § 384.84(3)(a)); cooperatives and small utilities follow rules not covered here. For a residential customer:
- (1) Notice: a written notice at least 12 days before the disconnection date, also sent to anyone the customer has designated, plus an attempt to reach the customer by phone or in person; from November 1 through April 1, if that fails, the utility posts a notice at the home at least a day ahead. If a renting customer can't be reached, the utility must try to contact you as landlord at least 48 hours before (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(a), (d)(2), (d)(5)).
- (2) Timing: 'Disconnection of a residential customer may take place only between the hours of 6 a.m. and 2 p.m. on a weekday and not on weekends or holidays' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(7)).
- (3) Cold: no disconnection of a home whose only heat depends on that service when the temperature or 24-hour forecast is 20 degrees Fahrenheit or colder (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(8)).
- (4) Winter assistance: 'a public utility furnishing gas or electricity shall not disconnect service from November 1 through April 1 to a residence which has a resident that has been certified under this paragraph' (Iowa Code § 476.20(3)(b)) as eligible for low-income energy or weatherization assistance; a household that may qualify gets 30 days to apply. This is a seasonal moratorium for certified households, not a longer notice period for everyone.
- (5) Health: a doctor's or public health official's verification of an especial danger to a resident's health postpones disconnection for 30 days (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(9)).
- (6) Military: no disconnection during a household head's deployment or for 90 days after, once the utility is told (Iowa Code § 476.20(3)(c)).
- (7) Disputes: paying the undisputed part delays disconnection up to 45 days (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(6)).

The gas rules are similar (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.4(14), version effective December 16, 2026). Iowa has no standing rule barring disconnection during a declared storm or other disaster, and no hot-weather rule.

City water, sewer and trash service may be cut off for delinquency after written notice and a chance for a hearing, and you can ask in writing to get a copy of the notice for your tenant's account (Iowa Code § 384.84(3)(c); `edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`).

A shutoff of the tenant's own account doesn't end your duties: you must still supply heat and water where the lease or Iowa Code § 562A.15 makes them yours (`edu-heating-ia`). For accounts in your name, see `edu-utility-landlord-account-ia`; for being copied on notices, `edu-utility-disconnection-notice-authorization-ia`.

title: Getting Copies of Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
Iowa lets a tenant who holds a gas or electric account name you to receive copies of disconnection notices. The Iowa Utilities Commission's rules require a rate-regulated utility, before disconnecting for nonpayment, to have 'Given the customer, and any other person or agency designated by the customer, written notice that the customer has at least 12 days in which to make settlement of the account to avoid disconnection' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(2)); the gas rules say the same (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.4(14)(d)(2), version effective December 16, 2026).

The designation is the customer's, made with the utility; no Iowa statute or held rule requires it to be in a separate document or forbids a lease term in which the tenant agrees to make it, and none obliges a utility to accept a lease clause in place of its own form. Separately, even without the tenant's consent, the utility must try to reach you at least 48 hours before disconnecting a renting customer it cannot contact (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(5)).

For city water, sewer, storm water and trash service you can ask yourself: 'If the account holder is a tenant, and if the owner or landlord of the property or premises has made a written request for notice, the notice shall also be given to the owner or landlord' (Iowa Code § 384.84(3)(c)); the same written request gets you notice of a lien certification and of a tenant's request to change the name on the account (Iowa Code § 384.84(3)(c), (4)(c); `edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`). Send that request to each city utility at the start of each tenancy.

The library's optional clause `utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co` applies in Iowa: the tenant authorizes you as an additional contact and agrees to sign the utility's form. Municipal utilities and cooperatives may have their own practices, not covered here. See also `edu-utility-shutoff-statute-ia`.

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText:
When a gas or electric account for the building or unit is in your name, you are the utility's customer, and the shutoff rules protect you as customer (12 days' written notice and the other limits in `edu-utility-shutoff-statute-ia`). Your tenants get one extra protection: 'If the disconnection will affect occupants of residential units leased from the customer, the premises of any building known by the utility to contain residential units affected by disconnection must be posted, at least two days prior to disconnection, with a notice informing any occupants of the date when service will be disconnected and the reasons for the disconnection' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(14)(d)(5)). The gas rules say the same (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.4(14)(d)(4), version effective December 16, 2026).

Your unpaid bill does not follow your tenants: a rate-regulated utility may not refuse service to a tenant who applies in their own name because of a previous occupant's debt, or because of an occupant's debt if the applicant is creditworthy and can pay any deposit, and it may not refuse someone service because they did not pay a bill they guaranteed for another customer (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(15)(a), (d), (h)).

Against you, the tenant has the remedies of the landlord-tenant act. If the lease or Iowa Code § 562A.15 makes heat, water, hot water or another essential service yours and you deliberately or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may give written notice and then 'Procure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services' (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)(a)) and deduct the cost from rent, or recover reduced rental value or rent paid for the period (Iowa Code § 562A.23(1)(b)-(c); `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`); a shutoff you cause willfully brings the remedies of Iowa Code § 562A.26 (`edu-utility-interruption-submeter-ia`).

Iowa has no statute letting tenants petition for a rent receiver to pay a landlord's utility bill, and no rule making a master-meter owner identify tenants to the utility; Iowa's receivership statutes (for example, abandoned buildings under Iowa Code § 657A.6 and mortgage foreclosure under Iowa Code § 654.14) are not tenant remedies. Unpaid city water, sewer and trash charges on a property can become a lien (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`).

Pay utilities in your name on time, and if you can't, tell your tenants before the utility posts the building.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Putting Utilities in the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
Iowa sets no deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name and gives you no right to cut off service that is still in your name because the tenant has not transferred it. A lease may require the transfer by a date you choose and repayment of what the provider charged you meanwhile (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)); the library's clause `utility-transfer-nj` does both and applies in Iowa.

But if you shut off or ask a provider to discontinue service to an occupied unit, you risk the remedies for a landlord who 'willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant' (Iowa Code § 562A.26): possession or termination, actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent and attorney fees (`edu-self-help-eviction-ia`). Recover unpaid reimbursements through the lease and the courts instead.

For city water, sewer and trash, protect yourself on paper: give the city utility written notice naming the tenant who is liable, the address and the date occupancy begins, renew it within 30 business days after each change of tenant, and ask in writing for notice of disconnection and of any request to change the name on the account (Iowa Code § 384.84(3)(c), (4)(d), (4)(e); for water, the lien exemption applies only if the unit's water is separately metered; `edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`). For gas and electricity, the tenant may also designate you to get copies of disconnection notices (`edu-utility-disconnection-notice-authorization-ia`).

If you keep an account in your name and bill the tenant, explain the charges before the lease is signed (`utility-charges-disclosure-ia`).

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilling Limits
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute capping what a landlord may rebill a tenant for utilities and no statute on utility allowances. The limit that exists is in the Iowa Utilities Commission's rules for gas and electricity from a master meter serving several units: you may include the cost in rent as an unidentified amount, or, 'if some other method of allocating the cost of the electric service is used, the total charge for electric service shall not exceed the total electric bill charged by the utility for the same period' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.3(1)(c)); the gas rule is the same (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-19.3(1)(c), version effective December 16, 2026).

Nothing requires you to use a fixed rent only. A utility allowance (you pay up to a set amount each month and the tenant repays the excess) is lawful. Use it where the meter serves only the tenant's unit, so that the excess is simply the provider's bill above the allowance; the optional clause `utility-allowance-ia` is drafted that way.

For a meter shared with other units or common areas, don't use an allowance; share the bill by a stated method that never collects more than the utility billed (`edu-utility-apportionment-ia`).

Either way, if the tenant pays you rather than the utility, you must fully explain the rates, charges and services before the lease is signed (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`). Payments the lease requires the tenant to make to you are rent under Iowa's definition (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`), so don't add late fees on top of an overage.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Utility Attachment Required
bodyText: Iowa does not require you to attach any utility document to the lease: no utility bill copies, rate schedules, past-usage history or average-cost statement, and no utility addendum. The one utility disclosure duty is to 'fully explain utility rates, charges and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed unless paid by the tenant directly to the utility company' (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4)). It applies only to utilities the tenant pays you for, and the statute doesn't require it in writing; the library's clause `utility-charges-disclosure-ia` records in the lease that you gave it, which is your evidence if a tenant later disputes a charge. A written utility addendum is lawful if you want one (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)), and you may keep the bills that support any charge you pass on. For utilities the tenant pays directly, you may still tell the tenant which services they must set up (`utilities-responsibility`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, which does require a written explanation; not covered here.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or held utility rule that lets a charge for energy-efficiency work stay with the meter and pass to the next customer, so there is no meter conservation charge to disclose to a new tenant and no rule letting a tenant deduct one from rent. Iowa also has no statute on landlord water submeters of the kind some states have (no city-rate rule, surcharge ban or monthly two-reading statement). What does limit you: for gas or electricity through a master meter, the total charged to occupants may not exceed the utility's bill (`edu-electric-submetering-ia`), which leaves no room for a meter surcharge; and the water utilities the Utilities Commission regulates do not permit submetering (`edu-utility-apportionment-ia`). If a utility program or loan you used for efficiency work shows up on a bill the tenant will pay, explain it before the lease is signed (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`).

title: Tenant Energy Data and Benchmarking
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy usage data to the owner: none authorizes a lease clause to do it, none requires it, and none forbids it. No Iowa city, county or the state building code commissioner may impose energy benchmarking on private property: 'A city shall not adopt or enforce an ordinance, motion, resolution, or amendment to require energy benchmarking requirements for a private property' (Iowa Code § 414.1(1)(g)); counties and the commissioner are barred the same way (Iowa Code § 331.301(23); Iowa Code § 103A.8D). In these statutes "energy benchmarking" means requiring a property to cut its average energy use or to use less than similar properties, so the bar does not reach an ordinance that only requires owners to measure or report energy use; local ordinances were not searched, so check your city's rules before assuming no reporting duty applies.

If you want usage data for an energy audit, a rebate application or your own records, get the tenant's consent: the library's optional clause `energy-data-release-wy` applies in Iowa. It works through the tenant's agreement to sign the utility's own release form, because a lease cannot make a utility hand over data, and each utility decides what consent it accepts. Use the data only for the stated purpose.

title: Utility Charges and Deposits
bodyText: Iowa's deposit statute doesn't name utility charges, but it covers them when the lease makes them payable to you: you may withhold amounts reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default in rent 'or of other funds due to the landlord pursuant to the rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(1)). Iowa has no rule keeping landlord-billed utilities out of rent; a payment the lease requires the tenant to make to you is rent under Iowa's definition (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`). What you may not withhold is a debt the tenant owes a utility company on the tenant's own account, unless the lease requires the tenant to repay you and you actually paid it. Itemize any utility deduction in the written statement within 30 days, with the bill to back it up (`security-deposit-return-ia`). If you collect a separate utility deposit yourself, it is a rental deposit (a deposit securing performance of the rental agreement): it counts toward the two-months'-rent cap and follows the same holding and return rules (`edu-deposit-cap-ia`). Deposits held by utilities follow their own rules. A rate-regulated gas or electric utility refunds a deposit after 12 consecutive months of prompt payment and pays interest on it (Iowa Admin. Code r. 199-20.4(4), (7)), and it must let someone other than the customer pay the deposit: 'Upon termination of service to such a customer, the deposit plus accumulated interest less any unpaid utility bill of the customer, shall be reimbursed to the person who made the deposit' (Iowa Code § 476.20(5)(c)). So if you pay a tenant's utility deposit, the refund at the end comes back to you, less the tenant's unpaid bill. City utilities set their own deposits (Iowa Code § 476.20(5)(a)); a city water deposit tied to your lien-protection notice is returned when the tenant moves out if the water charges are paid in full (Iowa Code § 384.84(4)(d)(2); `edu-municipal-utility-lien-ia`). Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Fire and Building Codes for Rentals
bodyText: Iowa has a state fire code and a state building code, but which one reaches your rental depends on the building and the city. Fire code: the state fire code is the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, with Iowa amendments (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)). The statute directs fire safety rules for 'apartment buildings, food establishments as defined in section 137F.1, and all other buildings or structures in which persons congregate from time to time, whether publicly or privately owned' (Iowa Code § 10A.523(1)). Violating a rule is a simple misdemeanor, and a serious misdemeanor if it is a clear and present danger to life and is not fixed within 30 days after written notice (Iowa Code § 10A.523(1)). A fire chief or trained fire inspector may enter at a reasonable hour and must order correction of a violation of the state rules or a local fire ordinance (Iowa Code § 10A.514; Iowa Code § 10A.515). Where a city adopts and enforces any edition of the International Fire Code with plan review and regular inspections, a building the city has verified as complying is deemed to comply with the state rules (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.11(1)). Whether the state fire code reaches a single-family rental house is not settled by the rules read; assume the local code does. Building code: the state building code (International Building Code, International Residential Code and International Existing Building Code, 2024 editions, with Iowa amendments; `edu-frozen-standard-incorporation-ia`) applies only where a city or county adopts it, in a city of more than 15,000 people without its own model-based code, and to state-owned and state-funded construction (Iowa Code § 103A.10(2)); elsewhere local building codes govern, except that the code's factory-built structure provisions, its energy-conservation and lighting-efficiency standards and, for new one- and two-family homes, its radon-mitigation provisions apply statewide (Iowa Code § 103A.10(3), (4); 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1124). A building's existing legal occupancy may continue except where the code or the state fire code specifically reaches it, and additions and alterations must meet current code (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.3(4); Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.10). Your duty under the lease law is to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1); `edu-habitability-ia`); tenants must comply with code duties that fall on tenants (Iowa Code § 562A.17(1)). Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms: `edu-alarm-duties-ia`. City housing codes and rental inspections (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others): `edu-rental-inspection-ia`. Grills: 'Charcoal burners and ash- or coal-producing devices shall not be operated on combustible balconies or within 10 feet of combustible construction' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)(d)), with exceptions for one- and two-family dwellings, a gas grill on one 20-pound LP container, and sprinklered buildings; the library's stricter clause `fire-safety-grilling` applies in Iowa.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Iowa Rentals
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or held rule requiring you to retrofit sprinklers into an existing rental. Sprinkler duties arise from construction: (1) New buildings under the state building code or state fire code: 'An automatic sprinkler system installed in accordance with section 903.3 shall be provided throughout all buildings with a Group R fire area' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.3(14)); the state fire code says the same (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)(h)). That reaches apartment buildings and other buildings built under the International Building Code. (2) One- and two-family houses and townhouses built under the residential code: Iowa deleted that code's sprinkler requirements for new one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.8(5), (6)). (3) High-rises: 'All buildings approved for construction after July 1, 1998, that exceed four stories in height, or seventy-five feet above grade, shall require the installation of an approved automatic fire extinguishing system' (Iowa Code § 10A.524(1)); buildings existing or under construction on August 15, 1975 are exempt unless later enlarged or altered beyond the height limits. (4) Alterations and additions must meet current code for the parts affected (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.10). The state building code applies only where adopted or required (`edu-fire-code-standard-ia`), and local codes may differ, though a city or county may not require sprinklers in a single-family detached dwelling or a dwelling with no more than two units as a condition of a home-based business (Iowa Code § 414.33(5); Iowa Code § 335.35(5)). If your building has a sprinkler system, keep it in good and safe working order like any facility you supply (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)), and use licensed fire protection system workers for installation and maintenance (Iowa Code § 100D.2(1)). The model codes adopted by reference were not read beyond the Iowa amendments.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Required
bodyText: Iowa has no statute or held rule requiring you to tell tenants, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has fire sprinklers, and no state grant, loan or tax credit for adding sprinklers to an existing rental. You may describe the building's fire protection in the lease if you wish (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)); if you do, keep it accurate. Where sprinklers exist, tenants must not damage or disable them (Iowa Code § 562A.17(6)), and you must keep them working (`edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-ia`). Some city housing codes and local fire codes may require notices or postings; check yours (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`).

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Iowa's state codes are frozen at the edition the rule names: 'The adoption of standards by reference to another publication or a part thereof shall not include adoption of any amendment, edition, or version of the publication subsequent to the effective date of the adoption' (Iowa Code § 17A.6(5)). A new edition of a model code binds you in Iowa only after the agency amends its rule, so check the rule's text, not the latest model code. The editions in force in the rules read for this library are: state fire code, International Fire Code 2024 (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)); state building code, International Building Code 2024, International Residential Code 2024 and International Existing Building Code 2024 (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.3, Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.8, Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.7); energy code, International Energy Conservation Code 2012, residential and commercial provisions (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.24, Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.25). The editions differ: the 2024 building and fire codes sit beside a 2012 energy code, and the energy code applies statewide to new construction even where a city hasn't adopted the state building code (Iowa Code § 103A.10(4)(a), (5)). Plumbing, mechanical and electrical codes are adopted by other boards in rule chapters not covered here. Cities adopt their own codes the same way: an ordinance must identify the code 'by subject matter, source and date' (Iowa Code § 380.10(1)), so a city's housing, building or fire code also stays at the edition it adopted until the city updates it (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). A building built lawfully under an older edition may generally keep its legal occupancy unless the current code or the state fire code specifically reaches it (`edu-fire-code-standard-ia`).

title: Heat in Iowa Rentals
bodyText:
You must 'Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6)).

Iowa sets no minimum indoor temperature and no heating season for rentals; a city housing code may (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`). You must also keep supplied heating equipment in good and safe working order (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)).

Shifting heat: where the tenant controls a unit-only furnace on the tenant's own gas or electric account, the heat duty falls outside your duty by the statute's own exception. Otherwise, only in a single family residence may you and the tenant agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant supplies heat (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)), for example a house heated by propane or fuel oil the tenant buys. For any other unit the duty stays with you; a tenant may take on specified repairs or tasks only by a separate signed writing with adequate consideration (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3); `maintenance-allocation-ia`), and a lease term waiving the duty is unenforceable (`edu-habitability-ia`).

If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable heat and deduct the cost from rent, or recover reduced rental value or rent paid for the period (Iowa Code § 562A.23; `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia`).

Boilers: the state boiler act requires periodic state inspection of boilers operating above 15 pounds per square inch, but exempts heating boilers in residences and low-pressure heating boilers in buildings other than places of public assembly, and small water heaters (Iowa Code § 89.3(1); Iowa Code § 89.4(1)(e), (g), (i)), so most apartment heating boilers need no state certificate.

Tenants must use heating equipment in a reasonable manner (Iowa Code § 562A.17(5)); the optional clause `heat-freeze-protection-ia` sets a minimum thermostat setting to protect pipes, and `extended-absence-notice-ks` covers winter absences. For utility shutoff protections in cold weather, see `edu-utility-shutoff-statute-ia`.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Iowa's statutes set no maximum or minimum water heater temperature and don't require you to reset a unit's water heater before each new tenant. Your duty is to supply 'reasonable amounts of hot water at all times' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6)) and keep the water heater you supply in good and safe working order (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)); if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply hot water, the tenant has the remedies in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ia` (Iowa Code § 562A.23). A household water heater of 120 gallons or less within the boiler act's limits needs no state boiler inspection (Iowa Code § 89.4(1)(i)). Installation standards for water heaters and fixtures, including any limit on hot water temperature, are in the state plumbing code, which is not covered here; follow it and the manufacturer's instructions when you install or replace a heater. Setting the heater at a safe temperature at each turnover is good practice to reduce scald risk, though no Iowa statute requires it.

title: No Window Guard Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no window-guard law for rentals. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to install window guards, window stops or other child fall-protection devices, to offer them to a household with young children, or to put a window-guard notice in the lease, and none regulates security or burglar bars or requires you to tell a tenant how bars release. Windows still fall under your general duties: you must 'Comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)) and 'Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2)); see `edu-habitability-ia`. Iowa's state building code adopts the International Residential Code and the International Building Code, 2024 editions, by reference (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.8, Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.3), and Iowa rewrote the house code's escape-window rule: 'every sleeping room have at least one operable emergency and rescue opening' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.8(7)), and 'The net clear opening dimensions are obtained by the normal operation of the emergency escape and rescue opening from the inside' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-301.8(7)). The state building code governs construction and alterations, and only where it applies: state buildings, cities and counties that accept it by ordinance, state-funded new construction, and cities over fifteen thousand people without their own national-code-based building code (Iowa Code § 103A.10(2)). The state fire code also adopts the International Fire Code (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)); see `edu-fire-code-standard-ia` for which code reaches your building. What the national codes themselves say about window fall protection and about bars or grilles over escape windows is national code text this library does not hold, so ask your building official before installing bars or relying on an exemption. Cities such as Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and Ames run their own housing codes and rental inspections under Iowa Code § 364.17 (`edu-rental-inspection-ia`), and those codes may say more. A safe course: never cover a bedroom escape window with bars or grilles that cannot be opened from inside without a key or tool, and if a tenant with young children asks for window stops or guards, you may agree in writing, choosing devices that do not block the escape opening.

title: Common Area Lighting
bodyText: Iowa has no statute that spells out how halls, stairs, entrances or parking areas of a rental building must be lit. Two general rules reach lighting. First, you must 'Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(3)) and comply with applicable building and housing codes (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1)); a dark stairway or a burned-out entry light can breach both. Second, the state fire marshal's rules must include 'standards relating to exits and exit lights' (Iowa Code § 10A.523(1)) for buildings including 'apartment buildings' (Iowa Code § 10A.523(1)), and the state fire code adopts the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, for all occupancies (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1); `edu-fire-code-standard-ia`). The fire code's own exit-sign and egress-lighting text is national code text this library does not hold; ask your fire official or city what applies to your building. City housing codes under Iowa Code § 364.17 (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and other cities; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) commonly set hallway and stair lighting standards. Iowa's one express hallway-lighting statute is for migrant labor camps, not ordinary rentals. No Iowa statute or held rule says whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric meter. A lease term sharing common-area electricity is not barred (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)); see `edu-utility-apportionment-ia` and `edu-electric-submetering-ia` for the limits on charging tenants for building utilities. A safer course is to keep hall, stair and exterior lights on a house meter you pay; if an existing light runs through a tenant's meter, tell the tenant in writing before the lease is signed and credit the cost or rewire it. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText:
Iowa law does not require you to supply a stove, oven, range or refrigerator. No Iowa statute or held rule lists them as part of a fit and habitable unit, and Iowa's landlord-tenant act names them only to define a roomer: a person in a unit that lacks a major bathroom or kitchen facility in a building where such facilities are shared, and a kitchen's major facility 'means refrigerator, stove or sink' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(14)). That label matters for one rule: unless the lease fixes a definite term, 'the tenancy shall be week-to-week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent' (Iowa Code § 562A.9(5)).

Once you supply an appliance, you must keep it working: you must 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)). The words 'and other facilities and appliances' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)) reach a stove or refrigerator you provide, and a lease cannot waive that duty (`edu-habitability-ia`).

Only in a single family residence may you and the tenant agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant does specified repairs (Iowa Code § 562A.15(2)); in other units a repair agreement needs a separate signed writing with adequate consideration (Iowa Code § 562A.15(3)); see `maintenance-allocation-ia`. The tenant must use supplied appliances reasonably (Iowa Code § 562A.17(5)).

List the appliances you supply in the lease with `appliances-included`, so it is clear which ones you must maintain.

City housing codes under Iowa Code § 364.17 (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may require cooking or refrigeration equipment, and a code that applies becomes part of your duty under Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1). Iowa's migrant labor camp statute does require refrigeration and stoves, but only for those camps.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no radiator-cover rule. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to cover or guard steam radiators or hot heating pipes, to offer covers to a tenant with young children, or to attach a radiator-cover rider to the lease; the word radiator appears in Iowa's statutes only in an insurance-coverage list. Your duties for heating equipment are the general ones: you must 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4)) that you supply, comply with applicable building and housing codes, and keep the unit fit and habitable (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(1), Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2); `edu-habitability-ia`), and you must supply 'reasonable heat' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6)) unless the tenant controls the system. A heating hazard that a building or housing code addresses, or that makes the unit unsafe, falls under those duties.
