Iowa's state boiler inspections do not reach most rental heating: the boiler chapter does not apply to 'Heating boilers in residences' (Iowa Code § 89.4(1)(e)) or to 'Low pressure heating boilers used in buildings other than those for public assembly' (Iowa Code § 89.4(1)(g)), so keeping a steam system safe is on you and your heating contractor. If you have steam radiators and a tenant with small children asks for covers, you may agree in writing (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)); choose covers made for the radiator so they do not block heat output or controls. City housing codes under Iowa Code § 364.17 (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may say more.

title: Pools and Spas at Iowa Rentals
bodyText:
If your rental property has a swimming pool, wading pool, spa (a hot tub or whirlpool) or spray pad for tenants, Iowa's pool law probably applies to it. The chapter 'applies to all spray pads, swimming pools, and spas owned or operated by ... commercial interests or private entities including but not limited to facilities operated by ... apartments, condominiums, and health or country clubs' (Iowa Code § 135I.2).

What it requires: 'A person shall not operate a spray pad, swimming pool, or spa without first having registered with the department' (Iowa Code § 135I.3), renewed every year. The Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing, or a local board of health by agreement, inspects pools and sets minimum safety and sanitation criteria by rule (Iowa Code § 135I.4). Pools 'operated by apartments, condominiums' (Iowa Code § 135I.4(3)) are exempt from the lifeguard requirements. Each day of a violation is a separate simple misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 135I.5), and the department or local board may order the pool closed until it is fixed (Iowa Code § 135I.6).

What it does not reach: 'facilities intended for single family use' (Iowa Code § 135I.2), so a pool or hot tub at a single-family rental house is outside the chapter; and a pool or spa run by a homeowners' association or housing cooperative of seventy-two or fewer units whose bylaws claim the exemption, provide for inspection by someone else and assume the liability, with bylaws that also apply to rental agreements for the units (Iowa Code § 135I.2).

No Iowa statute requires a pool-safety notice in the lease or a fence or barrier around a pool at a single-family rental. The barrier, gate and operating standards for covered pools are in the department's rules, and local building codes and ordinances commonly require fences for private pools; neither is quoted here, so check both before renting a property with a pool.

Your duty to keep common areas 'in a clean and safe condition' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(3)) covers a shared pool, and a lease cannot limit your liability for it (`edu-exculpatory-clauses-ia`). For pool rules in the lease, use `pool-use-ia`.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no balcony or deck inspection law. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to have balconies, decks, porches, exterior stairways or other elevated elements of a rental building inspected on a schedule, to hire an engineer or inspector for them, to file a report, or to tell tenants about an inspection. Your general duties still cover them: balconies, decks and outside stairs are part of the premises, so you must comply with applicable building and housing codes, keep the premises fit and habitable, and keep common areas 'in a clean and safe condition' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(3)); see `edu-habitability-ia`. A rotted deck or loose railing is a repair you owe. The one balcony rule in Iowa's held rules is a fire rule: under the state fire code, 'Charcoal burners and ash- or coal-producing devices shall not be operated on combustible balconies or within 10 feet of combustible construction' (Iowa Admin. Code r. 481-280.8(1)(d)), except at one- and two-family dwellings, for a gas grill on one 20-pound LP-gas container, and where the building, balconies and decks are sprinklered. The library's tenant grilling rule, `fire-safety-grilling`, is stricter than that and is lawful (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)). New and altered balconies and decks must meet the building code where the state code or a local code applies (`edu-fire-code-standard-ia`). City housing codes and rental inspection programs under Iowa Code § 364.17 (Des Moines, Iowa City, Cedar Rapids, Ames and others; `edu-rental-inspection-ia`) may inspect exterior elements during a rental inspection. A sound practice for wood balconies and decks on multi-unit buildings is to have them checked by a qualified contractor every few years and after any sign of rot or movement, and to keep the report.

title: Rentals Served by a Private Well
bodyText: Iowa does not require you to test a private well that serves a rental or to give tenants well-test results, and no statute or held rule requires a well notice in the lease. Two rules matter. First, size. A well system that serves enough people is a regulated public water system, whoever owns it: a public water supply system is one 'for the provision to the public of piped water for human consumption, if the system has at least fifteen service connections or regularly serves at least twenty-five individuals' (Iowa Code § 455B.171(26)). Operating one without a written permit from the Department of Natural Resources is unlawful (Iowa Code § 455B.183(1)(c)), and the department surveys and inspects these systems' monitoring and reporting (Iowa Code § 455B.174(2)). If your well serves an apartment complex, a group of rental houses or a manufactured home community at that scale, ask the department before renting. Below that size it is a private water supply (Iowa Code § 455B.171(24)). Second, the county. Each county board of health must regulate the private water supplies and private sewage disposal facilities in its jurisdiction (Iowa Code § 455B.172(4)), under standards at least as strict as the state's (Iowa Code § 455B.172(3)). County standards may reach well construction, location or testing; ask your county environmental health office. The state funds county board of health programs for testing private wells (Iowa Code § 135.11(20)); ask your county whether testing is available and at what cost. When you sell, Iowa's groundwater hazard statement must report known wells (Iowa Code § 558.69(1)(b)); that duty comes with a deed or real estate contract, not a lease. A sound practice for a rental on a private well: have the water tested for coliform bacteria and nitrate before each new tenancy and at least once a year, keep the results, and give the tenant a copy. Your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and to 'Supply running water' (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(6)) covers water from your own well; see `edu-habitability-ia`. Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Asbestos: No Tenant Notice Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no asbestos notice or disclosure duty for landlords. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, to tell tenants it is present, or to put an asbestos notice in the lease. Iowa's asbestos law regulates the work, not the tenancy. A business that removes or encapsulates asbestos 'shall hold a permit for that purpose unless the business entity is removing or encapsulating asbestos at its own facilities' (Iowa Code § 88B.3A(2)), and anyone who works on an asbestos project needs a state license (Iowa Code § 88B.6(2)(a)(1)); your own employees working on your own buildings are excused from licensing only if they are trained in removal procedures, safety and the applicable standards (Iowa Code § 88B.6(3)). Licensed inspectors and project designers are required for a 'public or commercial building' (Iowa Code § 88B.6(2)(a)), which 'means a building that is not a residential apartment building of fewer than ten units or a school building' (Iowa Code § 88B.1(7)), so an apartment building of ten or more units is covered. A willful violation can cost up to five thousand dollars per violation (Iowa Code § 88B.12(1)). Demolition and renovation are also subject to 'the federal national emission standard for asbestos under 40 C.F.R. pt. 61, subpt. M' (Iowa Code § 88B.2), enforced by the Department of Natural Resources, whose notification rules are not covered here. In practice: before renovating or demolishing an older building, have suspect materials tested, use a permitted contractor for any removal, give tenants the entry notice the law requires (`edu-landlord-entry-ia`), and keep work areas sealed off. Disturbed asbestos in a tenant's unit or a common area can breach your duty to keep the premises fit, habitable and safe (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2); `edu-habitability-ia`). If a tenant asks about asbestos, answer truthfully (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no defective-drywall disclosure law. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that a unit contains corrosive, imported or otherwise defective drywall, and the word drywall does not appear in Iowa's statutes or held rules. Iowa's seller disclosure statement is a sale document, not a lease document. It applies to a transfer, meaning 'the transfer or conveyance by sale, exchange, real estate contract, or any other method by which real estate and improvements are purchased' (Iowa Code § 558A.1(7)) for property with one to four dwelling units, and it must cover 'significant defects in the structural integrity of the structure' (Iowa Code § 558A.4(1)(a)). A lease is not a transfer under that definition. If a unit has drywall that corrodes wiring, plumbing or appliances or gives off odors, that is a repair you owe: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep supplied facilities and appliances in good and safe working order (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2), Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(4); `edu-habitability-ia`). If a tenant asks, answer truthfully (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). The disclosures Iowa does require at lease signing are listed in `edu-required-disclosures-ia`.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no chemical-exposure warning law like California's Proposition 65. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to post a warning that a rental property or its common areas expose people to chemicals that cause cancer or reproductive harm, or to put such a warning in the lease. Iowa does require some specific environmental disclosures, each covered in its own row: whether the property is listed in the federal hazardous-site system (`superfund-disclosure-ia`, `edu-superfund-ia`), and federal lead-based paint disclosure for older housing (`lead-based-paint`, `edu-no-lead-state-notices-ia`); see also `edu-radon-ia` and `edu-required-disclosures-ia`. Products and materials in the unit still fall under your general duties to keep the premises fit, habitable and safe (Iowa Code § 562A.15(1)(a)(2); `edu-habitability-ia`). If you or a contractor apply pesticides or other chemicals in a unit, give the entry notice the law requires (`edu-landlord-entry-ia`) and follow the product label. A California-style warning is not required in Iowa; adding one is lawful but has no legal effect here.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no military-installation or airport disclosure law for rentals. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that a rental is near a military air base, an Air National Guard field or an airport, or lies in a noise zone or accident potential zone, and there is no tenant right to end a lease on learning it. Iowa's airport law works through zoning, not disclosure: local governments with an airport hazard area may adopt airport zoning regulations that set permitted land uses and height limits (Iowa Code § 329.3), and the statute declares 'That the creation or establishment of an airport hazard is a public nuisance and an injury to the community served by the airport in question' (Iowa Code § 329.2(1)). Those regulations limit structures and uses near an airport; they do not require notice to tenants. If a property sits close to a runway or under a flight path, telling applicants is a sensible courtesy that can head off complaints, and you must answer truthfully if asked (`edu-consumer-protection-ia`). Iowa's servicemember lease protections are covered in `edu-servicemember-ia`.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Iowa requires none of the three disclosures grouped here. Ordnance: no Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell a tenant that a rental is near a former military ordnance or munitions site. Demolition: no Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that you have applied for, or intend to apply for, a demolition permit. If you plan to demolish, end the tenancy with the notice the lease and Iowa law require (`edu-end-of-term-ia`, `periodic-tenancy-notice-ia`). Iowa's retaliation statute lets you bring a possession action even after a tenant's code complaint if 'Compliance with the applicable building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit' (Iowa Code § 562A.36(3)(c)); see `edu-retaliation-ia`. Shared meters: no Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell a tenant that the meter for the tenant's unit also serves another unit or a common area. The utility rules require separate meters for each unit with listed exceptions and cap what you may collect for master-metered gas and electricity (`edu-electric-submetering-ia`); a tenant who pays you for utilities must have them fully explained before signing (Iowa Code § 562A.13(4); `utility-charges-disclosure-ia`); and sharing common-area electricity is covered in `edu-utility-apportionment-ia` and `edu-common-area-lighting-ia`. If a tenant's meter serves anything outside the unit, say so in writing before the lease is signed and adjust the charge.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no shoreline or beach-access disclosure for rentals. No Iowa statute or held rule requires you to tell an applicant or tenant whether a lake, river or beach next to the property is public or private, where public access lies, or what limits apply to docks or the shore. Iowa's water statutes regulate the shore itself, not leases: for example, a pier, dock or other structure on state-owned or state-managed waters needs a state permit, and, along the shores of those waters beyond the line of private ownership, no one may build in a way that blocks people walking the shore between the ordinary high-water mark and the water's edge without the commission's permission (Iowa Code § 461A.4(1)(a)). If you rent lakefront or riverfront property, tell the tenant in writing what the lease includes (dock, boat lift, beach) and any association, permit or state rules that limit its use, and pass on any association rules that bind the tenant (`hoa-compliance`).

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa does not require you to tell tenants or applicants about registered sex offenders, and no statute requires a registry notice in the lease or at a sale. The registry is public: the state 'shall maintain an internet site for the public and others to access relevant information about sex offenders' (Iowa Code § 692A.121(1)), searchable by name, county, city, ZIP code and distance, and anyone may sign up for free email alerts about registrations in a ZIP code or radius (Iowa Code § 692A.121(13)). Pointing applicants to the site is lawful and costs nothing. If you choose to tell other tenants that a particular neighbor is registered, repeat only what the public registry shows; the registry's other records are confidential (Iowa Code § 692A.121(14)). Iowa's residency restriction for certain offenders binds the offender, not you (`edu-sex-offender-ia`). Screening applicants for criminal history is covered by `edu-tenant-screening-ia` and `edu-fair-housing-ia`.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa has no occupancy disclosure for single-family leases. No Iowa statute or held rule makes a tenant's occupancy presumed unlawful because the lease is not notarized, was not signed by a licensed property manager or leaves out the landlord's phone number, and none requires a notice about such a presumption, at the top of the first page or in larger type. An Iowa lease needs no notarization to be valid; a lease longer than one year must be in writing and signed (`edu-statute-of-frauds-ia`). Iowa sets no font-size or first-page rule for residential leases (`edu-no-lease-type-size-ia`). Iowa does require you to disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the names and addresses of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices and service (`landlord-disclosure-ia`). Removing someone who moved in without permission goes through forcible entry and detainer: the action lies 'Where the defendant has by force, intimidation, fraud, or stealth entered upon the prior actual possession of another in real property, and detains the same' (Iowa Code § 648.1(1)), and that ground needs no three-day notice to quit (Iowa Code § 648.3(1)); see `edu-no-squatter-statute-ia`.

title: No Association Disclosure Required in Iowa Leases
bodyText:
Iowa does not require a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a homeowners' association to disclose the association's obligations, rules or documents to the tenant, or to carry any association statement.

You can get the documents easily, though. As a unit owner you may ask the association for its organizational documents, bylaws, rules and recent minutes, and it must provide them within ten business days of your request or your agent's (Iowa Code § 499C.2(1)), for a fee that may not exceed the estimated cost of production (Iowa Code § 499C.2(3)). Since July 1, 2026, you may also ask for a certification of whether dues and assessments are paid and a schedule of transfer fees (Iowa Code § 499C.2(1)(f), Iowa Code § 499C.2(1)(g), as amended by 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1055, § 1).

Give the tenant a copy of every association rule the tenant must follow before the lease is signed, and record it with `association-rules-receipt-ia`; the library's `hoa-compliance` clause then makes following those rules a lease term.

Your own landlord-tenant duties are not changed by the association: Iowa's landlord-tenant act excludes only 'Occupancy by an owner of a condominium unit or a holder of a proprietary lease in a cooperative' (Iowa Code § 562A.5(6)), not a tenant renting from an owner. A plain lease is not a sale, so the seller disclosure statement does not apply (`edu-no-drywall-disclosure-ia`); see `edu-hoa-ia` for other association rules.

title: Associations and Rented Units in Iowa
bodyText:
Iowa has no statute that governs how a homeowners' or condominium association treats rentals. Associations are organized under the horizontal property regime act (condominiums, Iowa Code ch. 499B), the cooperative chapter (Iowa Code ch. 499A) and, for record access, the common interest community chapter (Iowa Code ch. 499C), whose definition of a planned community 'includes property owner or homeowner associations' (Iowa Code § 499C.1(7)).

None of them sets a cap on association lease-approval or application fees, allows an association-held tenant deposit, lets the association demand rent from your tenant when you fall behind, limits rental restrictions to owners who buy after they are adopted, or protects a tenant's home child care against the association. Those questions turn on your declaration, bylaws and rules, and on case law; read them before you rent. The declaration, bylaws and rules stay in force while the regime exists unless amended (Iowa Code § 499B.21(1)).

What the statutes do say: unpaid condominium assessments are a lien on the unit, and if the association forecloses, the owner 'shall be required to pay a reasonable rental for the apartment if so provided in the bylaws, and the plaintiff in such foreclosure shall be entitled to the appointment of a receiver to collect the same' (Iowa Code § 499B.17), so a receiver, not the association directly, may end up collecting rent.

A small association or cooperative of seventy-two or fewer units may exempt its pool from state pool rules only through bylaws that 'also apply to a rental agreement relative to any of the dwelling units' (Iowa Code § 135I.2); see `edu-pool-safety-ia`.

A child care home, registered or not, may be run in a rented apartment or condominium unit (Iowa Code § 237A.3(3)), but the statute does not override association rules or your lease.

You remain liable to the association for assessments and fines on your unit; the `hoa-compliance` clause shifts fines caused by the tenant's own violations to the tenant. A lease with an option to buy is covered in `edu-lease-option-ia`.

title: Contractor Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText:
Iowa's mechanics' lien law gives a lien to anyone who furnishes labor or material to improve, alter or repair a building 'by virtue of any contract with the owner, owner-builder, general contractor, or subcontractor' (Iowa Code § 572.2(1)), and an owner is 'the legal or equitable titleholder of record' (Iowa Code § 572.1(8)). A tenant is not the owner.

When your tenant hires the work, the land is subject to the lien only 'to the extent of the interest therein of the person for whose benefit such material was furnished or labor performed' (Iowa Code § 572.5), that is, the tenant's lease. But the improvement itself is at risk: when that interest 'is only a leasehold, the forfeiture of the lease for the nonpayment of rent, or for noncompliance with any of the other conditions therein, shall not forfeit or impair the mechanic's lien upon such building or improvement' (Iowa Code § 572.6), which may be sold to satisfy the lien and removed by the buyer within thirty days.

Whether a landlord who required, approved or knew about a tenant's work can be treated as having contracted for it is a question for case law; assume it could happen. Iowa has no notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure: you cannot post or record a notice that keeps tenant work off your title, and no statute says a lease clause binds a contractor who never signed it. The practical protection is the lease clause `no-liens-ia` together with your alterations clause (`no-alterations`): the tenant must pay its contractors, tell them in writing that you are not paying, and clear any lien.

For work you order on a single- or two-family rental, Iowa's residential rules protect you: the general contractor must give you a written lien notice (Iowa Code § 572.13) and post a notice of commencement to the state's mechanics' notice and lien registry (Iowa Code § 572.13A), subcontractors post preliminary notices that the registry sends to you (Iowa Code § 572.13B(2)), and a subcontractor's lien is generally limited to what you still owe the general contractor when you receive that notice (Iowa Code § 572.13B(3)(a); Iowa Code § 572.16). Check the registry before final payment and get lien waivers.

Manufactured home community lots are governed by Iowa Code ch. 562B, not covered here.

title: Nuisance Law and Your Rental
bodyText: Iowa nuisance law can reach you for what tenants do on your property. Three statutes matter. General nuisances. 'Whatever is injurious to health, indecent, or unreasonably offensive to the senses, or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as essentially to interfere unreasonably with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, is a nuisance' (Iowa Code § 657.1(1)), and a civil action may be brought to abate it and recover damages. Listed nuisances include 'places resorted to by persons using controlled substances ... in violation of law, or houses where drunkenness, quarreling, fighting, or breaches of the peace are carried on or permitted to the disturbance of others' (Iowa Code § 657.2(6)). A person convicted of continuing a public or common nuisance commits an aggravated misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 657.3), and the court may order the nuisance abated at the defendant's expense (Iowa Code § 657.4). Prostitution and gambling. A person who 'owns, or leases any building, erection, or place used for the purpose of prostitution or gambling' (Iowa Code § 99.1A(1)) is guilty of a nuisance. The county attorney or any citizen of the county may sue to enjoin it and to stop 'the owner or agent of the building or ground upon which said nuisance exists, from further permitting such building or ground or both to be so used' (Iowa Code § 99.2). The general reputation of the place is prima facie evidence of the owners' and lessors' knowledge and acquiescence (Iowa Code § 99.14). If the nuisance is established, the court orders the building closed against any use for one year (Iowa Code § 99.21), unless you pay the costs and post a bond to abate it (Iowa Code § 99.26), and a three hundred dollar mulct tax is imposed on the building and ground and against you as owner (Iowa Code § 99.27); if you were not a party and did not appear, it is still imposed against the property (Iowa Code § 99.31). Renting to someone you know or have reason to know uses the place for prostitution, and not ending the tenancy or the practice at once, is a serious misdemeanor (Iowa Code § 725.4). Nuisance buildings. A court-appointed receiver for an abandoned or dangerous building can take over and collect rents under Iowa Code ch. 657A (Iowa Code § 657A.4, Iowa Code § 657A.6); see `edu-substandard-property-receivership-ia`. What Iowa does not have: no statute requires your lease to summarize a nuisance or crime statute, voids a lease because of a nuisance, or lets tenants or neighbors escrow rents or suspend a subsidy because of a drug nuisance. Act quickly on illegal activity: the lease clauses `criminal-activity-ia`, `residential-use-only` and `no-disturbance` make it a lease breach, the tenant must not disturb neighbors (Iowa Code § 562A.17(7)), and Iowa's termination procedures are in `edu-clear-present-danger-ia` and `edu-noncompliance-cure-ia`.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Addenda in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa neither requires nor regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. No Iowa statute or held rule makes you attach one, prescribes its wording, or requires a city crime-free program; any local program is a matter of local ordinance, not covered here. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules, not covered here. You may include drug and crime terms in the lease (Iowa Code § 562A.9(1)); the library's `criminal-activity-ia` clause does this job for Iowa, so you do not need a separate addendum. Whatever form you use, Iowa law limits what it can do. Fast termination is set by statute: you may end a tenancy on a single three-day 'written notice of termination and notice to quit stating the specific activity causing the clear and present danger' (Iowa Code § 562A.27A(1)) only for a clear and present danger, which includes '... Possession of a controlled substance unless the controlled substance was obtained directly from or pursuant to a valid prescription or order by a licensed medical practitioner' (Iowa Code § 562A.27A(2)(c)), and possession by a guest counts only if the tenant knew of it; the tenant keeps the statutory exemptions when someone else did it and the tenant acts against that person and gives you written proof before you sue (Iowa Code § 562A.27A(3)). See `edu-clear-present-danger-ia`. Other drug or crime violations are ordinary noncompliance with the cure and notice steps in `edu-noncompliance-cure-ia`. An addendum cannot waive those rights, except in a lease of a single family residence on land assessed as agricultural land in an unincorporated area (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a); `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`), and it cannot penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency help: Iowa voids any such waiver and imposes a civil penalty (`edu-emergency-assistance-ia`). Nuisance exposure for drug activity on your property is covered in `edu-nuisance-ia`.

title: Confession of Judgment Barred in Iowa Leases
bodyText: An Iowa lease may not let anyone confess judgment against the tenant (or the landlord). Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(b) says a rental agreement shall not provide that a party 'Authorizes a person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement'. Unlike the general waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a), this bar has no exception for farm homes. A prohibited term is unenforceable, and if you willfully use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Iowa's general procedure for a judgment by confession (Iowa Code ch. 676) does not change this for leases. The library offers no confession-of-judgment clause; to collect unpaid rent or damages, file in small claims or district court. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia`.

title: Arbitration Clauses Not Offered for Iowa Leases
bodyText: The library does not offer an arbitration clause for Iowa leases. Iowa's arbitration statute makes a contract term to arbitrate future disputes enforceable, but 'This subsection shall not apply to any of the following' (Iowa Code § 679A.1(2)), and the first item listed is 'A contract of adhesion' (Iowa Code § 679A.1(2)(a)). No Iowa statute defines a contract of adhesion, so whether a landlord's standard-form residential lease is one is a question for the courts. A pre-dispute arbitration term could also be read as a term by which the tenant agrees 'to waive or to forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)), which Iowa's landlord-tenant act bars; if a court agreed, willfully using a lease containing it could cost you the tenant's actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus the tenant's reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). Even an enforceable arbitration term does not reach injury and other tort claims unless 'a separate writing executed by all parties to the contract' (Iowa Code § 679A.1(2)(c)) says so. Once a dispute exists, you and the tenant may agree in a separate written agreement to arbitrate it: 'A written agreement to submit to arbitration an existing controversy is valid, enforceable, and irrevocable unless grounds exist at law or in equity for the revocation of the written agreement' (Iowa Code § 679A.1(1)). Possession cases go to court as forcible entry and detainer actions (Iowa Code ch. 648), and money claims within the small-claims limit can go to small claims (Iowa Code ch. 631). A landlord who wants an arbitration clause in an Iowa lease anyway should take legal advice first. Federal arbitration law may apply to some leases and is not covered here. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ia` and `edu-jury-waiver-ia`. The waiver bar in Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a) does not apply to a lease of a single-family residence on land assessed as agricultural land and located in an unincorporated area.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Iowa follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Iowa Code § 554.3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Iowa Code § 554.1308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Iowa Code ch. 562A searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Iowa's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
